## 1.9.6.2. Additional risk minimisation measures

Prior to launch of Povofortay in each Member State the Marketing Authorisation Holder (MAH) must agree about the content and format of the educational programme, including communication media, distribution modalities, and any other aspects of the programme, with the National Competent Authority.

The objective of the programme is to increase awareness of HCPs and patients on the risks of herpes zoster and other serious and opportunistic infections, embryofoetal toxicity following exposure in utero (pregnancy risk), malignancy, non-melanoma skin cancer, MACE, and VTE and how to manage these risks.

The MAH shall ensure that in each Member State where Povofortay is marketed, all healthcare professionals and patients/carers who are expected to prescribe, dispense or use Povofortay have access to/are provided with the following educational package:

## 2. Introduction

## 2.1 Therapeutic context

Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic disabling and debilitating inflammatory skin condition characterised by painful nodules and abscesses in early stages and draining tunnels (fistulas) and irreversible tissue damage and scarring in more severe disease. The lesions characteristically develop in the axillae and in the inframammary, inguinal, or gluteal regions. HS can lead to serious complications such as cellulitis, lymphedema, and systemic infections. HS negatively affects psychosocial well-being and has profound negative effects on patients' quality of life. Combining chronic pain with pus/drainage, unpleasant odor, and deformity of skin appearance can lead to social withdrawal, unemployment, depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts. HS is associated with significant comorbidities and increased mortality. Patients with HS have a higher prevalence of traditional cardiovascular risk factors, including obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and hypertension, which contribute to a significantly increased risk of developing cardiovascular disease compared with the general population.

Genetic predisposition, smoking, obesity, and hormonal factors are established etiologic factors for HS. The estimated prevalence of HS in Europe is approximately 1% in most well-conducted epidemiological studies. Approximately 30% to 70% of patients with HS have moderate to severe disease, which is assessed by Hurley staging or dynamic scores.

In general, first-line treatments of HS consist of antibiotics (topical and oral), antiseptic washes, intralesional corticosteroid injections, and lifestyle modification (e.g. smoking cessation), followed by second-line treatment with a biologic medicine. Currently, three monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) have been approved in the EU for the treatment of HS; adalimumab (anti-TNF-α); secukinumab (anti-IL-17A) and bimekizumab (anti-IL-17A/F). All three mAbs are indicated for the treatment of active moderate to severe HS in adults (adalimumab also in adolescents from 12 years of age) with an inadequate response to conventional systemic HS therapy. Third-line treatments include surgical intervention for patients with chronic lesions that do not respond to medication; however, there are multiple complications of surgery, including the risks of disease recurrence, scarring, infection, and wound healing difficulties.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

A significant proportion of patients do not respond to the approved biological medicines or their HS becomes refractory to therapies. The limitations of current treatments highlight the unmet need for safe and effective new treatment options for patients with active moderate to severe HS. In addition to a new mechanism of action, povorcitinib offers a different route of administration, i.e. QD oral tablet vs. subcutaneous injection with the mAbs.

## 2.2 Aspects of development

Povorcitinib, an oral Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) inhibitor, demonstrated initial proof of concept in HS patients in two Phase 2 studies (INCB 54707-202 and INCB 54707-203) at doses of 15, 30, 60, and 90 mg QD in 45 participants. A third Phase 2 study with povorcitinib (15, 45, and 75 mg QD) in 209 participants further demonstrated a clinical response across lesion count decrease, HiSCR, and improvement in several PROs (INCB 54707-204). The primary evaluation of the efficacy of povorcitinib is based on two identically designed pivotal phase 3 studies in adult participants with moderate to severe HS. Studies INCB 54707-301 (STOP-HS1) and INCB 54707-302 (STOP-HS-2) are double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled studies composed of a 12-week PC period and a 42-week extension period. The primary objective of both pivotal studies was to evaluate the efficacy of povorcitinib; the primary endpoint was the proportion of participants who achieve HiSCR50 at Week 12.

In addition to the ITT population of the phase 3 studies, the applicant has carried out efficacy analyses in the Post-Anti-TNF ITT population, which is the target population in the claimed indication.

## 2.3 Description of the product

Povorcitinib selectively inhibits JAK1. JAK1 is a member of the JAK family of intracellular enzymes, which also includes JAK2, JAK3, and tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2). JAKs transmit signals arising from cytokine- or growth factor-receptor interactions on the cellular membrane. Within the signalling pathway, JAKs phosphorylate and activate signal transducers and activators of transcription (STATs) which modulate gene expression. This influences cellular processes of immune cell function and haematopoiesis depending on the specific JAK isoforms involved. Povorcitinib modulates the JAK1 signalling pathway, preventing the phosphorylation and activation of associated STATs.

Povorcitinib inhibits signaling by JAK1-dependent cytokines (such as IL-6, IL-2, IL-22) thereby attenuating skin and systemic inflammation, and leading to the improvement of clinical signs and symptoms relevant to HS.

The approved indication is as follows:

Povoritinib is indicated for the treatment of active moderate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa (acne inversa) in adults who have responded inadequately to, or who are intolerant or contraindicated to an anti-TNF therapy.

The approved posology is as follows:

The dose is 45 mg or 75 mg once daily based on individual patient characteristics.

- A dose of 45 mg once daily is recommended for patients at higher risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and malignancy (see section 4.4).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

- A dose of 75 mg once daily may be appropriate for patients with high disease burden who are not at higher risk of VTE, MACE and malignancy (see section 4.4)
- A dose of 75 mg once daily may also be appropriate for patients with an inadequate response to 45 mg once daily.
- The lowest effective dose to maintain response should be used.

Consideration should be given to discontinuing treatment in patients who have shown no evidence of therapeutic benefit after 12 weeks of treatment. Patients with an initial partial response at week 12 may subsequently improve with continued treatment.

If retreatment with povorcitinib is indicated, the above guidance on dose and treatment duration should be followed.

## 3. Quality aspects

## 3.1 Introduction

The finished product is presented as film-coated tablets containing 45 mg and 75 mg of povorcitinib as active substance.

Other ingredients are microcrystalline cellulose, sodium starch glycolate, hydroxypropyl methylcellulose, magnesium stearate and film-coating layer ((hypromellose (E464), copovidone (E1208), titanium dioxide (E171), polyethylene glycol (E1521), medium chain triglycerides, iron oxide red (E172) (45 mg strength only), iron oxide yellow (E172), brilliant blue FCF (E133) (75 mg strength only)).

The product is available in PVC-PCTFE/Aluminium blister as described in section 6.5. of the SmPC.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 3.2 Active substance

## 3.2.1 General information

The chemical name of active substance is (S)-4-(3-(cyanomethyl)-3-(3',5'-dimethyl-1H,1'H-4,4'- bipyrazol-1-yl)azetidin-1-yl)-2,5-difluoro N-(1,1,1-trifluoropropan-2-yl)benzamide phosphate corresponding to the molecular formula C23H25F5N7O5P. It has a relative molecular mass of 605.45 g/mol and the following structure:

## Figure 1. Active substance structure

<!-- image -->

## 3.2.2 Manufacture, process controls and process development

## Description of manufacturing process and process controls

The manufacturing process of povorcitinib phosphate is conducted at two manufacturing sites. Satisfactory evidence of GMP compliance has been presented.

The active substance is synthesised in 10 main steps using five commercially available and welldefined starting materials with acceptable specifications.

The active substance convergent manufacturing process has been adequately described

## Control of materials

The proposed starting materials have been defined based on the EMA scientific advice. All the proposed starting material are acceptable, in line with the requirement of ICH Q11 and its Questions and Answers.

The proposed specifications for the starting materials include relevant testing parameters. The proposed limits are acceptable. The acceptance criteria for impurities are justified by process purge capabilities or by spike/purge studies. An adequate discussion regarding the potential carry-over of mutagenic compound has been presented. According to the information provided, for several potential impurities it is stated to be controlled as unspecified impurities in starting materials. A summary of validation data of the methods used for related substances testing in the starting materials is also provided.

## Control of critical steps and intermediates

Adequate in-process controls are applied during the synthesis, and critical steps have been defined. The specifications and control methods for intermediate products, starting materials and reagents have been presented.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Process validation

Brief information is provided that the process was validated. Process validation data of the active manufacturing process has not been presented; this approach is acceptable as the active substance is not sterile.

## Manufacturing process development

The commercial manufacturing process for the active substance was developed in parallel with the clinical development program. Critical quality attributes (CQAs) were identified. The originally used Process 1 was later changed to Process 2. Process 1 was used early in the development and batches manufactured by Process 1 were used for the GLP toxicology studies, the earlier human clinical trials, and as the primary reference standard. In fact, the Process 1 and Process 2 do not significantly differ. Changes introduced have been presented in sufficient detail and have been justified. At the end the Process 2 was extended to Process 2-MAA to cover more steps under GMP but without any change in the synthesis or quality of the used materials. Instead of three starting materials, five starting materials are proposed for the Process 2-MAA. The justification of the choice of starting materials has been provided. The quality of the active substance used in the various phases of the development is considered to be comparable with that produced by the proposed commercial process.

## 3.2.3 Characterisation and impurities

The characterisation of the active substance and its impurities are in accordance with the EU guideline on chemistry of active substances.

Potential and actual impurities are well discussed with regards to their origin and characterised.

The chemical structure of the active substance was elucidated by a combination of elemental analysis, single crystal X-Ray structure, infrared absorption spectrum (FT-IR), 1 H and 13 C NMR spectra. Mass spectrometry, and ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy (UV).

The active substance is a white to off-white non-hygroscopic solid. The active substance is classified as a BCS class 2 compound due to its limited in-vitro solubility over the pH range of 1 - 6.8 and is classified as low soluble compound with moderate-high permeability. Solubility of the active substance is highly pH dependent; and the solubility decreases sharply with increasing pH.

The active substance exhibits stereoisomerism due to the presence of one chiral centre with absolute configuration (S) indicated in the structural formula. The absolute configuration of the chiral center is controlled by chiral purity of the final active substance. Under current process conditions, there is no evidence of isomerisation of the chiral centre once it is established.

Polymorphism has been observed for the active substance

Eur.), residue on ignition (Ph. Eur.), crystallinity (Ph. Eur.), particle size distribution (Lasser Diffraction).

Batch analysis data of 22 pilot and commercial scale batches of the active substance are provided. The results are within the specifications and consistent from batch to batch.

## 3.2.5 Stability

The retest period proposed for the active substance in the proposed container is justified by the available stability data.

The commercial active substance is packaged in double low density polyethylene bags (food grade) secured with plastic zip ties packed in high-density polyethylene (HDPE) drum and HDPE lid with a sponge rubber gasket which complies with Commission Regulation (EU) 10/2011, as amended and with Ph. Eur. 3.1.3 Polyolefins. The information provided for the packaging is acceptable.

Stability data for batches of active substance from the proposed manufacturer(s) stored in the intended commercial package in a container closure system representative of that intended for the market under long term conditions (25 ºC / 60% RH) and under accelerated conditions (40 ºC / 75% RH) according to the ICH guidelines were provided.

Three batches with batch size smaller than the commercial were placed in the stability study. However, two additional batches are also placed in the stability study, that are near the proposed commercial batch size and the results are fully comparable. According to the information presented, primary batches are pilot-plant batches and supportive batches are plant confirmation batches. All batches are manufactured with the Process 2 that is applied for the commercialisation. So, the presented batches are considered satisfactorily representative.

The following parameters were tested: description, assay, chiral purity, related substances, water content, and crystallinity. The analytical methods used were the same as for release and were stability indicating.

For all batches, all results are within specification limits without any significant trends of any of the tested parameters under long term and accelerated conditions.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Stress stability studies were conducted to evaluate the susceptibility of the active substance to forced degradation conditions and to evaluate the stability indicating nature of the analytical method used for assay and related substances determinations. The active substance was stressed to assess the effects of oxidation, hydrolysis in acidic and basic media, exposure to UV light, and heat.

The active substance exhibits excellent stability under thermal and oxidation stress conditions. Under acidic and basic conditions, certain degradations were observed. Results of photostability testing of the active substance shows that it is stable when exposed to light. Additionally, these data demonstrate the specificity of the analytical procedure for the determination of the identity, assay and related substances of povorcitinib phosphate.

The stability results indicate that the active substance manufactured by the proposed suppliers is sufficiently stable. The stability results justify the proposed retest period.

The finished product is supplied as immediate release film-coated tablets for oral administration in strengths of 45 mg and 75 mg, and it is presented as:

· 75 mg tablet: light purple to purple oval tablets (16 mm by 8 mm) debossed with \"INCY\" on one side and \"75\" on the other side.

The only difference in the compositions of the tablets is the addition of varying levels of a nonfunctional coating intended to affect the tablet colour, with no change to the tablet cores.

Bioequivalence study waiver for the commercial formulation has been proposed. Dissolution studies were conducted to evaluate the clinical, registration stability, and proposed commercial tablets under a variety of pH conditions to assess tablet comparability. Comparative dissolution profiles among the clinical formulation, registration stability formulation and proposed commercial formulation for each strength have been performed, as well as with the QC method. The dissolution profiles obtained under these conditions were similar between the three tested formulations (f2&gt;50). Considering the totality of data, including the minor changes to the drug product formulation, the similarity of the dissolution profiles and the comparable product quality, in vitro dissolution comparability studies are considered appropriate for demonstrating comparability between the clinical, registration, and proposed commercial tablets, and, thus, the biowaiver was considered acceptable.

A dissolution method has been developed. The proposed dissolution test conditions have been justified. It has been demonstrated that the proposed dissolution method in combination with the proposed specification is discriminative towards differences in the active substance particle size. Proposed batch comparison (clinical versus registration versus commercial) was carried out. Batch sizes of the batches were provided to support comparability.

## Manufacturing process development

The manufacturing process is the same for both tablet strengths and uses conventional processes.

The manufacturing development has been evaluated using risk assessment to identify the critical product quality attributes and critical process parameters. Blend homogeneity has been adequately demonstrated. The product is focused on adult population, no specific considerations on excipients with relation to paediatric population is needed.

The manufacturing process has been evaluated using a combination of conventional univariate studies and design of experiment (DoE) studies.

A general overview of the changes made to the manufacturing process among the clinical, registration stability and intended commercial batches was provided. Dissolution profiles between the clinical, registration stability and intended commercial formulation were comparable.

## Specifications

The finished product release and shelf-life specifications include appropriate tests for this kind of dosage form: description (visual), identification (HPLC, UV), assay (HPLC), related substances (HPLC), uniformity of dosage (USP), water content (Ph. Eur.), dissolution (USP), and microbial limits (Ph. Eur.)

The proposed finished product specification generally includes appropriate test parameters for the applied dosage form.

The proposed analytical procedures and corresponding specification limits are adequate for routine control of the finished product. They are generally in line with ICH guidelines and Ph. Eur. and batch release data and stability data.

For the related substances test, two specified impurities are listed, which are limited to be NMT 0.2 %. Other impurities are covered by the limit for Individual Unspecified impurities. The maximum daily dose as per SmPC is 75 mg. According to the ICH guideline Q3B(R2), the identification threshold is 0.2% and qualification threshold 0.27 %.

The limits for impurities are set according to these thresholds and hence are acceptable. The limit for total impurities has been tightened to NMT 1.5% in line with batch and stability data.

Justification for omission of testing for identification of colorants, enantiomeric purity, residual solvents and elemental impurities is acceptable.

During evaluation, the proposed dissolution limit was not accepted The CHMP considered that from the batch data, this limit could be tightened as during the pharmaceutical development the dissolution behaviour of the product has had increasing trend and discriminative nature of the test should be maintained also for commercial batches and raised this as Major Objection (MO). As a response, dissolution limit was tightened and the MO was resolved. The microbiological quality skip testing is included in the finished product specifications in line with Ph. Eur. The proposed limits for microbiological quality are in line with the relevant Ph. Eur. monographs. Based on the provided information, skip testing is acceptable for microbial limits in the finished product.

The potential presence of elemental impurities in the finished product was assessed following a riskbased approach in line with the ICH Q3D Guideline for Elemental Impurities. In accordance with the ICH guideline Q3D (R1) Option 2b, on elemental impurities, a risk assessment was performed to determine if additional controls are needed to ensure that the finished product complies with the elemental impurities' limits set forth in ICH Q3D. The risk assessment supports the conclusion that no additional controls are needed, and that the levels of elemental impurities in the finished product are adequately controlled.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

A risk assessment for nitrosamine impurities was performed, including evaluation of the active substance, excipients, finished product manufacturing, bulk packaging and storage. Based on the risk assessment potential sources of nitrosamines were identified but not included in the specifications of the finished product. Therefore, justification was requested as MO by CHMP. Based on the presented data, the applicant has sufficiently demonstrated that formation of nitrosamines is not feasible in the presented reaction conditions, and the MO was considered resolved.

The analytical methods used have been adequately described and appropriately validated in accordance with the ICH guidelines. Satisfactory information regarding the reference standards used for testing has been presented.

The shelf life of 2 years for the product in blister cards without any storage conditions in the proposed container, as stated in the SmPC.

## Container closure system

The primary packaging is PVC-PCTFE/Aluminium blister. The material complies with Ph. Eur. and EC requirements. The choice of the container closure system has been validated by stability data and is adequate for the intended use of the product.

## Stability data

Initially, stability data from 6 pilot scale batches (3 batches per strength) of finished product stored for up to 9 months under long term conditions (25 °C / 60% RH) and for up to 6 months under accelerated conditions (40 °C / 75% RH) according to the ICH guidelines were provided. The batches differed from the commercial formulation. The batches were packed in the primary packaging proposed for marketing. CHMP considered that in line with ICH Q1A, the primary stability batches, should be of the same formulation as proposed for marketing. In this specific case, considering the similarity between the registration batches formulation and the proposed commercial formulation, bridging of stability data may be possible; however, this should be based on a comparison with results of the formal stability study performed on commercial formulation batches. Therefore, it was requested as MO that at least three months of stability data on at least two pilot scale or industrial scale batches (per strength) under ICH conditions for the proposed commercial formulation in the proposed commercial packaging should be provided. Furthermore, it was requested that the stability profile of the proposed commercial formulation is demonstrated to be similar to the registration stability batches. As requested, stability results of four batches (two batches per strength) covering 3 months at accelerated and long-term conditions have been provided. The batches have been manufactured according to the commercial manufacturing process; the commercial formulation was used. The batches have been packaged in the commercial packaging configuration of blister packages. It was, thus, demonstrated that the stability profile of the proposed commercial formulation is similar to the registration stability batches. The response was considered acceptable and the MO was resolved.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

A supportive stability study was performed on three pilot scale batches (per strength) packaged in HDPE bottles. The batches used for supportive stability study come from the same bulk tablets as used for registration stability study, but in different packaging. Stability data is available up to 12 months at long-term storage condition 25 °C / 60% RH and up to 6 months at accelerated storage condition 40 °C / 75% RH.

The following parameters were tested: description, assay, related substances, water content, dissolution, microbial limit. The analytical procedures used were the same as for release and were stability indicating as demonstrated through studies under forced conditions.

All tested parameters were within the specifications. No degradation products increased under long term and accelerated conditions.

Photostability testing following the ICH guideline Q1B was performed on 3 batches of both strengths. No needs to protect the product from light has been observed. The finished product is not sensitive to the light conditions tested.

A study for the finished product under stressed conditions has been provided. Acid, base, peroxide, metallic, heat, heat/humidity, light stressed samples were tested on peak purity, assay of active substance and degradation products. The stability indicating nature of the proposed HPLC method used for assay and related substances has been demonstrated.

Finished product bulk stability study has been performed on one batch per strength, packaged in double PE liners in fiber drums. Stability data is available at storage condition 20-25 °C. The updated bulk hold study on commercial formulation has been initiated on one batch per strength, packaged in double PE liners in fiber drums. Stability data is available up to 6 months at storage condition 20-25 °C. All of the obtained results are in line with the proposed specification limits.

Based on available stability data, the proposed shelf-life of 2 years without storage conditions as stated in the SmPC (section 6.3 and 6.4) are acceptable.

Three major objections were raised during the procedure concerning (1) dissolution limit of the finished product, (2) nitrosamines risk assessment, and (3) stability study of the finished product. In response to MO1, the dissolution limits were tightened as requested. In response to MO2, the applicant demonstrated that the presence of or nitrosamine impurity in the finished product was very unlikely. ## 4. Non-clinical aspects

## 4.1 Introduction

The non-clinical characterisation of orally administered povorcitinib includes in vitro and in vivo pharmacology (non-GLP) and safety pharmacology studies (GLP), in vitro and in vivo PK/ADME studies (non-GLP) and in vivo toxicokinetic and toxicology studies (GLP), following the ICH M3(R2) requirements.

An environmental risk assessment (ERA) in accordance with the updated 2024 guideline was also submitted.

## 4.2 Analytical methods

Samples obtained from non-GLP pharmacokinetic (PK) and toxicokinetic (TK) studies in multiple species (rat, dog, and cynomolgus monkey) were analysed for povorcitinib using an analytical method combining a protein precipitation extraction with 10% methanol in acetonitrile and LC/MS/MS analysis. The method has demonstrated a linear assay range from 1 to 2500 nM using 0.1 mL of study samples. The assay has been successfully applied to the analysis of plasma, urine, brain homogenate, cerebrospinal fluid, and serum protein binding samples. For GLP toxicity and safety pharmacology studies, plasma samples were analysed for povorcitinib in compliance with OECD principles of GLP, using validated methods for rat, dog, rabbit, and mouse plasma.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 4.3 Pharmacology

## 4.3.1 Pharmacodynamics

## 4.3.1.1 . Primary pharmacodynamics

A comprehensive set on in vitro and in vivo primary pharmacodynamic studies have been performed to study the mechanism of action and JAK1 over JAK2 selectivity of povorcitinib. These included in vitro characterisation of povorcitinib in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), primary human T-cells, human cell lines, and whole blood of mice, rats and dogs and in vivo rodent xenograft disease models of allergic diseases. Also, evaluation of povorcitinib selectivity within the JAK family, effect of povorcitinib in JAK/STAT activation and inhibition of cell growth and cytokine/chemokine production resulting from povorcitinib exposure were studied in vitro. In vivo, the different inflammatory rodent disease models were used to demonstrate that the inhibition of JAK1 signalling is suitable target in the treatment of inflammatory disease, such as HS.

In general, used non-GLP assays in the selected human inflammatory cell types and whole blood of mice, rats and dogs and mouse xenograft models are considered acceptable for the investigation of primary pharmacodynamics of povorcitinib.

## In vitro studies

## Povorcitinib selectivity within the JAK family

The studies on enzyme inhibition activity of povorcitinib of human JAK1, JAK2, JAK3 and TYK2 showed high selectivity towards JAK1. The inhibition activity for JAK1 (IC50 = 8.9 ± 1.7 nM) was 52-fold in comparison to inhibition activity for JAK2, &gt; 1000-fold in comparison to JAK3 and 45-fold over TYK2. On the other hand, metabolite M12 did not affect the activity of any JAK family member (IC50s&gt;25000 nM).

When povorcitinib was compared to marketed JAK1 inhibitors in biochemical (enzyme inhibition) and whole blood assays, the highest JAK1 selectivity over JAK2 was demonstrated for povorcitinib both in the enzymatic assays and human whole blood assays. The effects on other JAK family kinases (JAK3 and TYK2) were minor.

## Effect of povorcitinib on levels of phosphorylated JAKs and STATs

IC50 for IL-6 induced STAT3 phosphorylation was 690 ± 224 nM and for thrombopoietin (TPO) induced STAT3 phosphorylation &gt; 10 000, suggesting approximately 14-fold selectivity towards JAK1. Similar data was obtained from the whole blood of mice, rats and dogs. IC50 for IL-6 induced STAT1 phosphorylation was 360 ± 128 nM and for granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GMCSF) induced STAT5 phosphorylation &gt; 10 000, resulting in approximately 28-fold selectivity towards JAK1. Altogether, these data suggest a selectivity towards JAK1 pathway.

## Inhibition of cell growth and cytokine/chemokine production resulting from povorcitinib exposure

The effect of povorcitinib on cytokine-stimulated activation of JAK/STAT signalling and cell proliferation was studied in human T cells. The IC50 value of 29.6 ± 1.2 nM was recorded for the inhibition of IL-2 induced T cell proliferation by povorcitinib. The inhibition of cell growth by povorcitinib was also tested in HEK-293, HEPG2, HLF, HUVEC and SET-2 cell lines which are non-JAK dependent. No effects on proliferation were reported. The IC50 values of 17 nM were recorded for the inhibition of IL-17, 99 nM for the inhibition of IL-22 and 178 nM ± 57 nM for the inhibition of MCP-1.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The data presented support the proposed mechanism of action (JAK1 inhibition) for povorcitinib and the species selection (rat, dog) for pivotal toxicology program as JAK1 over JAK2 selectivity was suggested to be in the similar level in rat, dog and human whole blood assays.

## In vivo studies

The in vivo pharmacology program was performed in different inflammatory female rodent disease models. As no suitable non-clinical HS model is available, other JAK-dependent disease models were selected: arthritis (rat), cytokine induced inflammation (mouse) and delayed type hypersensitivity (mouse). In all models, povorcitinib induced a dose-dependent improvement in selected endpoints, and the recorded effect was independent from the administration route (SC, topical, oral).

A number of key proinflammatory JAK/STAT-dependent cytokines related to HS pathogenesis have been covered by in vivo pharmacology studies. It is demonstrated that the inhibition of JAK1 signalling is suitable target in the treatment of inflammatory diseases.

## 4.3.1.2 . Secondary pharmacodynamics

In the secondary pharmacodynamics screening study, potential targetfrom 70 receptors, enzymes and ion channels were included in the screening, including receptors involved in regulating cellular homeostasis, ion channel activity and inter-organelle communication. These receptors are linked to especially neurogenerative and cardiovascular diseases. As there were no adverse findings on CNS or cardiovascular functions in the safety pharmacology studies, off-target activities are not expected at the recommended dose of povorcitinib.

In the kinase profile screening towards 192 kinases, 200 nM povorcitinib demonstrated 70% inhibition of JAK2, while IC50 for JAK1 was 1.5 nM; confirming the selectivity of povorcitinib for JAK1 versus JAK2. No other JAK kinases were included in the screening. In a second kinase profiling study, povorcitinib demonstrated no selectivity towards 57 screened non-JAK family kinases.

## 4.3.1.3 . Safety pharmacology

Stand-alone safety pharmacology studies were conducted in rats and dogs in accordance with ICH S7A/B guidelines and GLP.

Cardiovascular effects were studied in in vitro hERG assay and 2 in vivo dog studies. In vitro hERG assay suggested IC50 value 11.8 µM, which is &gt;90-fold above the unbound Cmax in HS patients. In the dog studies, no cardiovascular adversity was recorded with dosing up to 15 mg/kg (plasma concentrations 9.19 ± 2.2 (4h) and 8.67 ± 2.2 (24h) µM). Based on unbound plasma concentration of 0.49 µM at 4-hour post-dose (calculated by using total concentration of 9.19 µM and unbound fraction of 5.3%), a safety margin of 3.8-fold was achieved in relation to unbound Cmax at the maximum recommended human dose.

Central nervous system effects were studied in the Irwin test in male and female rats. No effects were reported in dosing up to 200 mg/kg, corresponding to combined mean unbound Cmax was 4.34 µM (based on total Cmax of 81.8 µM and unbound fraction of 5.3%), which is &gt;33-fold higher than unbound Cmax at the maximum recommended clinical dose. Respiratory system effects (respiratory frequency, tidal volume and minute volume) were studied in male and female rats. Statistically significant decreases in tidal and minute volume were observed during the Phase 3 analysis (181-360 min postdose) at dose levels ≥60 mg/kg but these were not considered adverse. Therefore, NOAEL was set as 200 mg/kg. No TK analysis was included to this study.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

There were no concerns on CNS or respiratory system effects suggested in the studies conducted in rats.

## 4.3.1.4 . Pharmacodynamic drug interactions

No studies to investigate pharmacodynamic drug interactions were conducted.

## 4.3.2 Pharmacokinetics

## 4.3.2.1 . Absorption

Transport experiments in Caco-2 cell monolayers indicated concentration-dependent permeability and efflux of povorcitinib, suggesting the involvement of a saturable transport mechanism. The efflux ratio was reduced to unity with the addition of P-gp inhibitors, indicating that povorcitinib is a substrate for P-gp. Experiments with an P-gp inhibitor showed that povorcitinib is the inhibitor of P-gp as well.

The IV and oral PK of povorcitinib (as free base) after a single dose were evaluated in fasted SD rats, beagle dogs, and cynomolgus monkeys, and the results are summarised in Table 5.

## Toxicokinetics

The initial repeat-dose non-GLP toxicity studies were conducted using the free base of povorcitinib. Results of these bridging PK studies indicated that in rats the phosphate salt of povorcitinib could provide a slight increase (1.5 to 2.1-fold) in systemic exposure compared to the free base, while in dogs, both forms had similar exposure levels. Subsequently, repeat-dose GLP toxicity studies were conducted using the phosphate salt of povorcitinib. Details for TK from individual studies (single and repeat oral dose studies of up to 6 and 9 months in rats and dogs, developmental and reproductive toxicology studies in rats and rabbits, carcinogenicity studies in rats and mice) are assessed in Toxicology section below.

## Brain Penetration

The potential for povorcitinib to distribute into brain tissue was studied in nonpigmented male Spraque Dawley (SD) rats given an IV bolus of 1.3 mg/kg of povorcitinib followed by a 0.3 mg/h/kg IV infusion via the jugular vein for 4 h. The mean total brain and CSF concentrations of povorcitinib were 12% and 1% of the corresponding total plasma concentration.

## Tissue Distribution

Tissue distribution of 14 C-povorcitinib-derived radioactivity was extensive and generally consistent between sexes and strains. In nonpigmented male SD rats, tissues with the highest Cmax levels were the liver, adrenal gland, kidney cortex, Harderian gland, and kidney. In pigmented Long Evans (LE) rats, tissues with the highest Cmax values in male rats were the liver, adrenal gland, Harderian gland, kidney cortex, and brown fat. In pigmented female rats, tissues with the highest Cmax values were the liver, Harderian gland, adrenal gland, kidney cortex, and pancreas. The lowest levels of radioactivity (across all animals/groups) were generally observed in the central nervous system tissues, bone, and eye lens. In both SD and LE rats radioactivity levels in CNS tissues were low relative to plasma and other tissues, indicating limited CNS distribution. No strain-related differences were observed in CNS distribution. After maximum tissue concentrations at 4 h post-dose radioactivity was eliminated from tissues over time, with quantifiable concentrations of radioactivity observed in nine matrices at 72 hours post-dose in nonpigmented rats. In pigmented rats, radioactivity concentrations in the majority of tissues were below detectable levels by 48 hours post-dose. By 168 hours post-dose, only 6 tissues in males and 8 tissues in females had quantifiable levels of radioactivity, including the intervertebral ligaments, pigmented skin, liver, Meibomian gland, eye uveal tract, and hair follicle in both sexes, as well as the eye and adrenal gland in females. The longer persistence of radioactivity observed in pigmented rats was confined to melanin-containing tissues, consistent with melanin-associated retention.

There were no placenta transfer or excretion in milk studies.

## 4.3.2.3 . Metabolism

Clinically relevant CYP inductions/inhibitions and effects of povorcitinib on transporters are discussed in the clinical section 5.2.2.11 Pharmacokinetic interaction studies.

## In vitro metabolism

## Comparative In Vitro Metabolism of povorcitinib Across Species

The in vitro metabolism of povorcitinib was examined using cofactor-fortified hepatic microsomes and hepatic S9 fraction from SD rats, beagle dogs, cynomolgus monkeys and humans. An oxidative metabolite, M3 (hydroxylation of the dimethyl pyrazole) was the most abundant metabolite detected across in vitro systems. The in vitro metabolism profile of povorcitinib in hepatic microsomes and S9

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

fractions from rat, dog, and human was qualitatively similar and no human specific in vitro metabolites were identified.

## In Vitro Metabolism of povorcitinib

Because of low metabolic turnover in vitro, 14 C-povorcitinib was incubated in cryopreserved human hepatocytes using a relay method. Following 960 minutes of total incubation time (4 relays of 240 minutes each), intact povorcitinib made up 59.5% of the chromatographic radioactivity. Two metabolites accounting for &gt; 1% of chromatographic radioactivity were identified: M3 (oxidative) and M12 (N-glucuronidation of the dimethyl pyrazole moiety), accounting for 21.0% and 19.5% of chromatographic radioactivity, respectively.

The in vitro stability of the povorcitinib N-glucuronide metabolite M12 was investigated in human faecal homogenates. The results indicate that M12 can be deconjugated in the presence of human faeces, converting it back into povorcitinib. It was suggested that the deconjugation process is driven by bacterial activity in human faeces.

Neither povorcitinib nor any of its known in vitro human metabolites formed glutathione adducts in rat and human liver microsomes in the presence of NADPH, suggesting that povorcitinib does not generate reactive metabolites.

## In Vitro Metabolism of povorcitinib by Human rCYP and rUGT Enzymes

After incubation with human recombinant CYP (rCYP) and UGT (rUGT) enzymes povorcitinib was the most abundant drug-related material in human rCYP incubations with parent accounting for &gt; 94% of total drug-related peak area for all CYPs tested except for CYP3A4 (povorcitinib comprised 50.4% of the total drug-related peak area). In the presence of rCYP3A4, the most abundant metabolite generated was M3. Low levels of metabolite M1 (N-dealkylation cleavage of the trifluoropropyl moiety) was detected in the CYP3A4 incubates.

Intact povorcitinib was also the most abundant drug-related material detected after incubation with human rUGTs, contributing &gt; 97% of drug-related peak area in all incubations. M12 was the only metabolite identified in human rUGT incubates. The only isoforms that generated M12 at quantities ≥ 1% of parent peak area were UGT1A3 and UGT1A4; 1.0% and 2.3%, respectively.

## In Vitro Human rCYP Substrate Assay

Experiments using individual recombinant human CYPs (rCYP) showed that povorcitinib was primarily metabolised by CYP3A4. The metabolism of povorcitinib by CYP3A4 could not be confirmed using selective chemical inhibitors due to the low rate of metabolism of povorcitinib in human liver microsomes. The in vitro metabolism of povorcitinib by CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6 and CYP3A5 was low, thus, it was concluded that povorcitinib is predominately metabolised by CYP3A4.

## In vivo metabolism

Metabolite profiling was performed after a single oral dose of 14 C-povorcitinib in SD rats, beagle dogs and humans. Plasma, bile (rat and dog only), urine and faeces samples were analysed by LC-MS/MS with radiochemical detection for metabolite profiling and characterisation.

In TK study in male and female mice intact povorcitinib was the major analyte present in plasma. The two most abundant circulating metabolites, detected at 0.8% to 1.1% of the total integrated peak area, were M1 (N-dealkylation-derived loss of the trifluoropropyl moiety), and M3 (hydroxylation of the dimethyl pyrazole moiety of povorcitinib).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Ater single and multiple oral dosing in male and female rats the most abundant metabolite detected in plasma was metabolite M3 found at relative abundance levels &lt; 2.0% of parent. In urine, the most abundant metabolite detected was also metabolite M3. Plasma or urinary abundances of povorcitinib and its metabolites showed no sign of accumulation other than what would be expected based on steady-state PK. In faeces, povorcitinib or M3 were the most abundant drug-related materials detected, accounting for 25.2% - 33.7% of the administered radioactive dose in bile duct-intact animals and 9.6% - 25.6% of the administered radioactive dose in bile duct-cannulated (BDC) rats. Overall, the metabolic profile of povorcitinib was similar between male and female rats.

Ater single and multiple oral dosing in male and female beagle dogs at steady state, three metabolites were detected at trace abundance in plasma, including M3. Metabolites of povorcitinib showed no significant signs of accumulation. A total of 4 metabolites of povorcitinib were found and characterised in urine samples from male and female beagle dogs, with the most abundant being M3. In bile ductintact dogs, M3 was the most abundant drug-related material in faecal samples, accounting for 44.7% of the administered radioactive dose. In BDC dogs, povorcitinib was the most abundant drug-related material in faecal samples, accounting for 25.6% and 24.2% of the administered radioactive dose following an oral or IV dose.

In healthy adult participants at steady state no major circulating metabolites exceeding 10% of the total identified drug-related material were observed. M1 (N-dealkylation-derived loss of the trifluoropropyl moiety of povorcitinib) and M12 (N-glucuronidation of the dimethyl pyrazole moiety of povorcitinib) were detected at 2.2% and 3.2-3.6% of total known drug-related material. In urine, M3 and M12 were identified at levels ≥ 10% of the total known drug-related material. M1, M6 (hydrolysis of the amide moiety resulting in a carboxylic acid), M15 (N-dealkylation-associated cleavage of the azetidine moiety), and M16 (oxidative ring opening of the azetidine moiety in addition to oxidation of carbonitrile moiety to a carboxylic acid) accounted for ≥ 1% and &lt; 10% of the total drug-related material. Urinarily excreted povorcitinib and M12 accounted for 7.1% and 7.7% of the total radioactive administered dose over the 120-hour collection period analysed. In faeces, povorcitinib was the predominant drug-related material observed, accounting for 29.1% of the total administered radioactive dose. When considering both urine and faeces together, intact povorcitinib was the most abundant compound-related material excreted by humans following a single oral dose, accounting for 36.2% of the total administered radioactive dose and M3 was the most abundant human metabolite accounting for 11.7% of the total administered radioactive dose.

## 4.4 Toxicology

The nonclinical toxicology and safety pharmacology programs were designed in accordance with ICH M3(R2) (2009) and applicable ICH Safety Guidelines. povorcitinib refers to povorcitinib phosphate, the phosphate salt form, unless otherwise specified.

## 4.4.1 Single-dose toxicity

In male rats, a dose level of 500 mg/kg produced transient body weight loss suggesting that this dose level may not be tolerated in repeated dosing.

In dogs, povorcitinib administration at a single dose level of ≥50 mg/kg was associated with adverse clinical signs including limited use of the hind leg. Dose levels of ≤15 mg/kg were well tolerated.

## 4.4.2 Repeat-dose toxicity

Pivotal repeat-dose toxicity and TK studies were conducted in rats for up to 6 months, and in dogs for up to 9 months. A recovery group was included in the GLP studies to determine the reversibility of povorcitinib-related findings. In addition, a 28-day GLP toxicity study in CByB6F1 hybrid mice was conducted as a range-finding study for the 6-month carcinogenicity study in CByB6F1/Tg rasH2 hemizygous mice.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

In an investigational non-GLP 12-day dog study, high doses of povorcitinib (≥ 7.5 mg/kg/day) produced hind limb paresis and/or intermittent tremors and ataxia. Adverse inflammation of the GI tract was also noted in dogs at these dose levels and may have contributed to their poor condition. These findings occurred at exposures &gt; 7- fold higher than the estimated AUC for a dose of 75 mg QD in patients (based on population PK analysis).

In 28-day mice study, NOAEL was set as 100 mg/kg as adverse decrease in RCB count was observed with 300 mg/kg/day dosing of povorcitinib.

## Pivotal studies in rats

In the 28-day rat study, 2 females were found dead at 200 mg/kg, one due to severe bone marrow hypocellularity. Rats in the 200 mg/kg dosing showed signs of systemic stress and local irritation, lower prostate and pituitary weights and microscopic findings in the liver and ovaria. Reversible changes in haematology, clinical chemistry and immunophenotyping were observed with all dose levels but these changes were not considered adverse. Therefore, NOAEL was set as 60 mg/kg.

In the 3-month rat study, dose-dependent immunosuppression, lymphoid tissue depletion and haematologic changes were reported at all doses. Findings observed at lower doses were consistent with the intended pharmacology of povorcitinib, and NOAEL was set at 15 mg/kg as the effects observed with higher dosing were considered adverse. At 60 mg/kg, signs of general toxicity such as body weight reductions with associated lower food consumption, hair loss, scabbing, alopecia, skin lesions and oral discharge were reported.

In albino rats, light dependent retinal degeneration was observed in a 3-month toxicity study, but was determined to be species/strain specific, with no evidence of phototoxicity in vitro and no similar findings in pigmented animals or clinical studies.

In the 6-month rat study, NOAEL was set at 10 mg/kg, based on dose-dependent immunosuppression, lymphoid depletion, anaemia and general toxicity (i.e., systemic stress reactions) considered adverse in the 30 m/kg dosing. Safety margins derived from the NOAELs of rat 6-month study in comparison to clinical exposure are 5.4 (males) and 8.4 (females).

Transient and reversible microscopic findings in the bone were observed in a 1-month toxicity study in Sprague-Dawley rats and in a 3-month study in Long-Evans rats at an age comparable to adolescent humans ≥ 12 years; no bone findings were observed at similar doses in the 3- and 6-month rat toxicity studies.

## Pivotal studies in dogs

In the 28-day dog study, the highest dose (5 mg/kg) was set as NOAEL as no povorcitinib-related adversity was identified. In the 3-month dog study, 5 dogs died or were euthanised early due to secondary effects (e.g., skin lesions) of immunosuppression. Dose-dependent immunosuppression with secondary infections (Demodex), lymphoid tissue depletion, impaired erythropoiesis and systemic inflammatory responses were recorded. Povorcitinib-related adversity was reported in 2.5 and 5 mg/kg groups, and therefore the NOAEL was set as 1 mg/kg.

In the 9-month study, 7 deaths related to povorcitinib (immunosuppression) were reported in 0.6, 1.2 and 2.0 mg/kg/day groups. Main causes for these deaths were severe skin lesions, Demodex mite infestation and mixed inflammation in lymph nodes. Microscopic findings were observed in lymph nodes, Peyer's patches and bone marrow indicating systemic immunomodulation as well as skin, ears and paws caused by Demodex infection with mixed inflammation. The immune-related effects that were considered adverse occurred at ≥ 1.2 mg/kg/day, the NOAEL was set as 0.6 mg/kg/day. Safety margins derived from the NOAELs of dog 9-month study in comparison to clinical exposure are 0.5 (males) and 0.3 (females).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

No bone findings were observed in repeat-dose toxicity studies in dogs (comparable to adolescent humans ≥ 12 years.

## 4.4.3 Genotoxicity

The bacterial reverse mutation assay (Ames test utilising S.typhimurium and E.coli strains) showed negative results both with and without metabolic activation. Therefore, povorcitinib was considered non-mutagenic. In the in vitro chromosomal aberration test in human peripheral blood lymphocytes, povorcitinib was positive on polyploidy at concentrations ≥ 35 µg/ml in the 22-hr treatment without metabolic activation. In the in vivo rat bone marrow micronucleus assay, negative results were reported.

## 4.4.4 Carcinogenicity

The doses for a 6-month carcinogenicity study of povorcitinib in CByB6F1-Tg(HRAS)2Jic mice were selected based on results of a 28-day range-finding study. The high dose in this study was expected to achieve exposures ~30× the human therapeutic dose based on steady stated AUC. Non-neoplastic povorcitinib-related effects were noted in haematolymphoid tissues at ≥ 30 mg/kg/day in males and ≥ 10 mg/kg/day in females and included increased extramedullary haematopoiesis in the spleen; decreased lymphoid cellularity in the red and white pulp of the spleen; decreased lymphoid cellularity of thymus, submandibular lymph node, and mesenteric lymph node; and decreased cellularity of the bone marrow. These findings were largely similar to those observed in general repeat-dose toxicity studies in rodents. No carcinogenic effects related to povorcitinib administration was observed at any dose level. The highest dose 100 mg/kg/day was set as the NOAEL.

In a 2-year carcinogenicity study of povorcitinib by oral gavage in SD rats exposed to 1, 3 and 10 mg/kg/day there were no povorcitinib-related effects on mortality. Overall survival was comparable across treated and control groups. All other neoplastic macroscopic findings observed in the povorcitinib-exposed rats were considered incidental and unrelated to administration of the test article, due to these been commonly observed in this strain and age of rats, and/or were of similar incidence in control and treated animals. Similar findings in lymphoid tissues were observed as seen in 6-month mouse study. The NOAEL for carcinogenicity and systemic toxicity in rats was 10 mg/kg/day.

## 4.4.5 Developmental and reproductive toxicity

## Fertility and early embryonic development in rats

No deaths occurred in any group in the female fertility and early embryonic development rat study. For the mating and fertility analysis, severe impairment of fertility was reported as only 2 of 24 females became pregnant, and both of these pregnancies ended in early resorption (no viable embryos) in the 60 mg/kg/day group. For the implantation and embryonic survival, lower corpora lutea and implantation sites and markedly increased post-implantation loss was reported in the 15 mg/kg/day group. Ovary and reproductive tract findings were reported in the ≥ 15 mg/kg/day groups. The NOAEL for female reproductive performance and early embryonic toxicity was set as 3 mg/kg/day.

In the second rat study with reversibility assessment, similar findings were observed. No females delivered a litter in the 60 mg/kg/day group, and markedly reduced litter size was recorded for 15

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

mg/kg/day group. In the second mating phase after a 3-week recovery, all reproductive parameters in povorcitinib-treated groups were similar to controls, including mating performance, fertility, corpora lutea counts, implantation sites and viable foetuses and pre- or post-implantation loss, suggesting reversibility of povorcitinib-induced effects.

In the third rat study with an assessment of critical period of exposure, only mild and transient maternal toxicity was reported. When premating dosing was utilised, no effects on mating, fertility, pregnancy indices or precoital interval. When povorcitinib was dosed on GD0-3, higher postimplantation loss and lower number of viable embryos was reported in the 60 mg/kg/day group, indicating early embryonic sensitivity even to short exposure. povorcitinib dosing on GD0-7 resulted in significantly increased post-implantation loss and lower number of viable embryos in the 15 mg/kg/day group, and severe impairment of fertility and early embryonic survival in the 60 mg/kg/day group. No adversity was reported in the 3 mg/kg/day group.

In male rats, no povorcitinib-related effects on reproductive performance (male mating, fertility, and pregnancy indices), pre-coital intervals, or sperm parameters were reported at any dose level. The NOAEL for male reproductive toxicity and early embryonic development was set as 60 mg/kg/day. Safety margins for clinical exposure based on the NOAELs are 37 (males) and 0.9 (females).

## Embryo-fœtal development in rats

One female at 30 mg/kg/day died late in gestation (GD20), all other animals survived to scheduled necropsy. Increased post-implantation loss (15.5%; mainly early resorptions) resulting in fewer viable foetuses (84.5%) as well as lower mean foetal weight in the 30 mg/kg/day group. Also, non-adverse 14th rudimentary ribs were reported in this group. No adversity was reported in other povorcitinibtreated groups, and the NOAEL for maternal toxicity and embryo-foetal development was set as 10 mg/kg/day, resulting in safety margin 4.1 in comparison to clinical exposure.

## Embryo-fœtal development in rabbits

In the first rabbit study, two females in the 45 mg/kg/day group died before scheduled necropsy. In this high dose group, lower mean gravid uterine weight was reported. Haematological alterations, such as lower reticulocyte count, neutrophils and RBC count, were recorded in ≥ 15 mg/kg/day dosing, suggesting bone marrow or RBC production effects for povorcitinib. Increased post-implantation loss leading to fewer viable foetuses as well as reduced foetal body weights were reported in ≥ 15 mg/kg/day dosing. No external malformations or developmental variations were observed when rabbits were treated with povorcitinib.

In the second rabbit study, abortions and maternal mortality were reported ≥ 10 mg/kg/day doses of povorcitinib. Signs of maternal toxicity, such as body weight loss, low food intake and cool body were reported in these doses. For the low dose group (3 mg/kg/day), no signs of maternal toxicity were recorded. Increased post-implantation loss (34.2%), lower viable foetus count (5.9 vs 8.3), increased early and late resorptions, lower mean foetal body weights and increased external malformations (omphalocele) were reported in rabbits receiving 30 mg/kg/day povorcitinib. No developmental toxicity were reported in rabbits receiving ≤ 10 mg/kg/day povorcitinib. Maternal NOAEL 3 mg/kg/day and developmental NOAEL 10 mg/kg/day were established. Based on the NOAEL 10 mg/kg/day, safety margin 4.9 in comparison to clinical exposure was established.

## Prenatal and postnatal development in rats

In the F0 generation, severe maternal toxicity was observed in 25 mg/kg/day povorcitinib dosing, resulting in euthanasia in extremis, total litter loss and dead, stillborn or cannibalised pups. High postimplantation loss was reported in this dosing. For the 3 and 10 mg/kg/day povorcitinib dosing, no maternal toxicity was observed.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Povorcitinib exposure was confirmed in offspring during the lactation period. The mean F1 pups to F0 females ratio of povorcitinib plasma concentration at 2 hours post-dose on PND10 ranged from 0.08 to 0.2.

In the F1 generation developmental toxicity analysis, severe effects on pup survival and growth were reported in 25 mg/kg/day group. Very low viability and birth weights as well as developmental delay (pinna detachment) and neuromuscular/limb abnormalities consistent with necropsy findings of malrotated paws, bent/misshapen bones) were observed resulting in early termination of offspring at PND21. Postweaning evaluations were not performed due to the preweaning toxicity. For the 10 mg/kg/day dosing, some effects on pup body weights were noted but not considered adverse as no associated clinical or structural abnormalities were reported. For the 3 mg/kg/day dosing, no adverse effects on survival, growth, developmental or skeletal findings were recorded.

In the F1 generation reproductive performance assessment, no povorcitinib-related effects were observed in povorcitinib dosing 3 and 10 mg/kg/day. No changes in F2 embryo survival and reproductive indices were noted at these dose levels.

## 4.4.6 Local tolerance

Local tolerance studies have not been performed with povorcitinib. In line with the 'Guideline on nonclinical local tolerance testing of medicinal products (EMA 2015)', local tolerance evaluation (GI) was included as part of the general toxicity studies.

## 4.4.7 Other toxicity studies

A total of 54 povorcitinib-related substances identified as potential impurities were evaluated for potential mutagenicity using a rules-based expert system (Derek Nexus) and a statistical-based methodology (Sarah Nexus). Of the 54 compounds evaluated, 50 were assigned as ICH M7 Class 5 based on in silico assessment. Of the remaining 4 compounds, one was classified as ICH M7 class 5 compound based on negative result in Ames mutagenicity assay and the remaining three compounds were ICH M7 Class 3 and will be treated as a genotoxic impurities.

Enhanced Ames Test was undertaken to investigate the mutagenic potential of the povorcitinib impurity INCB210416. Weak positive response was only seen in one strain, Salmonella typhimurium TA1535 in the absence of metabolic activation.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The phototoxicity potential of povorcitinib was evaluated by measuring by the relative reduction in viability of BALB/c 3T3 mouse fibroblasts exposed to povorcitinib and ultraviolet radiation (+UVR), as compared with the viability of fibroblasts exposed to povorcitinib in the absence of ultraviolet radiation (-UVR). Povorcitinib toxicity was observed in the presence UVR (+UVR), but not in the absence of UVR (-UVR). The resulting PIF was &gt; 1, suggesting phototoxic potential. However, the MPE values were &lt; 0.15, which are of questionable toxicological relevance for systemic drugs (Note 4 of the ICH S10). It was concluded that povorcitinib does not present a risk for phototoxicity in patients.
