## 4.5 Overall discussion and conclusions on non-clinical aspects

## 4.5.1 Discussion

The nonclinical development of povorcitinib has followed ICH M3 guideline and is thus accepted.

## Pharmacology

## Primary pharmacodynamics

A comprehensive set of in vitro and in vivo primary pharmacodynamic studies have been performed to study the mechanism of action and JAK1 over JAK2 selectivity of povorcitinib. These studies include in vitro evaluation of povorcitinib selectivity within the JAK family, effect of povorcitinib in JAK/STAT activation and inhibition of cell growth and cytokine/chemokine production resulting from povorcitinib exposure. In vivo, the different inflammatory rat and mouse disease models were used to demonstrate that the inhibition of JAK1 signalling is a suitable target in the treatment of inflammatory diseases, such as HS.

The selected human inflammatory cell types and whole blood of mice, rats and dogs and mouse xenograft models are overall considered acceptable for the investigation of primary pharmacodynamics and demonstration of proof-of-concept for povorcitinib.

## In vitro studies

## Povorcitinib selectivity within the JAK family

Enzyme inhibition activity analyses of povorcitinib of human JAK1, JAK2, JAK3 and TYK2 demonstrated high selectivity towards JAK1. The inhibition activity for JAK1 (IC50 = 8.9 ± 1.7 nM) was 52-fold in comparison to inhibition activity for JAK2. Although the number of experiments for the JAK3 and TYK2 inhibition were low (n=2), the results suggest &gt; 1000-fold selectivity for JAK1 over JAK3 and 45-fold selectivity for JAK1 over TYK2. Further, metabolite M12 did not affect the activity of any JAK family member (IC50s &gt; 25000 nM).

When povorcitinib was compared to marketed JAK1 inhibitors in biochemical and whole blood assays, a high JAK1 selectivity over JAK2 was demonstrated for povorcitinib both in the enzymatic assays and human whole blood assays. The effects of povorcitinib on other JAK family kinases (JAK3 and TYK2) were minor. Among JAK inhibitors used, povorcitinib demonstrated the highest selectivity ratio (JAK1/JAK2 inhibition) in all experiments.

## Effect of povorcitinib on levels of phosphorylated JAKs and STATs

The inhibition of IL-6 mediated STAT3 phosphorylation was interpreted as inhibition of JAK1 and inhibition of thrombopoietin (TPO) mediated STAT3 phosphorylation as inhibition of JAK2. This is agreed as JAK1 is known to be an important mediator for IL-6 induced and JAK2 for TPO induced STAT3 activation. IC50 for IL-6 induced STAT3 phosphorylation was 690 ± 224 nM and for TOP induced STAT3 phosphorylation &gt; 10 000, suggesting approximately 14-fold selectivity towards JAK1 pathway. Similar data was obtained from the whole blood of mice, rats and dogs. Thus, a cross-reactivity among animal species is adequately demonstrated.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

When using granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) as a stimulus, IC50 for IL-6 induced STAT1 phosphorylation was 360 ± 128 nM and for GM-CSF induced STAT5 phosphorylation &gt; 10 000, resulting in approximately 28-fold selectivity towards JAK1. Results suggest selectivity towards JAK1 pathway.

## Inhibition of cell growth and cytokine/chemokine production resulting from povorcitinib exposure

The IC50 value of 29.6 ± 1.2 nM was recorded for the inhibition of IL-2 induced T cell proliferation by povorcitinib. The inhibition of cell growth by povorcitinib was also tested in HEK-293, HEPG2, HLF, HUVEC and SET-2 cell lines which are not JAK dependent. No effects on proliferation in these cell lines was reported. The IC50 values of 17 nM was recorded for the inhibition of IL-17 (n=2) and 99 nM for the inhibition of IL-22 (n=2). The IC50 values of 178 nM ± 57 nM were recorded for the inhibition of MCP-1 (n=3). It should be noted that these results should be interpreted with caution as n was only 2 or 3 and interindividual variation in human primary cells may be high. This data are thus considered as supportive data for inhibition of JAK1 by povorcitinib.

## In vivo studies

In all used inflammatory disease models, povorcitinib induced a dose-dependent improvement in selected endpoints, and the recorded effect was independent from the administration route (SC, topical, oral). Overall, a number of key proinflammatory JAK/STAT-dependent cytokines related to HS pathogenesis have been covered by in vivo pharmacology studies. Therefore, the observed efficacy of povorcitinib in animal inflammatory models is likely associated with positive effects in HS.

## Secondary pharmacodynamics

In the secondary pharmacodynamics screening study, sigma-1 receptor was identified as potential target from 70 receptors, enzymes and ion channels included in the screening. The activity of povorcitinib on sigma-1 receptor was then further studied and IC50 of 0.675 μM was determined for the sigma-1 inhibition. Sigma-1 receptors are involved in regulating cellular homeostasis, ion channel activity and inter-organelle communication, especially in neurogenerative and cardiovascular diseases. A 6.3-fold safety margin towards expected clinical exposure was presented, supported with absence of adverse findings on CNS or cardiovascular functions in the safety pharmacology studies.

In the kinase profile screening towards 192 kinases, povorcitinib at 200 nM demonstrated 70% inhibition of JAK2, while IC50 for JAK1 was 1.5 nM. This again confirms the selectivity of povorcitinib for JAK1 versus JAK2. No other JAK kinases were included in the screening. In a second kinase profiling study, povorcitinib demonstrated no selectivity towards 57 screened non-JAK family kinases.

## Safety pharmacology

The safety pharmacology studies are considered adequate, even if TK analysis was not incorporated to all studies.

Cardiovascular effects were studied in in vitro hERG assay and two in vivo dog studies. In vitro hERG assay suggested IC50 value of 11.8 µM, which is &gt;90-fold above the unbound Cmax in HS patients. In the dog studies, no cardiovascular adversity was recorded with dosing up to 15 mg/kg (plasma concentrations 9.19 ± 2.2 (4h) and 8.67 ± 2.2 (24h) µM), resulting in unbound plasma concentration of 0.49 µM at 4-hour post-dose. This provides a safety margin of 3.8-fold in relation to unbound Cmax at the maximum recommended human dose.

Due to relatively low safety margin in beagle dogs, the potential risk for human use cannot be completely excluded from a non-clinical point of view. However, the totality of data suggests that administration of povorcitinib at the recommended clinical dose is not likely associated with adverse effects on cardiovascular system (also see clinical safety section).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

There were no concerns on CNS or respiratory system effects suggested in the studies conducted in rats.

Pharmacodynamic drug interactions

Pharmacodynamic drug interaction studies were not conducted. This is accepted.

## Pharmacokinetics

## Absorption

PK parameters were measured after a single oral or intravenous administration of povorcitinib free base in rats, dogs and monkeys.

Across rat, dog and monkey, povorcitinib was rapidly and completely absorbed following oral administration, with complete bioavailability consistent with its low clearance profile after IV dosing. The systemic exposure increased with dose across species. The main difference between animal species was terminal half-life, being approximately 4h in rats, 13h in monkeys and &gt;22h in dogs. Due to suboptimal sampling period (up to 24h post-dose), t1/2 estimations should be carefully interpreted, especially in dogs. The bridging studies were conducted to compare exposures between free base and phosphate salt forms of povorcitinib. In rats, Cmax and AUC values were greater (in the range from 1.5- to 2.1-fold) when using the phosphate salt, while no significant difference in exposure was observed in dogs. Because of limited number of animals (n=1/sex/dose) and indirect comparison using dose-normalised exposures (different dose levels were used for free base and phosphate salt), the validity of conclusions in dogs is questionable. Since all pivotal repeat-dose toxicity studies were conducted with povorcitinib in the phosphate salt form, this issue is not pursued further. Transport studies in Caco-2 cell monolayers indicated concentration-dependent permeability and efflux of povorcitinib, suggesting the involvement of a saturable transport mechanism. Experiments further demonstrated that povorcitinib is both a substrate and inhibitor of P-gp, a finding that provides insight into its limited penetration into the central nervous system and its potential to influence intestinal efflux of co-administered P-gp substrates.

## Distribution

The distribution of povorcitinib is characterised by moderate plasma protein binding, largely mediated by albumin, without evidence of saturation in the concentration ranges tested. An average unbound fraction was 5.3, 5.3 and 8.2% in rat, dog and human, respectively. Pharmacologically inactive human metabolite M12 did not exhibit concentration dependent plasma protein binding, fu ranging from 26.96% to 30.48% across all dose concentrations with an average fu of 28.96%. Povorcitinib binds to both HSA and α1 acid glycoprotein and the extent of binding is independent of povorcitinib concentration. The distribution into blood cells was minimal. In in vitro experiments with human skin homogenate the binding of povorcitinib was not concentration dependent and indicated non-saturable or non-specific. CNS penetration of povorcitinib was minimal in rats, attributed to active efflux via P-gp and BCRP, which are known to be expressed in rat choroid plexus epithelial cells. When male rats were intravenously administered with povorcitinib, the mean total brain and CSF concentrations of povorcitinib were 12% and 1% of the corresponding total plasma concentration. A similar expression of P-gp and BCRP at the blood brain barrier and choroid plexus epithelial cells of humans may result in modest distribution of povorcitinib into human brain and CSF. Tissue distribution studies confirmed widespread distribution except to CNS tissues, bone and lens. In SD non-pigmented rats, the radioactivity was widely distributed into various tissues, in accordance with estimated volume of distribution exceeding total body water. The tissue radioactivity generally declined below the limit of quantitation up to 72 hours after dosing. In LE pigmented rats, extensive distribution and very slow elimination of radioactivity (measurable levels at 168 hours post-dose) were noted in eye uveal tract, pigmented skin and hair follicle. Thus, povorcitinib shows a great affinity for melanin-containing tissues. Although placental and milk transfer studies were not conducted, mechanistic considerations and embryo-foetal/postnatal toxicity findings support the contraindication during pregnancy and breastfeeding, as reflected in SmPC section 4.3.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Metabolism and excretion

When analysing hepatic microsomes and S9 fractions pre-incubated with povorcitinib for 60 minutes, the metabolic turnover was moderate and qualitatively similar metabolic profiles were observed between human and animal species. Metabolite M3 represented the main fraction (accounted for &gt;10% of the parent compound only in cynomolgus monkey), with M1, M2 and M4 being commonly identified in rat, dog, monkey and human microsomes and S9. No human unique metabolites were identified. Incubation in the presence of glutathione (GSH) revealed no reactive conjugates. After 960-minute incubation of [ 14 C]-povorcitinib with cryopreserved human hepatocytes using a relay method, unchanged compound represented up to 59.5% of chromatographic radioactivity. Two other significant metabolites were detected over the course of the study: M3 (oxidative) and M12 (N-glucuronidation of the dimethyl pyrazole moiety) accounted for 21.0% and 19.5% of chromatographic radioactivity, respectively. While unchanged povorcitinib represented the major moiety in animal and human plasma, M3 was the predominant metabolite in animal species. M12 was the major metabolite detected in human plasma and urine, exceeding 10% of total radioactivity in plasma. Since M12 was shown to be pharmacologically inactive and N-glucuronide conjugates are generally not of toxicological concern due to well-known detoxification pathway (greater polarity leading to easier excretion), no additional toxicological characterisation was required. Excretion occurs primarily via bile and faeces across species, including humans. Overall, the PK profile is well delineated and does not indicate a need for additional non-clinical DDI evaluations beyond those performed by the applicant in support of this application.

## Drug-drug interactions

Povorcitinib is not considered a substrate for human OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OAT1, OAT3, or OCT2. Consequently, a clinical DDI study to evaluate the impact of concomitant medications that are known OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OAT1, OAT3, or OCT2 inhibitors on the PK of povorcitinib is not warranted in accordance with ICH12. Povorcitinib is not considered a substrate for human renal efflux transporters MATE1 or MATE2-K.

CYP3A4 is the principal metabolising CYP isoform involved in povorcitinib metabolism. povorcitinib did not meaningfully induce or inhibit major CYP isoforms at clinically relevant concentrations, except for weak in vitro inhibition of CYP2C8/2C9. The risk of DDIs by strong CYP3A inhibitors and inducers has been included in the SmPC section 4.5.

For discussion on PK drug-drug interactions from clinical point of view, see the section Clinical pharmacology.

## Toxicology

## General Toxicity

Single-dose studies identified transient weight loss in rats and neuromuscular signs in dogs at high doses, with lower doses being well tolerated. Pivotal GLP-compliant repeat-dose studies in rats (up to 6 months) and dogs (up to 9 months) identified dose-limiting toxicities including unscheduled deaths primarily mediated by JAK-pathway immunosuppression, including lymphoid depletion, bone marrow hypocellularity, and secondary infections. Some of the findings persisted during the recovery period, which was included in GLP studies. In the non-pivotal 12-day dog study, high dose levels (≥ 7.5 mg/kg/day) resulted in hind limb paresis and/or intermittent tremors and ataxia. Adverse gastrointestinal inflammation was also observed at these dose levels and may have contributed to the animals' poor clinical condition. These effects occurred at exposures exceeding approximately sevenfold the estimated AUC associated with a 75 mg once-daily dose in patients, based on population pharmacokinetic analysis, and are not considered relevant for clinical settings. In long-term dog studies, prolonged immune suppression precipitated demodectic mange, a species-specific susceptibility that is not considered to be clinically relevant in humans. Toxicokinetic analyses confirmed adequate systemic exposure to support safety evaluations, dogs being the most sensitive species. povorcitinib accumulation as steady-state was attained.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

In albino rats, light-dependent retinal degeneration was observed in a 3-month toxicity study, but was determined to be species/strain-specific, with no evidence of phototoxicity in vitro and no similar findings in pigmented animals or clinical studies. Therefore, these retinal findings are not considered relevant to human risk assessment.

Relevant findings related to general toxicity were adequately described in SmPC section 5.3.

## Genotoxicity and Carcinogenicity

Genotoxicity of povorcitinib was assessed in accordance with ICH S2(R1).

In bacterial reverse mutation assay S.typhimurium and E.coli strains were used. Povorcitinib did not cause a positive increase in the number of revertants per plate with any tester strain in the presence or absence of metabolic activation and thus met the criteria for a negative response.

The in vitro chromosome aberration assay indicated structural aberrations under certain conditions, and povorcitinib was considered positive for inducing structural aberrations in cultured human peripheral blood lymphocytes at high concentrations without metabolic activation.

The in vivo micronucleus test of povorcitinib was negative. The applicant concludes that in accordance with ICH S2(R1), if polyploidy, but no structural aberrations are seen in an in vitro assay, generally a negative in vivo micronucleus assay with assurance of appropriate exposure would provide sufficient assurance of lack of potential for aneuploidy induction. TK data confirmed exposure of the rats to povorcitinib. However, the mean Cmax and AUC0-24 values increased only marginally with a 4-fold increase in dose. Additionally, the systemic exposures at 500 mg/kg from this current study were less than corresponding dose normalised values on the first day of dosing at 200 mg/kg in the 28-day rat study, reflective of pharmacokinetic nonlinearity at high doses in micronucleus test. However, sufficient systemic exposure was achieved in in vivo test. The applicant's view is supported by the CHMP, and no further examination of genotoxicity was thus deemed warranted.

Povorcitinib revealed no oncogenic potential in 6-month carcinogenicity study in CByB6F1Tg(HRAS)2Jic mice and 2-year carcinogenicity study in SD rats.

## Developmental and reproductive Toxicity

Studies were conducted to assess effects on male and female fertility and early embryonic development in rats, embryo-foetal development in rats and rabbits, and pre- and postnatal development in rats.

Female fertility was adversely affected at high doses, specifically during the peri implantation window, but effects were reversible after a recovery period. No effects on male reproductive parameters were observed. Embryo-foetal toxicity was demonstrated in both rats and rabbits, including increased post implantation loss and reduced foetal weight at maternally toxic dose levels. In rabbits lower mean foetal body weights were followed by secondary effects on foetal morphology (omphalocele) at high dose. It is acknowledged that this malformation can be caused by some aspects of maternal toxicity, nevertheless, there is clear dose-response, and safety margin at NOAEL of less than 5. Pre- and postnatal development studies showed limb dysfunction and skeletal abnormalities in pups exposed postnatally via lactation at high doses; these findings were absent in embryo foetal studies, confirming their postnatal origin. The findings in the EFD and PPND studies and low safety margins support contraindication during pregnancy and breastfeeding set in the SmPC section 4.3. In addition, relevant findings related to reproductive and development toxicity were adequately described in SmPC section 5.3.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Toxicokinetics

Toxicokinetic analyses were included in all pivotal safety studies. Overall, the exposure levels reached were adequate to assess the povorcitinib-related safety findings.

At the NOAELs from the 9-month dog and 6-month rat GLP studies (0.6 mg/kg/day in dogs and 10 mg/kg/day in rats), plasma AUC values were 0.3 to 8.4-fold the estimated human AUC for a dose of 75 mg QD (based on population PK analysis). The dog was the most sensitive species. The low AUC margins in dogs (0.5 × for males; 0.3 × for females) were driven by secondary effects of immunosuppression (i.e., demodectic mange) subsequent to JAK inhibition. Demodectic mange observed in longer-term dog studies is not expected to occur in humans.

## Other studies

No separate local tolerance studies, antigenicity studies or toxicological studies for metabolites have been conducted and are not required. No separate immunotoxicity studies have been conducted, but the immunotoxicity endpoints were assessed in the repeat-dose toxicity studies.

No special dependence studies were conducted. Povorcitinib inhibited sigma-1 receptor in enzyme assays, but no effects related to sigma-1 receptor in human are expected.

Povorcitinib is not considered pose a risk for phototoxicity in patients.

## Environmental risk assessment

Povorcitinib is not expected to pose a risk to the environment.

## 4.5.2 Conclusions

In conclusion, the applicant provided a comprehensive evaluation of pharmacologic, pharmacokinetic and toxicologic properties of povorcitinib. Overall, povorcitinib is considered to be approvable from a non-clinical point.

## 5.2 Clinical pharmacology

## 5.2.1 Methods

Two LC/MS/MS methods were validated for the determination of povorcitinib in human plasma: a method from Incyte Corporation, that was used in Phase 2, Phase 3 and most of Phase 1 clinical studies, and a method from QPS that was used in the remaining Phase 1 studies. These two methods were cross validated. In addition, the methods for the determination of povorcitinib in human skin and human dialysate were validated by QPS and Incyte, respectively. The urine sample concentrations were determined using a non-validated, qualified, fit-for-purpose method that adapted Incyte plasma method. Other methods were developed and validated for quantifying of drugs co-administered with povorcitinib in drug-drug interaction and in QT/QTc studies. All methods were suitable for the intended use and demonstrated reliable performance.

In two Phase 1 clinical studies, levels of pSTAT3, a pharmacodynamic marker of JAK1 signalling, were quantified using a commercially available sandwich ELISA kit. Exploratory blood and skin biomarkers were assessed in patients with HS in some Phase 2 and 3 clinical studies.

## 5.2.2 Pharmacokinetics

## 5.2.2.1 Introduction

Pharmacokinetic (PK) data were mainly used for descriptive purposes. The PK data were generated in 12 phase 1 studies but also in phase 2 and both phase 3 studies for healthy volunteers, target patient population and special populations to characterise drug disposition, identify subgroups with potentially altered exposure, and evaluate possible drug-drug interactions. Data were also incorporated into population pharmacokinetic (popPK) and exposure-response (E-R) analyses.

## 5.2.2.2 Evaluation and qualification of models

## 5.2.2.2.1 Population pharmacokinetics

Two popPK models in healthy adults and patients with HS were developed to investigate impact of covariates:

## Study DMB-19.205.1 (popPK model)

This popPK model was based on data from 2 phase 1 studies with healthy participants (INCB 54707-101 and INCB 54707-102) and data from 2 phase 2 studies with HS participants (INCB 54707-202 and INCB 54707-203).

Final popPK model was two-compartment model with a linear elimination and a first order absorption with a lag time. Predictor variables in popPK model included body weight, sex, participant population and age.

Final popPK model was parametrised by Tlag, ka, CL/F, Vc/F, Q/F and Vp/F where interindividual variability (IIV) was estimated for parameters CL/F, Vc/F and ka.

Values of shrinkage for IIV was reasonable for CL (3.69%) and ka (12.7%), respectively, as this was below 30% compared to IIV for Vc/F (31.8%) which could have impact on

predictions. However, predictions for individual participants were in good agreement with observed data. Moreover, visual predictive check graphs for HS participants resulting from final popPK model sufficiently covered majority of observed concentrations within range from 5th to 95th percentile.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Study CPP-25.44.1 (popPK model)

This popPK model was based on data from 12 Phase 1 studies (INCB 54707-101, -102, -103, -104, - 105, -106, -107,-108, -109, -110, -111, and -112), 5 Phase 2 studies (INCB 54707-202, -203, -204, - 205, and -206), and 2 Phase 3 studies (INCB 54707-301 and -302). These studies included participants with HS, prurigo nodularis, vitiligo and healthy participants.

The data for the popPK analysis included 2029 participants (pooled from 19 studies) contributing 14,202 povorcitinib concentration measurements following povorcitinib doses ranging from 6 to 225 mg.

Final popPK model was two-compartment disposition model with linear elimination and a five-transit compartment absorption model. Predictor variables in popPK model included body weight, participant population (HS, prurigo nodularis [PN], vitiligo [VO], healthy), IGFR, total bilirubin, fed status (yes vs. no/unknown) and race (Japanese vs. Non-Japanese).

Predictor variables identified for CL/F were body weight, participant population, IGRF and total bilirubin, for Q/F was body weight, for V2/F were body weight and race, for V3/F was body weight, for KTR was fed status, and for F1 was fed status. Regarding CL/F, healthy participants had higher CL/F compared to HS participants, participants with VO or PN had lower CL/F compared HS participants, CL/F increased if IGRF increased and CL/F decreased if total bilirubin decreased. Regarding Q/F, Q/F decreased if body weight increased. Regarding V2/F, Japanese race had lower V2/F compared to non-Japanese race and V2/F decreased if body weight increased. Regarding V3/F, V3/F decreased if body weight increased. Regarding KTR, fed participants had decreased KTR compared to fasting/unknown fed status participants. Regarding F1, fed participants had increased F1 compared to fasting/unknown fed status participants.

## 5.2.2.2.2 Physiology based pharmacokinetic model

PBPK models of povorcitinib based on the available in vitro and in vivo data including clinical PK data were developed to predict DDI liability - study CPP-25.47.1

PBPK model was developed based on data from 2 phase 1 studies (INCB 54707-101 and INCB 54707-104). Consequently, PBPK model was verified on 4 phase 1 studies (INCB 54707-101, INCB 54707-102, INCB 54707-104 and INCB 54707-109).

Minimal PBPK model with an optional single adjusted compartment was used as final PBPK model. Predicted values for PK parameters were in agreement with observed values for PK parameters as all predicted values were within 1.5-fold of observed values.

Final PBPK model was used for prediction of DDIs of povorcitinib 75 mg single dose as CYP3A substrate with weak to moderate CYP3A inhibitors erythromycin 250 mg four times in a day (QID), erythromicyn 500 mg QID, fluconazole 200 mg once daily (QD), cimetidine 400 mg twice a day (BID) and moderate CYP3A inducer efavirenz 600 mg QD. Predicted DDIs had less than 1.25-fold increase for weak inhibitors, from 1.25-fold to 2-fold increase for moderate inhibitors, and from 50% to 80% decrease for moderate inducers.

## 5.2.2.3 Absorption

Absorption of povorcitinib in humans was fast, with median Tmax values from 2 to 4 hours with a delay of app. 2 hours following administration with food.

Based on the one in vitro study conducted in Caco-2 cells monolayer povorcitinib exhibits an apparent permeability (Papp) value of 4.5 × 10-6 cm/sec at 50 μM.

Transport experiments indicated povorcitinib is a P-gp and BCRP substrate.

Povorcitinib exhibits pH-dependent solubility, with low solubility at pH values greater than 3. Nevertheless, a dedicated clinical study (INCB 54707-104) evaluating coadministration with a proton pump inhibitor (esomeprazole 40 mg) demonstrated no clinically meaningful impact on the single-dose PK of povorcitinib.

Absolute bioavailability study for povorcitinib was not performed. Based on mass balance data minimally 60.6% of the drug was absorbed (recovery was 89.7% and 29.1% excreted in faeces as povorcitinib), but most likely around 80-90% of the drug is absorbed as only app. 7% of intact povorcitinib was excreted in faeces in first 48 hours and the remaining amount in later phase most likely due to the biliary excretion and back conversion from metabolite M12.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The overall data, from in vitro experiments and in vivo studies including the mass-balance data, imply moderate high to almost complete drug absorption of povorcitinib.

The effect of food was first evaluated as a part of study INCB 54707-101. Following administration of 30 mg povorcitinib with high fat meal there was slight increase in PK parameters Cmax, AUC0-t, and AUC0-∞ by approximately 10%, 12%, and 12%, respectively and Tmax was app. 2 hours delayed. The data showed negligible impact of food on absorption of povorcitinib.

The effect of a standardised high-fat meal on the absorption of povorcitinib administered in a single dose of 45 mg and 75 mg was evaluated in an open-label, randomised, single-center, cross-over study (INCB 54707-109).

The results of study INCB 54707-109 indicate that the exposure (Cmax, AUC0-t, and AUC0-∞) of povorcitinib was increased approximately by 13%, 14%, and 14% when a dose of 75 mg was administered with a high-fat breakfast as compared to administration in the fasted state. After administration of a single dose of povorcitinib 45 mg, a high-fat meal had negligible effect on povorcitinib exposure, increasing Cmax, AUC0-t and AUC0-∞ by 6%, 8% and 8%, respectively.

Both studies confirmed negligible effect of co-administration with a high-fat meal on povorcitinib PK. No dosage adjustments or time restrictions with regard to meal and drug intake are necessary.

## 5.2.2.4 Bioequivalence

No bioequivalence study was performed. The applicant summarised formulations used during the drug development. In most clinical studies, 15 mg, 45 mg and 75 mg tablets were used with the same excipients and 15 mg and 75 mg were made from common blend.

The main difference between formulations used in the clinical trials and to be marketed formulation is the presence of non-functional film coating; otherwise, the formulations are identical.

## 5.2.2.5 Distribution

Plasma protein binding of povorcitinib was high in man over 90 % of the drug was bound to plasma proteins with fu 6.4%. Similar values were obtained in vitro also in other species tested (rat 5.8% and dog 5.3%)

Povorcitinib has limited distribution into blood cells, with a blood-to-plasma total radioactivity ratio of 0.656 to 0.887.

Volume of distribution calculated based on studies 101 and 102 was moderate (Vz/F: 129-323 L). The typical value of the volume of distribution (Vd/F) for povorcitinib based on PopPK analysis was 285.9 L in patients with HS suggesting broad distribution of povorcitinib into tissues.

Distribution of povorcitinib into skin tissues has been evaluated in the study INCB 54707-112. Both plasma and skin samples were collected. The results of the study confirmed povorcitinib is well distributed to skin tissues and similar concentrations were observed in tissue samples as in plasma for at least 7 days and the same exposure (ratio 0.95). The elimination half-life of povorcitinib in skin (39.9 hours) was also comparable to that of plasma. The concentrations in skin tissues were over IC 50 for IL6 up to 48 hours. At predose of day 10 and at 24 hours (proposed once daily administration) the concentrations were safely above IC 50 for IL6. povorcitinib is highly bound to skin proteins, with an unbound fraction of 4.2% in dermatome (epidermis plus dermis) human skin homogenate.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 5.2.2.6 Metabolism

In vitro metabolic profiling of povorcitinib was performed in human hepatocytes as well as hepatocytes of different animal species (see non-clinical section). Based on in vitro investigations povorcitinib was found to be predominantly metabolised by CYP3A4 with lesser amount metabolised by UGT1A3,4.

## In vivo metabolism

Based on the mass-balance study (INCB 54707-103) results it can be concluded that the majority of the recovered radioactivity was characterised.

The exposure to the parent drug accounted for approximately 69.3% of circulating plasma total radioactivity based on AUC(0-t)/MW.

One major metabolite in plasma was observed, M12 (N-glucuronidation of the dimethyl pyrazole moiety), accounting for 25.9% of total plasma radioactivity was the most abundant metabolite. No other metabolite accounted for more than 10% of the total plasma radioactivity. The other identified circulating metabolites were M1 (1.6%), M3 (2%) and M22 (1.1%).

In excreta parent povorcitinib was the predominant drug-related moiety accounting for 36.2% and the most abundant metabolite was M3 (hydroxylation of the dimethyl bipyrazole moiety) accounting for 11.7% (5.5% in urine and 6.2% in faeces) of the total administered radioactive dose. The most abundant metabolite in urine is metabolite M12 and this metabolite was not detected in faeces most likely due to back conversion to parent drug in the intestine.

## 5.2.2.7 Elimination

A radiolabelled mass balance study INCB 54707-103 was conducted under fasting conditions in 7 healthy subjects. The selected dose 75 mg is the higher therapeutically proposed dose, and the design is considered acceptable to assess the ADME of povorcitinib.

The total recovery of radioactivity was 89.7% almost reaching 90% recommended in the EMA guideline and is considered adequate. Most of the circulating material was identified.

Majority of the drug was recovered in faeces (59.2%) and 30.6% were recovered in urine. povorcitinib was the predominant drug related material in excreta.

Most of the faecal recovery of povorcitinib was recovered at later time points of this study (i.e., due to the biliary excretion of the drug and its metabolites and not due to the unabsorbed drug). In first 48 hours 7.7% of radioactivity was recovered.

Intact povorcitinib was the most abundant analyte detected in human excreta (7.1% in urine and 29.1% in faeces). The most abundant metabolite in human excreta was metabolite M3 accounting for 11.7% of drug related material (5.5% in urine and 6.2% in faeces).

The elimination half-life ranged from 27 to 35 hours in clinical trials.

## 5.2.2.8 Dose proportionality and time dependency

Three phase I studies provided clinical PK data relevant for the assessment of linearity of PK of povorcitinib:

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Study INCB 54707-101 - was first in human ascending dose study evaluating a single-dose administration of doses from 6 mg up to 405 mg. The number of subjects (8) per treatment group was adequate for this type of study. PK of povorcitinib was tested in broad range of single doses starting from 6 mg going up to 405 mg. The PK parameters AUC and Cmax increased linearly with increasing dose up to 150 mg and slightly less than dose proportional increase was observed at higher doses.

Study INCB 54707-102 - was a multiple-ascending dose study evaluating once-daily administration at doses 30 mg, 60 mg, or 120 mg. The PK parameters were evaluated following first dose and at steady state at day 10. The study design was appropriate. Following multiple doses 30, 60 and 120 mg the exposure increased in linear manner with maximal plasma levels slightly less than dose proportional in the highest dose tested of 120 mg. The results of the study showed povorcitinib accumulates following once daily dosing with Rac app. 2.5 (2.2- to 2.6-fold increase). The accumulation was similar at different dose levels tested. The steady state was achieved at day 9.

Study INCB 54707-108 - similar trend has been seen in PK in this study in healthy Japanese participants at the two dose levels tested 45 mg and 90 mg the increase in PK was dose proportional.

The PK of povorcitinib is considered linear in therapeutic dose range and linearity can be concluded up to 225 mg following single dose administration.

## 5.2.2.9 Pharmacokinetics in the target population

The PK data in target patient population with HS were collected in PK population in both main phase 3 studies and in three phase 2 studies. The sparse data collected were evaluated in the popPK analysis and average exposure data were generated and compared with healthy subjects data. There were no significant differences in PK observed between healthy subject population and target patient population. The PK data generated in healthy subjects are well applicable to target population.
