## 5.2.2.10 Special population

The effect of gender on PK was not identified as a significant covariate in the population analysis.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

No dose adjustments are needed based on gender.

The applicant conducted a study in healthy Japanese subjects (108) to evaluate PK and potential differences in this population. Two dose levels were tested 45 mg and 90 mg after both single and repeated dosing. The PK were comparable with data obtained from previously conducted studies (101, 102) in predominantly Caucasian subjects.

In the popPK analysis impact of race on povorcitinib PK was evaluated in dataset of patients with HS. The exposures were comparable across race (ie, White, Black or African American, and Asian, Japanese and non-Japanese participants).

No dose modification based on race/ethnicity is required.

The effect of bodyweight was tested in popPK analysis, as expected, exposure decreased with increasing bodyweight, but the differences are of a small magnitude and can be considered not clinically relevant, no dose adjustments based on bodyweight are necessary.

The effect of age was tested in popPK analysis and was not identified as a significant covariate. Also, no dose modification is needed in patients with decreased renal functions that are common in elderly patients. No dose modification is needed in this population.

## Renal impairment

The effect of renal impairment on PK of povorcitinib was evaluated in a dedicated single-dose study in patients with severe renal impairment and patients with ESRD on hemodialysis. In the severe renal impairment group, absorption was similar (median tmax approximately 2.5-3 hours). Modest decrease in Cmax of 21% and modest increase in AUC0-inf of 20% was observed in patients with severe renal impairment versus matched normal renal function control. Participants with severe impairment exhibited a longer terminal half-life (geometric mean 51.7 vs. 35.5 hours) and slightly lower apparent oral clearance (CL/F; 4.28 vs. 5.15 L/h). Urinary PK demonstrated low renal excretion overall (fraction excreted unchanged in urine approximately 3-7%) and a decline in renal clearance with decreasing renal function (e.g., CLR ~0.347 L/h in normal vs. ~0.152 L/h in severe impairment over the 0-144 h window), supporting that renal clearance is not a major route of elimination for povorcitinib. Plasma protein binding was independent of renal function.

Povorcitinib plasma exposures in the ESRD group were approximately 31% to 36% lower for Cmax and 26% to 40% lower for AUCs compared with the healthy-matched participants. Comparison of PK exposures between ESRD before hemodialysis and ESRD after hemodialysis indicates that timing of hemodialysis had no impact on the PK of povorcitinib. Less than 1% of the dose administered was removed by dialysis.

## Hepatic impairment

To evaluate the effect of hepatic impairment on the exposure of povorcitinib, a single-dose parallel group study (INCB 54707-105) was conducted in patients with moderate and severe hepatic impairment. The exposure of povorcitinib was comparable in participants with moderate hepatic impairment and participants with normal hepatic function and no dose adjustment is recommended.

In participants with severe impairment, total povorcitinib Cmax was approximately 20% lower and similar AUCs when compared to healthy participants with normal hepatic function. There was approximately 75% increase in unbound fraction of povorcitinib in plasma. As a result, plasma exposure of unbound povorcitinib was approximately 40% to 76% higher compared with participants with normal hepatic function. For participants with severe hepatic impairment the maximum recommended dose is 45 mg povorcitinib per day.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 5.2.2.11 Pharmacokinetic interaction studies

## PK drug-drug interactions

## In vitro

Povorcitinib showed no clinically relevant inhibition of major CYP enzymes; weak CYP and UGT inhibition observed at supratherapeutic concentrations did not meet ICH M12 thresholds at the clinically relevant dose of 75 mg. A formal signal for potential intestinal CYP3A4 inhibition cannot be excluded based on in vitro data, although this was not considered clinically meaningful. Povorcitinib did not induce CYP1A2, CYP2B6 or CYP3A4. A ≥2-fold increase in CYP3A4 mRNA was observed in a single donor at 0.1 and 0.5 µM; however, the effect was not concentration-dependent. A concentration-dependent decrease in CYP2B6 mRNA expression was noted across donors at supratherapeutic concentrations (≥5 µM); given the absence of cytotoxicity and the exposure margin relative to clinical concentrations, this finding was considered non-specific and not indicative of a clinically relevant DDI risk. Although the N-glucuronide metabolite M12 was a major circulating metabolite, no dedicated DDI studies were conducted for this metabolite. It is considered pharmacologically inactive and unlikely to inhibit or induce CYP or UGT enzymes; therefore, it is not expected to contribute to clinically relevant DDIs. Transporter studies showed that povorcitinib is a substrate of P-gp and BCRP, but not of hepatic or renal uptake transporters. PBPK modelling and clinical data indicate that intestinal efflux transporters have a limited impact on povorcitinib absorption. In vitro data identified povorcitinib as an inhibitor of P-gp, BCRP and MATE1, whereas inhibition of the other evaluated transporters was less pronounced. The potential for transporter-mediated drug interactions was further investigated in dedicated clinical and modelling studies. Povorcitinib was not investigated as a substrate or inhibitor of OCT1. However, based on the totality of safety information and a positive signal for OCT2 inhibition, OCT1 inhibition experiments are not warranted. Additionally, povorcitinib as BSEP inhibitor was also not tested. However, povorcitinib's molecule class and safety profile do not suggest a specific concern for BSEP inhibition or cholestatic liver signals. In conclusion, at a clinically relevant dose of 75 mg, povorcitinib has the potential to cause clinical drug interactions involving P-gp and BCRP inhibition in the gut, but not systemically, as well as inhibition of OCT2 and MATE1 transporters.

## In vivo

Based on positive signals from in vitro studies, the potential of povorcitinib to cause or to be subject of DDIs was investigated in three clinical studies (INCB 54707-104, INCB 54707-110 and INCB 54707-111). The effect of strong CYP3A4 inhibitor and inducer, PPI and UGT inhibitor probenecid on povorcitinib PK was investigated. Moreover, inhibitory potential of povorcitinib on P-gp, BCRP and OCT2/MATE transporters was evaluated. Additionally, since povorcitinib is also intended for women of child-bearing potential, the possible DDI with oral contraceptives containing LNG and EE was also assessed in study INCB 54707-111.

## Povorcitinib as a victim

Administration after multiple doses of a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor (itraconazole) did not have a clinically important impact on povorcitinib Cmax but significantly increased AUC0-t and AUC0-inf, with GMRs (90% CIs) of 1.88 (1.75, 2.02) and 1.83 (1.70, 1.97), respectively. The elimination half-life increased from 31.8 hours when povorcitinib was administered alone to 42.9 hours when administered with itraconazole. There was no significant change in povorcitinib tmax. Based on the results, the recommendation to reduce povorcitinib dose to 45 mg once daily for patients receiving chronic treatment with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors is therefore proposed. The effect of moderate and weak CYP3A4 inhibitors was predicted using PBPK modelling approach and based on the predictions, no dose adjustment is recommended.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The effect of multiple doses of a strong CYP3A4 inducer, rifampin, on the single-dose of povorcitinib was investigated in a fixed-sequence study. Co-administration of rifampin significantly decreased povorcitinib Cmax, AUC0-t, and AUC0-∞, with GMRs (90% CIs) of 0.542 (0.501, 0.586), 0.203 (0.191, 0.216), and 0.198 (0.186, 0.212), respectively, and led to the decrease in elimination half-life from 27.8 hours to 10.5 hours. Tmax was unaffected. The magnitude of observed effect supports proposed labelling recommendations to avoid co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inducers. Additionally, the effect of moderate CYP3A4 inducers was predicted in PBPK simulation and no dose adjustment is proposed by the applicant.

The effect of PPIs and probenecid on the exposure of povorcitinib was minimal and not considered clinically relevant.

## Povorcitinib as a perpetrator

When co-administered with P-gp sensitive substrate, digoxin, povorcitinib increased digoxin Cmax, AUC0t, and AUC0-∞, with GMRs (90% CIs) of 1.38 (1.14, 1.67), 1.26 (1.12, 1.41), and 1.10 (1.05, 1.14), respectively. The observed increase in exposure was not considered as clinically significant by the applicant.

Administration of rosuvastatin alone or in combination with a single dose of povorcitinib resulted in overall comparable rosuvastatin exposure, indicating no impact of povorcitinib on BCRP substrates. Similarly, administration of OCT2/MATE2-K substrate metformin alone or co-administered with povorcitinib in a steady-state resulted in comparable metformin AUC0-t and AUC0-inf between the 2 treatments and Cmax reduced by approximately 11%. Negligible impact of povorcitinib on metformin PK was observed when co-administered.

The effect of multiple doses of povorcitinib on the single-dose PK of LNG and EE was evaluated in study INCB 5477-111. Following a single-dose of combined oral contraceptive with and without administration of povorcitinib, the LNG Cmax was approximately 15% lower when co-administered with povorcitinib and AUCs were comparable between the two treatments. The plasma levels of EE were unaffected by povorcitinib administration.

## 5.2.3 Pharmacodynamics

## 5.2.3.1 Mechanism of action

Povorcitinib selectively inhibits Janus kinase (JAK) 1. JAK1 is a member of the JAK family of intracellular enzymes, which also includes JAK2, JAK3, and tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2). JAKs transmit signals arising from cytokine- or growth factor-receptor interactions on the cell membrane. Within the signalling pathway, JAKs phosphorylate and activate signal transducers and activators of transcription (STATs) which modulate gene expression. This influences cellular processes of immune cell function and haematopoiesis depending on the specific JAK isoforms involved. Povorcitinib modulates the JAK1 signalling pathway, preventing the phosphorylation and activation of associated STATs. Povorcitinib inhibits signalling by JAK1-dependent cytokines (such as IL-6, IL-2, IL-22) thereby attenuating skin and systemic inflammation relevant to HS.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 5.2.3.2 Primary and secondary pharmacology

## PD studies in healthy subjects

In healthy volunteer studies (INCB 54707-101,102), the effect of povorcitinib on cytokine-stimulated pSTAT3 following single and multiple ascending doses was evaluated. The results showed a more pronounced inhibition of IL-6-stimulated pSTAT3 compared to TPO-induced pSTAT3, indicating selectivity for JAK1 over JAK2. The inhibition was dose-dependent and peaked around maximum plasma levels of povorcitinib (1-6 hours following administration of drug).

## PD studies in patients with HS

In addition to the clinical endpoints and PK assessments performed in the context of INCB 54707-204, -301 and -302 studies, exploratory analyses were conducted to provide mechanistic and biological insights into the PD effects of JAK1-pathway inhibition by povorcitinib. For these analyses, serum samples were analysed using Olink Target 48 and Olink Explore proteomic panels.

In the Target 48 assay, reductions were observed in a broad range of markers, including chemokines, cytokines and proteases.

In the Explore assay, a wide range of markers were reduced, including markers of T cell and NK cell activation (e.g. IL-2RA and granzyme B), markers related to B cell activation BAFF and CXCL13, the neutrophil marker lipocalin-2 (LCN2), proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines (e.g., TNFα, LTA, CCL19, IL-12, IL-19), as well as proteases involved in tissue remodelling.

Using the values extracted from the clinical laboratory dataset, decreases from baseline in highsensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), an inflammatory marker induced by IL-6 signaling through the JAK-1 pathway, were observed with povorcitinib already at 3 weeks (i.e. first study visit in INCB 54707-301 and -302 studies).

## Effects of povorcitinib on the QT interval duration

A dedicated study (INCB 54707-107) was conducted to evaluate the effect of therapeutic (225 mg) and supra-therapeutic (450 mg) single doses of povorcitinib on the QTc interval in ECGs from healthy volunteers with control arms placebo and the active comparator moxifloxacine 400 mg.

Using concentration-QTc analysis, a QTcF effect exceeding 10 ms could be excluded within the observed range of povorcitinib plasma concentrations. The study results fulfilled the requirements to conclude that povorcitinib meets the ICH E14 criteria for a negative QT/QTc study since the upper limits of two-sided 90% CI for povorcitinib-placebo difference in QTcF prolongation at all post-dose time points were below 10 msec.

## 5.2.3.3 Pharmacodynamic interactions with other medicinal products or substances

No clinical studies to evaluate the pharmacodynamic interactions with other medicinal products or substances have been submitted.

## 5.2.3.4 Genetic differences in PD response

No data on genetic differences in PD response has been provided.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 5.2.3.5 Immunological events

Not applicable.

## 5.2.4 Pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD)

Two exposure-response analysis evaluating the two dose levels 45 mg and 75 mg and impact of exposure on efficacy and safety were presented by the applicant:

## Study CPP-25.45.1

This study investigated exposure-response relationship at Week 12 during placebo-controlled treatment period for two efficacy endpoints (reduction by HiSCR50 and reduction by Skin Pain NRS30) and for two safety endpoints (acne, and infections and infestations). Efficacy endpoints were investigated in two populations (full analysis population, post-anti-TNF population) and safety endpoints were investigated in three safety populations (1, 1b, 2). All these endpoints were assessed by logistic regression model (LRM) with parameter estimates based on Bayesian methodology.

In case of both efficacy endpoints, it was concluded based on 95% credible interval (CrI) for odds ratio (OR) that 1) each dose (45 mg and 75 mg) had significantly higher odds to achieve reduction than placebo (PBO) in both populations and that 2) dose 75 mg had significantly higher odds to achieve reduction than dose 45 mg in both populations. Significances were achieved based on the fact that 95% CrI for OR had all values higher than 1.

Regarding the safety endpoint acne, it was concluded based on 95% CrI for OR that 1) each dose (45 mg and 75 mg) had significantly higher odds of getting acne than PBO in safety populations 1 and 2, and that 2) dose 75 mg had significantly higher odds of getting acne than dose 45 mg in all safety populations.

Regarding the safety endpoint infections and infestations (IN), it was concluded based on 95% CrI for OR that 1) each dose (45 mg and 75 mg) had significantly higher odds of getting IN than PBO only in safety populations 1 and 2, and that 2) dose 75 mg had significantly higher odds of getting IN than dose 45 mg in safety populations 1 and 2. Significances were achieved based on fact that 95% CrI for OR had all values higher than 1.

Lastly, observed and estimated percentage of acne event from LRM both for PBO and povorcitinib doses (45 mg and 75 mg) was generally much lower that percentage of IN event.

In conclusion, reduction given by efficacy endpoints (HiSCR50, Skin Pain NRS30) was significantly more probable for povorcitinib dose than for PBO and more probable for dose 75 mg than for dose 45 mg. Similarly, adverse event (acne, and infections and infestations) was in most cases significantly more probable for povorcitinib dose than for PBO and more probable for dose 75 mg than for dose 45 mg.

## Study CPP-25.50.1

This study investigated relationship between povorcitinib exposure and clinical efficacy responses derived based on draining tunnel count (DTC) over 12-week treatment period. Derived endpoints were given by percentage decrease in DTC count (DT50 - at least 50%, DT75 - at least 75%, DT100 - at least 100%) and by 1-unit increase in DTC count (worsening of disease).

Based 90% confidence interval (CI) for OR, there was not statistically significant difference between dose 75 mg and 45 mg for all investigated endpoints (DT50, DT75, DT100, worsening of disease) for each used baseline DTC category (1-4 or ≥5). In this case, 90% CI for OR included 1 which meant that both higher odds and lower odds for achievement of DT50/DT75/DT100/worsening of disease for dose 75 mg compared to 45 mg could not be excluded.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

On the other hand, it was concluded based on 90% CI for OR that there was significantly higher odds of getting DTC decrease for dose 75 mg compared to PBO for endpoints DT50, DT75 and DT100 for each used baseline DTC category (1-4 or ≥5) as all values of 90% CI for OR were higher than 1. In case that DTC ≥5 was used, significantly lower odds of worsening disease was concluded for dose 75 mg compared to PBO as all values of 90% for OR were lower than 1. There were also additional significant differences which were not, however, common for majority of investigated endpoints and not for both baseline DTC categories (1-4 or ≥5). These additional significances were for comparison of dose 45 mg vs. PBO in case of DTC 1-4 for DT75 (higher odds of decrease for dose) and worsening of disease (lower odds of worsening for dose) and in case of DTC ≥5 for DT50 (higher odds of decrease for dose), DT75 (higher odds of decrease for dose) and worsening of disease (lower odds of worsening for dose).

Lastly, values of OR alone reflected that 1) odds of decrease in DTC was higher for both doses compared to PBO and for dose 75 mg compared to dose 45 mg, and 2) odds of increase in DTC was lower for both doses compared to PBO and for dose 75 mg compared to 45 mg.

In conclusion, DTC decrease was rather related with povorcitinib dose than with PBO and worsening of disease was rather related to PBO than to dose. There was not significant difference between dose 75 mg and 45 mg.

## 5.2.5 Dose selection and therapeutic window

The recommended dose is 45 mg or 75 mg once daily based on individual patient characteristics.

Exposure-response analysis was conducted to evaluate dose dependency of efficacy and safety.

Based on the results for both proposed strengths statistically significant improvement compared to placebo can be concluded. A minor, but statistically significant improvement for 75 mg strength vs. 45 mg was also seen, i.e. odds Ratios were 1.05 for HiSCR50 and 1.08 Skin Pain NRS30 in the full analysis population and 1.13 and 1.18, respectively, in the post-anti-TNF population.

E-R analysis for Draining Tunnel count showed positive trend with increasing dose/exposure and the difference was most pronounced in participants with a baseline dT counts ≥ 5 favouring 75 mg dose in these patients.

Evaluation of safety endpoints acne, and infections and infestations showed higher posterior probability that 75 mg was connected more with these events compared to 45 mg.

To conclude there is similar efficacy and safety for both doses with positive pattern for several endpoints for higher dose of 75 mg and some subpopulation can benefit from the higher dose.

## 5.2.6 Overall discussion and conclusions on clinical pharmacology

## 5.2.6.1 Discussion

The clinical pharmacology program consisted of 12 clinical studies including single and multiple ascending dose studies (INCB 54707-101, INCB 54707-102), mass-balance study (INCB 54707-103), food effect study (INCB 54707-109), drug-drug interaction studies (INCB 54707-104, INCB 54707-

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

110, INCB 54707-111), studies in patients with hepatic and renal impairment (INCB 54707-105, INCB 54707-106), an ascending dose PK study in Japanese participants (INCB 54707-

108), QT/QTc study (INCB 54707-107), skin PK study (INCB 54707-112) and 2 population PK studies (CPP-25.44.1, DMB-19.205.11) and PBPK study (CPP-25.47.1).

## Bioanalytics

The povorcitinib clinical development program included bioanalytical methods for the quantification of povorcitinib in plasma, skin, and dialysate. Cross-validation of the plasma analytical methods was performed supporting the comparability and reliability of the analytical results across laboratories. Overall, the validated PK analytical methods are considered fit for purpose, and the resulting PK data are deemed reliable and suitable to support the clinical evaluation of povorcitinib.

The bioanalytical methods applied in the DDI and QT/QTc studies were validated LC/MS/MS methods. The validation data for these assays were considered adequate and the analytical performance acceptable.

The applicant sufficiently clarified the analytical platforms used for exploratory pharmacodynamic biomarker analyses and described the validation, quality control and measures implemented to ensure data reliability, supported by extensive documentation.

ADME: Absorption of povorcitinib was fast, with a Tmax seen in most of studies from 2-4h.

No data about the absolute bioavailability of povorcitinib are provided since no IV formulation was developed and utilised within the clinical pharmacology program. However, the overall data, from in vitro experiments and in vivo animal and human including the mass-balance data, imply moderate high to almost complete drug absorption of povorcitinib, consistent with its classification as a BCS Class II, with limited impact of efflux transport processes in the intestine.

The data from studies INCB 54707-101 and INCB 54707-109 showed negligible impact of food on absorption of povorcitinib. In the pivotal phase III studies INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 povorcitinib 45 or 75 mg tablets were administered orally at approximately the same time each day either with or without food. The recommendation in SmPC Section 4.2 that povorcitinib tablets may be taken with or without food is therefore supported.

No bioequivalence study was performed. In most of the clinical studies 15 mg, 45 mg and 75 mg tablets were used with the same excipients and 15 mg and 75 mg were made from common blend. The main difference between formulations used in the clinical trials and to be marketed formulation is the presence of non-functional film coating otherwise the formulations were identical. Dissolution data are sufficient to support this minor change in formulation, and no BE study is needed (also see section on quality aspects).

The PK of povorcitinib can be considered linear in therapeutic dose range and linearity can be concluded up to 225 mg following single dose administration with slightly less than dose proportional increase in higher doses.

Povorcitinib accumulates following once daily dosing with Rac app. 2.5 (2.2-to 2.6-fold increase). The accumulation was similar at different dose levels tested. The steady state was achieved within day 9.

Plasma protein binding of povorcitinib was high in man over 90 % of the drug was bound to plasma proteins with average fraction unbound (fu) 6.7%. Two ex vivo studies (DMB-23.163, DMB-24.91) evaluated plasma protein binding in healthy subjects and in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, reporting an average fraction unbound of 6.2%-6.7%.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The typical value of the volume of distribution (Vd/F) for povorcitinib based on PopPK analysis was 285.9 L in patients with HS suggesting broad distribution of povorcitinib into tissues. Povorcitinib is broadly distributed to skin tissues and similar concentrations were observed in tissue samples as in plasma.

Based on in vitro investigations povorcitinib was found to be predominantly metabolised by CYP3A4 with lesser amount metabolised by UGT1A3 and UGT1A4. The radiolabelled mass balance study study INCB 54707-103 was acceptable in terms of study design and data obtained. The exposure to the parent drug accounted for approximately 69.3% of circulating plasma total radioactivity and one major metabolite in plasma was observed, M12 (N-glucuronidation of the dimethyl pyrazole moiety), accounting for 25.9% of total plasma radioactivity.

The PK properties of metabolites of povorcitinib were not discussed and no data were provided by the applicant. Nevertheless, M12 is an N-glucuronide and is considered pharmacologically inactive; furthermore, it is not expected to inhibit or induce CYP or UGT enzymes. Therefore, the absence of quantitative plasma exposure data for M12 is not considered to impact the interpretation of the PK or DDI assessments for povorcitinib.

Majority of the drug was recovered in faeces 59.2% and 30.6% were recovered in urine. Povorcitinib was the predominant drug related material in excreta.

The elimination half-life of povorcitinib was app. 32 hours.

In conclusion, the conducted mass-balance study is considered acceptable in terms of its study design and data obtained. The information provided in SmPC section 5.2 is adequate.

Povorcitinib possesses a chiral center, but chiral inversion of S-povorcitinib to R-enantiomer is improbable under in vivo conditions.

## Genetic polymorphism

Povorcitinib is predominantly metabolised by CYP3A4, an enzyme not affected by genetic polymorphism. Minor contributions to povorcitinib metabolism are mediated by UGT1A4 and UGT1A3, both of which are polymorphic. However, given the limited role of these UGTs in overall povorcitinib clearance, the clinical impact of their genetic variability is expected to be minimal (see in vivo DDI section). Accordingly, the risk of clinically significant variability due to genetic polymorphisms is considered low.

## Population PK

The applicant developed two popPK models in healthy adults and patients with HS to investigate impact of covariates: DMB-19.205.1 and CPP-25.44.1.

The first popPK model study DMB-19.205.1 was based on limited number of studies (data from 4 studies included) and was followed by a second study (CPP-25.44.1) which included PK data from all performed trials.

In study CPP-25.44.1, the development of popPK model was based on data from 12 Phase 1 studies (INCB 54707-101, -102, -103, -104, -105, -106, -107, -108, -109, -110, -111, and -112), 5 Phase 2 studies (INCB 54707-202, -203, -204, -205, and -206), and 2 Phase 3 studies (INCB 54707-301 and -302). These studies included participants with HS, prurigo nodularis, vitiligo and healthy participants.

The data for the popPK analysis included 2029 participants (pooled from 19 studies) contributing 14,202 povorcitinib concentration measurements following povorcitinib doses ranging from 6 to 225 mg. Out of 2029 participants, 1352 participants were HS patients (66.63%). Out of 14202 samples,

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

831 samples were BLQ samples (5.85%) and these samples were excluded during the model development which is considered acceptable by the CHMP. The dataset is considered of appropriate size for the purpose of describing PK in the HS target population.

The covariates distributions are considered reasonable with respect to demographic variables such as age (median: 38 years, range: 18 to 81 years), body weight (median: 89 kg, range: 42.1 to 228 kg), sex (out of 2029 participants, 1167 females [42.48%] and 862 males [57.52%]) and race (out of 2029 participants, 1443 Whites [71.12%], 333 Blacks or African Americans [16.41%], 115 Asians [5.67%], 92 American Indians/Alaskan Natives/Native Hawaiians/Pacific Islanders/other [4.53%] and 46 unknowns [2.27%]).

Out of 2029 participants, limited number of subjects had moderate (8 participants, 0.39%) or severe (no participant) hepatic impairment, as well as moderate (17 participants, 0.84%) or severe (13 participants, 0.64%) renal impairment. Nevertheless, the impact of renal and hepatic impairment on povorcitinib PK has been evaluated in dedicated studies.

Out of 2029 participants, number of participants taking mild (35 participants, 1.72%), moderate (19 participants, 0.94%) and strong (1 participant, 0.05%) CYP3A4 inducers was limited. Similarly, out of 2029 participants, number of participants taking moderate (19 participants, 0.94%) and strong (1 participant, 0.05%) CYP3A4 inhibitors was also limited. Number of participants taking mild CYP3A4 inhibitors (217 participants, 10.69%) and number of participants taking proton pump inhibitor (199 participants, 9.81%) were relatively high.

The effects of concomitant administration of strong CYP3A4 inducers and inhibitors, as well as proton pump inhibitors were evaluated in a dedicated study.

The final popPK model was two-compartment disposition model with linear elimination and a fivetransit compartment absorption model. Covariates in population PK model included body weight (BW), participant population (HS, prurigo nodularis [PN], vitiligo [VO], healthy), IGFR, total bilirubin, fed status (yes vs. no/unknown) and race (Japanese vs. Non-Japanese). Covariate modelling approach is considered appropriate. Goodness-of-fit plots do not indicate any model misspecification, and the provided model provides good description of povorcitinib data. Final popPK model parameters were estimated with good precision both for fixed effects and for random effects.

Based on final popPK model, values of shrinkage for IIV of V2/F (45.5%), V3/F (71.8%) and KTR (42.8%), respectively, were higher than 30% compared to shrinkage for IIV of CL/F (5.65%) which could have impact on predictions. High shrinkage values for V2/F, V3/F, and KTR, respectively, were likely due to the large number of sparse PK samples from Phase 2 and 3 studies. However, individual predicted concentrations and population predicted concentrations obtained from final popPK model were in relatively good agreement with observed concentrations not only across all participants (HS, PN, VO, healthy) but also for HS participants. The same was concluded by prediction-corrected visual predictive check graphs (pcVPCs) from final popPK model as majority of observed concentrations was covered by range from 5th to 95th percentile derived from simulated concentrations. Thus, high shrinkage values for V2/F, V3/F and KTR is not considered problematic for prediction.

Nevertheless, since BW was found to be influential covariate on povorcitinib exposure, pcVPCs stratified by body weight groups were provided. They confirmed that the popPK model adequately describes observed concentrations across the full body weight range.

The model is considered to be sufficient for its intended purpose, i.e. to investigate PK and impact of covariates in patients with HS. Estimated covariate effects were modest.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## PK in target population

There were no significant differences in PK observed between healthy subject population and HS target patient population. The PK data generated in healthy subjects are well applicable to HS target population.

## Special populations

The effect of gender, ethnicity on PK was not identified as a significant covariate in the population analysis. No dose adjustments are needed.

Body weight inversely affected povorcitinib exposure. At the lower end of body weight range investigated (45 kg, 10th percentile) Cmax,ss was 1.36-fold higher than for the 97 kg reference patient. The applicant also simulated povorcitinib exposures for patients weighing 30-40 kg and, in those patients, predicted Cmax,ss was 1.5-fold higher than for the reference patient. This increase in exposure is within observed PK variability and is not considered clinically relevant, therefore no dose adjustments are required based on bodyweight.

Additionally, simulations of povorcitinib Cavg,ss were conducted at the 95th, 97.5th, 99th percentile and at the maximum observed body weight (228 kg). It is agreed that reduction in exposure at the upper body weight extremes (up to 0.82-fold) is modest and does not require dose adjustment.

The effect of age was tested in popPK analysis and was not identified as a significant covariate. Also, no dose modification is needed in patients with decreased renal functions that are common in elderly patients. Therefore, no dose modification would be needed in elderly population based on these data. However, from the safety point of view and in line with the Art. 20 referral, the use of lower 45 mg dose is recommended for elderly patients (see discussion on clinical safety).

## Renal impairment

The effect of renal impairment was assessed in subjects with severe renal impairment and with endstage renal disease (ESRD) on hemodialysis. The results showed modest changes in exposure for severe impairment (slightly lower Cmax (21% lower), AUC0-inf increased by 20%) and lower exposure in ESRD (Cmax reduced by 31-36%, AUC reduced by 26-40%). Dialysis contributed minimally to drug removal (&lt;1% of the dose) and timing of haemodialysis had no impact on the povorcitinib PK. No dose adjustment has been proposed by the applicant for patients with severe renal impairment, and none is deemed necessary based on the available data. There is no safety concern detected for patients with ESRD.

## Hepatic impairment

Moderate hepatic impairment had no clinically relevant impact on total or unbound povorcitinib exposure, with Cmax and AUC values comparable to those in subjects with normal hepatic function. No adjustment is needed for moderate impairment. Although no clinically meaningful change in total plasma povorcitinib exposure was observed in patients with severe hepatic impairment, the unbound fraction increased by about 75%, resulting in unbound povorcitinib exposure increased by approximately 40%, 68%, and 76% for Cmax,u, AUC0-t,u, and AUC0-inf,u, respectively. This information is adequately stated in SmPC section 5.2, and the posology is restricted in subjects with severe hepatic impairment in SmPC section 4.2 to 45 mg dose QD, which is supported.

## Pharmacokinetic DDI

## In vitro

Overall, the available in vitro data indicate a low potential for clinically relevant CYP- or UGT-mediated perpetrator drug-drug interactions. Povorcitinib did not show clinically relevant inhibition or induction of major CYP enzymes at exposures relevant to the clinical dose, and weak CYP and UGT inhibition observed at supratherapeutic concentrations did not exceed ICH M12 thresholds. The major circulating metabolite M12 is considered pharmacologically inactive and is not expected to contribute to clinically relevant CYP- or UGT-mediated interactions. In vitro transporter studies identified P-gp, BCRP and MATE1 as the main potential transporter-mediated interaction pathways, whereas inhibition of other evaluated transporters was less pronounced.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## In vivo

Clinical DDI studies demonstrate that povorcitinib is sensitive to modulation of CYP3A4 activity. Coadministration with itraconazole increased povorcitinib AUC0-inf by 83% and prolonged elimination half-life (from 32 to 43 hours), while the absence of changes in Cmax or tmax indicates that inhibition of intestinal P-gp or BCRP does not affect the rate of absorption. The SmPC recommends reducing the povorcitinib dose to 45 mg once daily when combined with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. This is agreed.

The effect of moderate and weak CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, fluconazole and cimetidine) was evaluated using a PBPK model, which predicted increases in povorcitinib exposure of up to approximately 1.7-fold with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors. The SmPC includes information on the increase in povorcitinib exposure when co-administered with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors. No dose adjustment is recommended for moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, as the currently available data are not considered sufficient to support a specific dose reduction. Rifampin, a strong CYP3A4 inducer, markedly reduced exposure (Cmax decreased by approx.46%, AUC decreased by ~80%, half-life shortened to ~10.5 hours), supporting the SmPC recommendation to avoid co-administration with strong inducers. The effect of moderate CYP3A4 inducer (efavirenz) was evaluated using a PBPK model. In view of the PBPK-predicted reduction in povorcitinib exposure following co-administration with moderate systemic CYP3A4 inducers (approximately 15% and 58% decrease in Cmax and AUC, respectively), recommendation to monitor for changes in disease activity has been added to the SmPC by the applicant and is agreed. Povorcitinib exhibits pH-dependent solubility, with low solubility at pH values greater than 3. Nevertheless, a dedicated clinical study (INCB 54707-104) evaluating co-administration with a proton pump inhibitor esomeprazole 40 mg demonstrated no clinically relevant impact on the single-dose PK of povorcitinib. Accordingly, no warning is included in the SmPC, which is considered acceptable. UGT1A4 inhibitor probenecid decreased povorcitinib exposure by about 25% (AUC) and 18% (Cmax), which is not considered clinically relevant and therefore no dose modification is proposed in the SmPC.

As a perpetrator, povorcitinib showed weak intestinal P-gp inhibition, increasing digoxin exposure by 38% (Cmax) and 26% (AUC0-t) after a single dose. Although systemic inhibition was considered unlikely based on in vitro data, the borderline increase observed after a single dose and in the absence of multiple-dose data, a more pronounced inhibitory effect at steady state cannot be excluded. Accordingly, the SmPC has been updated to include a precautionary statement advising caution when povorcitinib is co-administered with P-gp substrates with a narrow therapeutic index.

Povorcitinib did not significantly affect rosuvastatin (BCRP substrate) or metformin (OCT2/MATEs substrate) exposure, and no dose restrictions in the SmPC are therefore warranted. Although the rosuvastatin study was conducted as a single-dose, the absence of any increase in rosuvastatin exposure, together with the lack of an in vitro signal indicating systemic BCRP inhibition, support that the single-dose data are sufficient to exclude a clinically relevant interaction. Therefore, while the study does not fully capture potential steady-state effects, this limitation is not further pursued, as the totality of evidence does not indicate a systemic inhibitory risk. Similarly, co-administration with oral contraceptives containing levonorgestrel and ethinyl estradiol did not result in clinically meaningful changes in exposure, supporting that no dose restrictions are required.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Pharmacodynamics

The mechanism of action of povorcitinib has been sufficiently characterised. The STAT3 transcription factor is directly phosphorylated by JAKs in response to cytokine stimulation and can be used as a pharmacodynamic marker for JAK activation levels. In healthy volunteer studies, the applicant evaluated the effect of povorcitinib on cytokine-stimulated pSTAT3 following single and multiple ascending doses. The results showed a more pronounced inhibition of IL-6-stimulated pSTAT3 compared to TPO-induced pSTAT3, indicating selectivity for JAK1 over JAK2. The inhibition was dosedependent and peaked around maximum plasma levels of povorcitinib (1-6 hours following administration of drug). This information was considered clinically relevant for prescribers and hence its inclusion in SmPC section 5.1 was agreed.

In addition, as part of the INCB 54707-204, -301 and -302 studies, exploratory analyses of several biomarkers were conducted to provide mechanistic and biological insights into the PD effects of JAK1pathway inhibition by povorcitinib that are relevant for HS. Decreases from baseline in hs-CRP, an inflammatory marker induced by IL-6 signaling through the JAK-1 pathway, were observed with povorcitinib already at 3 weeks (i.e. first study visit in INCB 54707-301 and -302 studies). This information was considered clinically relevant for prescribers and hence its inclusion in SmPC section 5.1 was also agreed.

## QT interval

A dedicated study (INCB 54707-107) was conducted to evaluate the effect of therapeutic (225 mg) and supra-therapeutic (450 mg) single doses of povorcitinib on the QTc interval. The design was in line with ICH E14 guideline and the parallel design of the study is considered adequate. The study results fulfilled the requirements to conclude that povorcitinib meets the ICH E14 criteria for a negative QT/QTc study since the upper limits of two-sided 90% CI for povorcitinib-placebo difference in QTcF prolongation at all post-dose time points were below 10 msec. Povorcitinib in the single dose up to 450 mg did not prolong the QT interval. The SmPC section 5.1 was updated to reflect the absence of clinically relevant effect on the QTc interval.

## PD interactions

No clinical studies to evaluate the pharmacodynamic interactions with other medicinal products or substances were submitted by the applicant. Upon CHMP request, the applicant added an appropriate warning to SmPC section 4.4 stating that \"Combination with biologic immunomodulators, potent immunosuppressants such as ciclosporin or other Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors has not been studied. Their concomitant use with povorcitinib is not recommended as a risk of additive immunosuppression cannot be excluded\".

## PK/PD and dose justification

Exposure-response analyses were provided in support of dose selection of povorcitinib in HS patients.

## Exposure-efficacy

Exposure-efficacy analysis in the full population included 1226 participants from two Phase 3 studies. Analysis in the Post-Anti-TNF population included a subgroup of 328 participants from those two studies. Povorcitinib exposure was derived from the individual empirical Bayes estimates obtained from the popPK model. Cavg,ss was selected as the exposure metric of interest, which is acceptable.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The E-R analysis on efficacy was conducted on the primary efficacy endpoint (HiSCR50 at Week 12) and one of the key secondary efficacy endpoints (Skin Pain NRS30 at Week 12) (Study CPP-25.45.1). Additionally, ad hoc E-R analysis of efficacy was conducted on a secondary endpoint of percentage change-from-baseline in dT counts (Study CPP.25.50.1).

A log-linear E-R relationship with Cavg,ss was used for all endpoints in exposure-efficacy analysis. The observed data mostly showed a positive association between the first three quartiles of povorcitinib exposure and both endpoints (HiSCR50 and Skin Pain NRS30) for the full analysis and post-anti-TNF populations. Posterior predictive checks used for model evaluation indicate that the model does not capture well the central tendency of the observed data, i.e. at some concentrations the model is overpredicting, at others the model is underpredicting the response. Therefore, any results obtained from the model simulations should be interpreted with caution.

In study CPP-25.45.1, both povorcitinib doses demonstrated significantly greater efficacy compared to placebo for HiSCR50 and Skin Pain NRS30, in both the full analysis and post-anti-TNF populations. The odds of achieving these efficacy endpoints were higher with the 75 mg dose than with the 45 mg dose; however, the difference between the two active doses was minor, as reflected by odds ratios of 1.05 for HiSCR50 and 1.08 for Skin Pain NRS30 in the full analysis population and 1.13 and 1.18, respectively, in the post-anti-TNF population. It is noted that the observed Phase 3 data showed similar response rate for HiSCR50 and Skin Pain NRS30 scores between 45 mg and 75 mg dose in the full population. In the Post-Anti-TNF population, the response rates appeared to be even slightly lower for the higher 75 mg dose. Simulated probabilities of HiSCR50 and Skin Pain NRS30 scores suggest slightly higher responses with the 75 mg dose compared to 45 mg, both in the full population and Post-Anti-TNF population. Given the discordance with the observed results and issues observed in posterior predictive checks, these results do not sufficiently justify benefits of 75 mg over 45 mg dose.

The second study (CPP-25.50.1) assessed the relationship between povorcitinib exposure and clinical efficacy responses based on dT count over a 12-week treatment period. No statistically significant difference was observed between the 75 mg and 45 mg doses for the evaluated endpoints across baseline dT count categories. Nevertheless, both doses were superior to placebo, and the odds of improvement were generally higher with the 75 mg dose, particularly in patients with higher baseline disease activity (i.e. baseline dT counts ≥ 5). Although these results suggest 75 mg dose might be useful in patients with higher disease burden, given the exploratory nature of this analysis, the results should be interpreted with caution. Moreover, no details on model development and model evaluation were presented by the applicant.

## Exposure-safety

The dataset for exposure-safety analysis comprised 12 weeks of safety data from PC period from three phase 2 studies and two phase 3 studies in HS. Regarding safety endpoints (acne, infections and infestations), both active doses were associated with a higher probability of adverse events compared to placebo. The 75 mg dose showed a slightly higher probability of these adverse events than the 45 mg dose.

In conclusion, both the 45 mg and 75 mg doses of povorcitinib provide significant efficacy and acceptable safety compared to placebo. The 75 mg dose may offer additional benefit in certain subpopulations, such as those with high disease burden, although the overall difference between the two doses is small (see Efficacy section for further details).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 5.2.6.2 Conclusions

Overall, the clinical pharmacology program is comprehensive, and the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of povorcitinib were adequately characterised.

The information and results obtained in the clinical pharmacology programme have been adequately reflected in the SmPC.

## 5.3 Clinical efficacy

## 5.3.1 Dose response study INCB 54707-204

## Study Design and Methods

Study INCB 54707-204 was a randomised, parallel-group, PC, dose-ranging study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of povorcitinib (15, 45, and 75 mg QD) in adult participants with HS (Hurley Stages I, II, and III). The study schema is shown in Figure 4.

Figure 4. INCB 54707-204 Study Design

<!-- image -->

EOS = end of study; EOT = end of treatment.

The primary efficacy endpoint was the mean change in AN count at Week 16 relative to baseline, with HISCR50 as the key secondary endpoint.

The primary efficacy analysis compared povorcitinib 75 mg versus placebo on the mean change from baseline in AN count at Week 16 using MMRM based on the ITT Population in the PC period through Week 16. The MMRM included the fixed effects of treatment group, stratification factors Hurley Stage [I, II, and III] and geographical region [North America and outside of North America]), visit (Weeks 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, and 16), treatment by visit interaction, and covariates of baseline measurement and baseline measurement by visit interaction. Unstructured covariance matrix was assumed.

## Results

Of the 209 enrolled participants, 207 participants were randomised and treated in the PC period; 174 participants (83.3%) completed treatment through Week 16, and 35 participants (16.7%) discontinued from treatment during the PC period. The majority of discontinuations from treatment during the PC period were due to participant choice (7.7%).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

During the OLE period, 175 participants took at least 1 dose of povorcitinib and 121 (69.1%) completed treatment through Week 52. Consistent with the PC period, discontinuations from treatment during the OLE period were most frequently due to participant choice (11.4%). During the LTE period, 97 participants took at least 1 dose of povorcitinib and 68 (70.1%) completed treatment through Week 100. As in the PC and OLE periods, discontinuations from treatment during the LTE period were most frequently due to participant choice (9.3%).

Demographic characteristics were generally well-balanced across treatment groups. The median age of participants was 36.0 years (range: 19-70 years). The majority of participants were North American (81.8%) and not Hispanic or Latino (85.6%); 70.3% were White and 24.4% were Black. The majority of participants were current or former nicotine users (43.5% and 14.4%, respectively) and were obese (BMI ≥ 30 mg/kg2; 74.7%) or severely obese (BMI ≥ 40 mg/kg2; 30.2%).

Treatment groups were generally well-balanced in terms of disease severity at baseline; however, the povorcitinib 75-mg group had somewhat lesser disease severity across several baseline measures. The mean and median AN counts were slightly lower in the povorcitinib 75-mg group (10.6 and 8.0, respectively) than for the other treatment groups (ranging from 11.2 to 12.9 and 9.5 to 10.0, respectively). Participants in the povorcitinib 15-mg group had slightly lower scores on QoL measures as compared with the other treatment groups.

## 5.3.2 Main studies

The phase 3 studies INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 were identical in design and therefore are described together.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 5.3.2.1.1 Study title

INCB 54707-301: \"Selective Treatment of Oral povorcitinib in Hidradenitis Suppurativa Study 1 (STOPHS1); A Phase 3, Double-Blind, Randomised, Placebo-Controlled, Efficacy and Safety Study of povorcitinib (INCB054707) in Participants With Moderate to Severe Hidradenitis Suppurativa\"

INCB 54707-302: \"Selective Treatment of Oral povorcitinib in Hidradenitis Suppurativa Study 2 (STOPHS2); A Phase 3, Double-Blind, Randomised, Placebo-Controlled, Efficacy and Safety Study of povorcitinib (INCB054707) in Participants With Moderate to Severe Hidradenitis Suppurativa\"

## 5.3.2.1.2 Study design

Studies INCB 54707-301 and 54707-302 were identically designed, randomised, double-blind studies composed of sequential PC and extension periods lasting 12 and 42 weeks, respectively. Patients were randomised 1:1:1 to receive povorcitinib (45 or 75 mg QD) or placebo QD during the PC period; patients who completed the PC period were eligible to continue to a 42-week double-blind extension period with povorcitinib 45 or 75 mg QD. Patients were stratified based on ANdT count (&lt; 11 or ≥ 11) at baseline and previous treatment of HS with a biologic medicine. Participants randomised to povorcitinib at baseline remained at their respective dose level (45 or 75 mg) throughout the PC and extension periods, while participants randomised to placebo received povorcitinib 45 or 75 mg (1:1 ratio) at the week 12 visit onward, after completion of the PC period.

Figure 5. Pivotal studies INCB 54707-301 and -302 study schema

<!-- image -->

AN=abscess and inflammatory nodule, EOS=end of study, EOT=end of treatment, HS=hidradenitis suppurativa, QD=once daily

## 5.3.2.1.3 Treatment

Povorcitinib 45 mg or 75 mg or placebo was administered for 12 weeks. Patients who completed the PC period could continue to a 42-week double-blind extension period with povorcitinib 45 mg or 75 mg (Figure 5).

Povorcitinib or matching placebo was taken orally QD, preferably in the morning and at about the same time each day, with a full glass of water, with or without food.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Povorcitinib was provided as 45 mg or 75 mg tablets; both strengths matched each other in smell, taste, and appearance. Placebo tablets matched the povorcitinib tablets in smell, taste, and appearance.

## 5.3.2.1.4 Concomitant and rescue therapy

Use of systemic and topical antibiotics for HS, and certain topical antiseptics for HS (i.e. diluted bleach or topical washes containing gluconate or benzoyl peroxide), were prohibited during the PC period, except in cases of protocol-specified systemic antibiotic rescue therapy. Throughout the study, other prohibited medications included systemic immunomodulators (except for short courses and for nondermatological indications), HS surgery, laser or other phototherapy, live-attenuated vaccines, investigational medications (other than the study drug), strong systemic CYP3A4 inhibitors, and strong or moderate systemic CYP3A4 inducers.

Allowed medications included analgesics (opioid or non-opioid) and wound care dressings (alginates, hydrocolloids, and hydrogels) for HS. Participants who elected to receive non-live attenuated types of COVID-19 vaccines during the study could continue study drug administration. In the event of a particularly painful HS lesion that necessitated an acute intervention, two types of lesion rescue treatment were allowed as per protocol-specific criteria, i.e. injection with intralesional corticosteroid, and incision and drainage of the lesion.

## 5.3.2.1.5 Randomisation

During the PC period, all patients were centrally assigned to study treatment using Interactive Response Technology (IRT) system in a 2:2:1:1 ratio to receive one of the following treatments:

- Povorcitinib 45 mg QD
- Povorcitinib 75 mg QD
- placebo to povorcitinib 45 mg QD
- placebo to povorcitinib 75 mg QD

The 2:2:1:1 randomisation ratio was equivalent to the overall randomisation ratio of 1:1:1 to povorcitinib (45 or 75 mg) or placebo for the 12-week PC period.

Randomisation was stratified by ANdT count (&lt; 11 or ≥ 11) and previous treatment of HS with a biologic drug (yes or no).

Participants randomised to povorcitinib at baseline remained at their respective dose level (45 or 75 mg QD) throughout the PC and extension periods, while participants randomised to placebo received povorcitinib 45 or 75 mg QD (1:1 ratio) from the Week 12 visit onward, after completion of the PC period.

## 5.3.2.1.6 Blinding

After the database lock for the primary analysis (Week 12), the sponsor was unblinded, but investigators and participants remained blinded to individual treatment assignments through study completion.

Emergency unblinding would occur if an AE requires the investigator to be made aware of the participant's treatment assignment (in case of a medical emergency for patient's safety). The decision to break the treatment code in an emergency situation resides at the sole discretion of the investigator.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 5.3.2.1.7 Patient population

The study population consisted of patients ≥ 18 years of age who had a clinical diagnosis of moderate to severe HS (Hurley Stage II or III) for at least 3 months at the time of screening and who had a documented history of inadequate response to at least a 3-month course of at least 1 conventional systemic therapy (oral antibiotic or biologic drug) for HS (or demonstrated intolerance to, or had a contraindication to, a conventional systemic therapy for treatment of their HS), with HS lesions in at least 2 distinct anatomical areas and total AN count of at least 5.

The following definitions were used to define Hurley stage II and III:

- Stage II: One or more widely separated recurrent abscesses with tunnel (draining or nondraining) formation and cicatrisation (scarring)
- Stage III: Multiple interconnected tunnels (draining or nondraining) and abscesses across the entire area, with diffuse or near-diffuse involvement

The key eligibility criteria of the INCB 54707-301 and 54707-302 studies were identical and summarised below.

## Inclusion criteria

1. Ability to comprehend and willingness to sign a written ICF for the study.
2. Age ≥ 18 years at the time of signing the ICF.
3. Diagnosis of moderate to severe HS for at least 3 months prior to the screening visit.
4. Total abscess and inflammatory nodule count of at least 5 at both the screening and baseline visits.
5. HS lesions in at least 2 distinct anatomical areas, 1 of which must be at least Hurley Stage II or Hurley Stage III, at both the screening and baseline visits.
6. Documented history of inadequate response to at least a 3-month course of at least 1 conventional systemic therapy (oral antibiotic or biologic drug) for HS (or demonstrated intolerance to, or have a contraindication to, a conventional systemic therapy for treatment of their HS).
7. Agreement to NOT use topical and systemic antibiotics for treatment of HS during the placebocontrolled period (unless the systemic antibiotic rescue criterion is met).
8. Agreement to NOT use a diluted bleach bath or topical antiseptic washes containing chlorhexidine gluconate or benzoyl peroxide on the areas affected by HS lesions during the placebo-controlled period.
9. Agreement to use appropriate contraception, as specified in the protocol.
10. Willing and able to comply with the study protocol and procedures.

## Exclusion criteria

1. Presence of &gt; 20 draining tunnels (fistulas) at either the screening or baseline visit.
2. Women who are pregnant (or who are considering pregnancy) or breastfeeding.
3. Concurrent conditions or history of other diseases, as follows:
- a) Thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, or platelet dysfunction.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

- b) Venous and arterial thrombosis, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, stroke, moderate to severe heart failure (NYHA Class III or IV), cerebrovascular accident, myocardial infarction, coronary stenting, or coronary arterial revascularization with bypass graft surgery (CABG).
- c) Diagnosis of other significant cardiovascular diseases, as specified in the protocol.
- d) Uncontrolled hypertension, as defined by a confirmed systolic blood pressure &gt; 160 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure &gt; 100 mm Hg.
- e) Participants who are permanently bedridden or wheelchair assisted.
- f) Recipient of an organ transplant that requires continued immunosuppression.
- g) Any malignancies or history of malignancies with the exception of adequately treated or excised nonmetastatic basal cell or squamous cell cancer of the skin.
- h) Conditions that could interfere with drug absorption, including but not limited to short-bowel syndrome.
- i) Chronic or recurrent infectious disease, as specified in the protocol.
- j) Current or history of disseminated herpes zoster, or recurrent (more than 1 episode of) dermatomal herpes zoster.
- k) Current or history of disseminated herpes simplex.
- l) Active systemic infection or any active infection that, based on the investigator's clinical assessment, makes the participant an unsuitable candidate for the study.
- m) Any other active skin disease or condition that may interfere with the course, severity, or assessments of HS.
- n) Any clinically significant medical condition (other than HS) or any other reason that the investigator determines would interfere with the participant's participation in this study or would make the participant an unsuitable candidate to receive study drug or would put the participant at risk by participating in the study.
- o) Any clinically significant medical condition other than HS, as determined by the investigator, that is not adequately controlled with appropriate treatment or may interfere with the course, severity, or assessments of HS.
- p) Albinism.
4. A screening 12-lead ECG that demonstrates clinically significant abnormalities requiring treatment or that is indicative of serious underlying heart disease or criteria associated with Q wave interval (QT)/Fridericia-corrected Q wave interval (QTcF) abnormalities.
5. Have undergone significant trauma or major surgery (per investigator's assessment) within 30 days preceding the screening visit.
6. History of clinically significant (per investigator's judgment) drug or alcohol abuse within 6 months preceding the screening visit.
7. History of treatment failure with any systemic or topical JAK inhibitor for HS or any other inflammatory condition.
8. Receipt of medical treatment or investigational drugs within the following interval before the baseline visit:

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

- a) &lt; 12 weeks or 5 half-lives (if known), whichever is longer, for any investigational or experimental treatments.
- b) &lt; 12 weeks or 5 half-lives (if known), whichever is longer, for immunomodulating biologic drugs.
- c) &lt; 8 weeks for live vaccine, or planning to receive live vaccine during the course of the study or within 8 weeks after the last dose of study drug.
- d) &lt; 4 weeks for any topical or systemic JAK inhibitor.
- e) &lt; 4 weeks for systemic immunosuppressive or immunomodulating small-molecule drugs

Note 1: Use of corticosteroid inhalers and intranasal sprays is allowed.

Note 2: Use of oral corticosteroids for non-dermatologic conditions is allowed for no longer than 7 days if deemed acceptable by the investigator and the sponsor (or designee).

- f) &lt; 4 weeks for surgical, laser, or any phototherapy intervention in areas with HS lesions.
- g) &lt; 2 weeks for other systemic therapies for HS with potential therapeutic impact.

Note: Per discretion of the investigator (or designee), these drugs are allowed during the study if not prescribed for HS treatment and if at a stable dose and the dose is not anticipated to change during the course of the study.

- h) &lt; 2 weeks for systemic anti-infectives for HS treatment.
- i) &lt; 1 week for any oral or topical PDE4 inhibitor.
- j) &lt; 1 week for topical anti-infectives for HS lesions.
- k) &lt; 1 week for topical products containing chlorhexidine gluconate, or benzoyl peroxide, and topical diluted bleach bath to treat HS.
- l) &lt; 1 week for any topical drug applied onto HS lesions.
- m) &lt; 1 week for topical or intralesional corticosteroids.

Note: Use of topical corticosteroids for dermatologic diseases other than HS is allowed for areas not being treated for HS. The total body surface area involvement for other dermatologic diseases should not interfere with the safety of the participant or the HS assessments.

- n) &lt; 1 week or 5 half-lives (if known), whichever is longer, for strong systemic CYP3A4 inhibitors and strong and moderate systemic CYP3A4 inducers.
9. At the screening visit, any of the following laboratory abnormalities.

Hematology:

- Platelets &lt; 100 × 109/L
- Hemoglobin &lt; 9 g/dL
- Absolute neutrophil count (ANC) &lt; 1.5 × 109/L
- Total white blood cell (WBC) count (leukocyte count) &lt; 3.0 × 109/L
- Absolute lymphocyte count &lt; 0.8 × 109/L

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Hepatic:

- ALT &gt; 2 × ULN
- AST &gt; 2 × ULN
- Total bilirubin &gt; 1.5 × ULN (Note: Participants with clinical diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome may have a direct bilirubin measured and would be eligible provided the direct bilirubin is &lt; ULN

Renal:

- Estimated glomerular filtration rate &lt; 45 mL/min per 1.73 m2 (Note: Based on the simplified 4-variable Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD) formula)
10. Evidence of infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (i.e., TB).
11. Active HIV or acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. Active HIV is defined as confirmed positive anti-HIV antibody test.
12. Evidence of HBV or HCV infection or risk of reactivation.
13. Known hypersensitivity or severe reaction to povorcitinib or excipients of povorcitinib (refer to the IB) and/or other products in the same class.
14. Any condition, laboratory result, or result of screening assessments that would, in the investigator's and sponsor's (or designee's) judgment, interfere with full participation in the study, including administration of study drug and attending required study visits, pose a significant risk to the participant, or interfere with interpretation of study data.
15. The following participants are excluded in France: vulnerable populations according to article L.1121-6 of the French Public Health Code and adults under legal protection or who are unable to express their consent per article L.1121-8 of the French Public Health Code.

The study INCB 54707-301 was conducted at 88 study centers in Austria, Belgium, Canada, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Greece, Japan, Netherlands, Poland, Spain, and United States (US).

The study INCB 54707-302 was conducted at 96 study centers in Australia, Bulgaria, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain, United Kingdom (UK), and United States (US).

## 5.3.2.1.8 Study assessments

The following key assessments were used when evaluating the efficacy of povorcitinib in the phase 3 studies:

## Hidradenitis Suppurativa Clinical Response (HiSCR)

The HiSCR is a validated clinical endpoint defined by the status of 3 types of lesions: abscess, inflammatory nodules, and draining tunnels.

The definition of response (HiSCR50) requires the 3 criteria below to be met, relative to baseline:

- At least 50% decrease in abscess plus inflammatory nodule (AN) count; and
- No increase in abscess count; and
- No increase in draining tunnel count

HiSCR75, HiSCR90, and HiSCR100 are respectively defined as at least a 75%, 90%, and 100% reduction from baseline in the total AN count, with no increase in abscess or draining tunnel count.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Skin Pain NRS - PRO

Patients answered the Skin Pain NRS question daily via eDiary from screening through Week 54 based on a 24-hour recall period.

The Skin Pain NRS ranges from 0 (no skin pain) to 10 (skin pain as bad as you can imagine) and evaluates the worst level of skin pain due to the patient's HS.

Skin Pain NRS30 is defined as at least a 30% reduction and at least a 1-unit reduction from baseline in the Skin Pain NRS and was calculated for patients with a Skin Pain NRS of at least 3 at baseline.

## Flare

Flare is defined as at least a 25% increase and a 2-unit increase in the total AN count relative to baseline.

## Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy - Fatigue Scale (FACIT-F) - PRO

The FACIT-F scale is a 13-item questionnaire originally designed to assess fatigue, over a 7-day recall period, in patients with chronic disease. Each item uses a 5-point scale ranging from \"4 = not at all\" to \"0 = very much.\" The total FACIT-F score ranges from 0 (maximum fatigue) to 52 (no fatigue). An increase in FACIT-F score represents a decrease in fatigue (i.e. better QoL).

## Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) - PRO

The DLQI is a 10-question, validated questionnaire to measure how much the skin problem has affected the patient over the previous 7 days, across symptoms and feelings, daily activities, leisure, work and school, personal relations, and treatment. The DLQI score ranges from 0 to 30, with higher scores indicating a greater impact on QoL.

The PRO questionnaires FACIT-F and DLQI were completed by the patients at study visits before site personnel perform any clinic assessments to avoid biasing the participant's response.

## Other (selected) efficacy assessments

International Hidradenitis Suppurativa Severity Score System (IHS4): The IHS4 is a composite, dynamic score and validated tool used to determine HS severity. It employs a weighted scale that sums the number of inflammatory nodules (multiplied by 1), the number of abscesses (multiplied by 2), and the number of draining tunnels (multiplied by 4).

Itch NRS - PRO: The Itch NRS is a validated as a single-item PRO of itch severity that asks patients to rate their itching severity based on their worst level of itching. The scale ranges from 0 (no itch) to 10 (worst itch imaginable).

Hidradenitis Suppurativa Quality of Life (HiSQoL) - PRO: The HiSQoL is a 17-item HS-specific healthrelated QoL instrument with a 7-day recall period, and it will be used to assess HS symptoms and the impact of HS problems on QoL through 3 domains (symptoms, activities and adaptations, and psychosocial).

## 5.3.2.1.9 Objectives and estimands

## Primary objective

The primary objective in the phase 3 studies was to evaluate the efficacy of povorcitinib (45 mg and 75 mg) versus placebo in patients with moderate to severe HS.

## Statistical methods for estimation and sensitivity analysis on primary estimand

## Analysis of the efficacy endpoints

In each phase 3 study, the statistical null hypothesis for primary endpoint (superiority of each povorcitinib treatment group [75 and 45 mg] compared with the placebo group) in the ITT Population - all randomised subjects - was tested at a 2-sided α = 0.025 using the CMH test, stratified by randomisation stratification factors. The corresponding p-value was provided. Rate difference between each povorcitinib dose group (45 and 75 mg) versus placebo and the associated 95% Wald CI was computed using Mantel-Haenszel stratum weights and Sato's variance. The stratified common odds ratio with the 95% CI was provided. HiSCR50 rates at Week 12 along with 95% exact CIs based on the Clopper-Pearson method were also reported.

Participants who discontinued treatment or who initiated systemic antibiotic rescue therapy or prohibited medication with effect on HS outcomes were considered as nonresponders for all subsequent visits through Week 12. Also, participants who missed a post-baseline value at a visit (i.e., true missing values due to data not collected) were imputed as nonresponders for that visit only.

A sensitivity analysis was conducted with all data included regardless of occurrence of any intercurrent event, followed by multiple imputation of missing values using a fully conditional specification of joint distribution of treatment, stratification factors, baseline and scheduled post-baseline values of HiSCR components up to Week 12. Also, a tipping point analysis was performed to examine the potential effects of how many of the participants with missing data are assumed to be responders.

As a post-hoc analysis, a modified nonresponder imputation analysis was performed that considered participants who received systemic treatment with a potential effect on HS during the PC period, or who discontinued study treatment due to an adverse event or lack of efficacy, as nonresponders. All

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

other missing data for HiSCR50/75/90/100 were imputed using the multiple imputation fully conditional specification method.

In addition, the primary estimand was performed using the same stratified CMH test in the PP Population - those sufficiently compliant with the protocol- as a supportive analysis.

## Secondary objectives

The key secondary objectives were to further evaluate the efficacy of povorcitinib (45 mg and 75 mg) versus placebo in moderate to severe HS (i.e. proportion of patients who achieve HiSCR75 at week 12), to evaluate the effect of povorcitinib in reducing the incidence of flares (i.e. proportion of patients with flare by week 12) and to evaluate the effect of povorcitinib in decreasing skin pain (i.e. proportion of participants who achieve Skin Pain NRS30 at week 12 among patients with baseline Skin Pain NRS score ≥ 3).

## Statistical methods for estimation and sensitivity analysis on the secondary estimands

All the key secondary endpoints and other efficacy endpoints were analysed using the stratified CMH method, similar to that specified in the primary analysis. Similar to the primary analysis, participants who had true missing values due to data not collected were imputed as nonresponders for that visit only for the response endpoints.

## Error probabilities and adjustment for multiplicity

For the primary and key secondary endpoints on the ITT Population, the overall familywise Type I error rate was 2-sided α = 0.05. Graphic approach as outlined in Figure 6 was used in the primary and key secondary endpoints. In Step 1, within Family 1, the null hypothesis for each povorcitinib group vs. placebo was tested on the primary endpoint at 2-sided α = 0.025. If any null hypothesis was rejected, its significance level was transferred to the subsequent tests. This iterative process was to continue until no further hypotheses could be tested within Family 1.

In Step 2, if all 4 null hypotheses within Family 1 were rejected, the null hypotheses of skin response and flare for povorcitinib 75 mg vs. placebo would be tested, in this order, at 2-sided α = 0.05. If both were rejected, in Step 3, the null hypotheses of skin response and flare for povorcitinib 45 mg vs. placebo would be tested using the gatekeeping procedure at 2-sided α = 0.05.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Hxy,0 refers to null hypothesis of equal proportion of responders in povorcitinib dose and placebo. Index x=1 refers to povorcitinib 75 mg and x=2 refers to povorcitinib 45 mg.

## 5.3.2.1.10 Sample size

Based on the observed HiSCR rates at Weeks 8 and 12 reported in a Phase 2, randomised, doseranging study of INCB 54707-204, it was assumed that the HiSCR rates at Week 12 would be 48%, 45%, and 30% for the 75 mg, 45 mg and placebo groups, respectively. A sample size of 200 participants per group was to achieve approximately 93% and 80.7% power to detect a difference in the 75 mg and 45 mg, respectively, vs the placebo group at a 2-sided α = 0.025.

No power estimates or sample size calculations have been presented for the Post-Anti-TNF subgroup.

## 5.3.2.1.12 Results

## 5.3.2.1.13 Participant flow and numbers analysed

The study initiation dates (first patient dosed) in INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 studies were 19 December 2022 and 22 February 2023, respectively.

Altogether 864 and 877 patients were screened, and 608 and 619 were randomised in the INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 studies, respectively. All randomised patients were included in the ITT population.

Altogether 517/608 (85.0%) and 531/619 (85.8%) of patients in the INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 studies were included in PP population, respectively. Altogether 553 (91.0%) and 554 (89.5%) of patients, respectively, took povorcitinib at least once during the extension period and were included in Extension-Evaluable Population.

## Compliance to treatment

Treatment compliance in phase 3 studies was assessed by tablet count at each study visit.

Mean treatment compliance during the PC period in the placebo and povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg groups was 97.4-98.4% in study INCB 54707-301 and 97.9-98.1% in study INCB 54707-302.

Mean treatment compliance during the extension period for those who crossed over from placebo to povorcitinib was ≥ 98.9% and ≥ 97.9% in studies INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302, respectively.

Mean treatment compliance for participants who took povorcitinib throughout the study was ≥ 97.7% and ≥ 97.6% in studies INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302, respectively.

## 5.3.2.1.14 Deviations from study plan

## Protocol amendments

Two identical amendments affecting participating EU countries were made to the protocols of INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 studies. The primary purpose (rationale) of all changes in amendment 1 (10 April 2023) and amendment 2 (01 May 2023) was to address regulatory requests provided after review by the EU national health authorities. The following changes were made:

## Amendment 1

1. Title Page: Revised the binding statement that the clinical trial will be conducted in compliance with Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) No. 536/2014.
2. Removed \"cervical carcinoma in situ\" from the exclusion criteria.
3. Revised guidance to describe management of ALT/AST elevations.
4. Revised guidance regarding COVID-19 management.
5. Revised to include \"any malignancy\" as a criterion for the patients to be removed from the study.
6. Clarified rationale on why rifampin/rifampicin is prohibited for systemic antibiotic rescue therapy (i.e. due to potential drug-drug interactions with the study drug).
7. Clarified aspects related to post-study access to study drug (i.e. extension study).
8. Reporting of SAEs: Updated directive reference.

## Amendment 2

1. Clarified aspects related to post-study access to study drug (i.e. extension study).
2. Included statement regarding the benefits and risks of participating in this study for potential patients who are current or past long-time smokers.
3. Revised guidance to describe management of CPK elevations.
4. Included statement explaining that the ICF will describe the potential risks associated with participation in this study and treatment with the investigational product for patients who are current or past long-time smokers.

In addition, the protocols were amended in countries outside EU/EEA (between 21-Aug-2023 and 29Jan-2024) to include information about the extension study available for eligible and consenting patients who complete the initial 54 weeks of treatment.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

All protocol amendments included administrative changes that were incorporated throughout the protocol.

## Protocol deviations

Placebo-controlled period

Study INCB 54707-301: During the PC period, protocol deviations occurred in 81.4% of total patients; minor deviations were reported for 65.1% of patients and major deviations were reported for 61.0% of patients. Critical protocol deviations (exclusion criteria) were reported for 5 patients (0.8%; 2 patients each in the placebo and povorcitinib 45 mg groups and 1 patient in the povorcitinib 75 mg group). The major protocol deviations that were most frequently reported among all patients were related to PROs (23.5%), laboratory assessment (20.2%), and visit schedule (14.1%) (Table 26).

A total of 91 patients in study INCB 54707-301 (24, 31, and 36 patients in the placebo, povorcitinib 45 mg, and 75 mg groups, respectively) had deviations that affected the primary endpoint and were excluded from the PP Population. Reasons for exclusion were as follows (note that some patients were excluded from the PP Population for more than 1 reason):

- Mis-stratification based on ANdT count and/or previous treatment of HS with a biologic drug (51 patients).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

- Lesion count evaluator performed baseline and/or Week 12 assessments prior to completing required training, or did not use the Protocol-specific forms for lesion count or lesion rescue (16 patients).
- Use of a prohibited therapy or procedure during the PC period (12 patients).
- Full eligibility was not met on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria (10 patients).
- Week 12 visit was performed outside of window (11 days or longer; 8 patients).
- Study drug bottle was not returned 2 or more times/visits during the PC period (2 patients).

INCB 54707-302 study: During the PC period, protocol deviations occurred in 85.9% of total patients; minor deviations were reported for 71.2% of patients and major deviations were reported for 64.6% of patients. No critical protocol deviations were reported.
