## Extension period

INCB 54707-301 study: During the extension period, protocol deviations occurred in 89.3% of total patients; minor deviations were reported for 71.8% of patients and major deviations were reported for 74.0%of patients. Critical protocol deviations (efficacy) were reported for 3 patients (0.5%; 1 each in the placebo to povorcitinib 75 mg group, povorcitinib 45 mg group, and povorcitinib 75 mg group). The most frequent major protocol deviations among total patients were related to visit schedule (36.0%), PROs (27.1%), participant investigational product compliance (24.2%), and laboratory assessment (21.3%).

INCB 54707-302 study: During the extension period, protocol deviations occurred in 92.6% of total patients; minor deviations were reported for 81.2% of patients and major deviations were reported for 77.6% of patients. No critical protocol deviations were reported. The major protocol deviations most frequently reported among total patients were related to visit schedule (35.9%), PROs (34.8%), laboratory assessments (27.8%), and participant investigational product compliance (24.7%).

## Medical history

INCB 54707-301 study: Most patients (96.2%) had a general medical history including at least 1 medical condition or procedure, with similar incidences between the treatment groups (97.0% in the placebo group, 96.6% in the povorcitinib 45 mg group, and 95.0% in the povorcitinib 75 mg group). Medical history findings were most frequently (i.e., ≥ 20% overall) reported from the following SOCs: infections and infestations (68.6%); skin and subcutaneous disorders (50.3%), metabolism and nutrition disorders (47.7%); psychiatric disorders (33.4%); immune system disorders (23.5%); vascular disorders (23.0%); gastrointestinal disorders (21.4%); and respiratory, thoracic, and mediastinal disorders (21.1%).

The most frequently (≥ 10% overall) reported MedDRA PTs were COVID-19 (39.3%), varicella (37.7%), acne (34.5%), obesity (32.7%), hypertension (20.9%), depression (19.2%), anxiety (16.8%), asthma (12.8%), seasonal allergy (11.7%), and gastroesophageal reflux disease (11.7%).

INCB 54707-302 study: Most patients (93.7%) had a general medical history including at least 1 medical condition or procedure, with similar incidences between the treatment groups (93.1% in the placebo group, 93.3% in the povorcitinib 45 mg group, and 94.7% in the povorcitinib 75 mg group). Medical history findings were most frequently (i.e., ≥ 20% overall) reported from the following SOCs: infections and infestations (73.2%), skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders (53.0%), metabolism and nutrition disorders (43.3%), psychiatric disorders (31.3%), and vascular disorders (21.3%).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The most frequently reported MedDRA PTs (≥ 10% overall) were COVID-19 (47.2%), varicella (47.0%), acne (42.3%), obesity (28.4%), hypertension (20.0%), depression (16.6%), anxiety (15.7%), and seasonal allergy (11.3%).

## Prior medications

In INCB 54707-301 study, 96.2% of patients, and in INCB 54707-302 study, 94.8% of patients received oral antibiotics before the study. The incidence of prior biologic use was 35.9% and 38.6%, most commonly anti-TNF, which had been used by 27.5% and 31.8% of patients in INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 studies, respectively.

## 5.3.2.1.15 Outcomes and estimation

In this section, the results of the primary, key secondary efficacy endpoints and selected secondary endpoints are described separately for the INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 studies for the ITT population. Considering that the indication proposed by the applicant is restricted to the Post-Anti-TNF population, additional efficacy results are presented in Section 5.3.6, including comparison of the pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT population vs. pooled ITT population.

## Primary endpoint

The efficacy results for the primary endpoint in the phase 3 studies INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 in the ITT population is summarised in Table 36. The proportion of patients achieving HiSCR50 at week 12 was 40.2% and 40.6% vs. 29.7% in study INCB 54707-301, and 42.3% and 42.3% vs. 28.6% in study INCB 54707-302 for povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg vs. placebo groups, respectively.

The primary endpoint for each dose was considered statistically significant if the 2-sided p-value was ≤ 0.025. Therefore, the primary endpoint was met in both studies at 45 mg and 75 mg dose levels.

## Sensitivity analyses of the primary endpoint

A sensitivity analysis was performed, with all observed data included regardless of occurrence of any intercurrent event, followed by multiple imputation of missing values. In study INCB 54707-301, Week 12 HiSCR was evaluated for 12 (18%) out of 65 participants with intercurrent event. Among them no HiSCR responses were observed. In study INCB 54707-302, Week 12 HiSCR was evaluated for 8 (12%) out of 67 participants with intercurrent event. Among them 2 HiSCR responses were observed. Based on the observed data, HiSCR response rates at Week 3, 6 and 9 were generally similar in participants with and without intercurrent events. In this sensitivity analysis, the estimated HiSCR50 response rates in study INCB 54707-301 were 44.5%, 45.7% and 32.7 for the povorcitinib 45 mg, 75 mg and placebo groups, respectively. This resulted in a difference in the response rate of 11.9 (95% CI 2.3, 21.6, p=0.0157) for the povorcitinib 45 mg and 13.1 (95% CI 3.2, 23.1, p=0.0098) for the povorcitinib 75 mg groups vs. placebo. In study INCB 54707-302, the corresponding estimated HiSCR50 response rates were 47.6%, 47.3% and 32.0 for the povorcitinib 45 mg, 75 mg and placebo groups, respectively. This resulted in a difference in the response rate of 15.7 (95% CI 5.9, 25.4, p=0.0020) for the povorcitinib 45 mg and 15.3 (95% CI 5.7, 25.0, p=0.0022) for the povorcitinib 75 mg groups vs. placebo.

In second sensitivity analysis, patients who received systemic treatment with a potential effect on HS during the PC period, or discontinued study treatment due to an adverse event or lack of efficacy were considered nonresponders and all other missing data for HiSCR50 were imputed using the multiple imputation fully conditional specification method. In this analysis, the difference in response rates were 11.5% (95% CI 2.2, 20.9, p=0.0160) and 12.8% (95% CI 3.2, 22.4, p=0.0092) in study INCB 54707-301, and 14.7% (95% CI 5.1, 24.3, p=0.0030) and 14.7% (95% CI 5.1, 24.4, p=0.0031) in study INCB 54707-302 for the povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg groups vs. placebo, respectively.

e Skin pain endpoints were measured for participants with a baseline Skin Pain NRS score ≥ 3. Skin Pain NRS30 was defined as at least a 30% reduction and at least 1-unit reduction from baseline in the Skin Pain NRS score.

f A flare was defined as at least a 25% increase in the total AN count relative to baseline and an increase of at least 2 in the total AN count relative to baseline.

Note: the results for selected secondary and exploratory endpoints are presented for the pooled phase 3 ITT population in section 6.3.6.

## Need for rescue lesional treatment

Altogether 8.9%, 13.2% and 12.9% of patients in study INCB 54707-301 and 9.9%, 4.8% and 6.7% of patients in study INCB 54707-302 required rescue lesional treatment during the PC period in the placebo and povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg groups, respectively.

## Need for systemic antibiotic rescue therapy:

During the PC period, 2.0%, 2.9% and 3.0% of patients in study INCB 54707-301 and 1.5%, 1.4% and 1.9% of patients in study INCB 54707-301 required systemic antibiotic rescue therapy in the placebo and povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg groups, respectively.

## Participant-reported analgesic and opioid use

An analgesic use diary was used to track the use of pain medication (over-the-counter and prescribed) for HS-related pain. The first question asked if the patient had taken any pain medication (nonopioid or opioid) for HS-related pain in the past 24 hours; if the answer was yes, a second question asked if the medication was an opioid.

The use of analgesics and opioids during the PC period in study INCB 54707-301 are shown in Table 38 and in Table 39, and in study INCB 54707-302 in Table 40 and Table 41, respectively.

## 5.3.4 Supportive studies

## INCB 54707-202

Study design and methods Study INCB 54707-202 was a Phase 2, multicenter, open-label, single-arm study to assess the preliminary safety, PK, and efficacy of povorcitinib 15 mg QD over 8 weeks in adults with moderate to severe HS. A total of 10 patients were assigned to treatment with povorcitinib and 7 patients (70.0%) completed the study.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Results

At week 8, three patients (42.9%) each achieved HiSCR50 and an AN count of 0 to 2. The mean change from baseline in IHS4 was -2.1, the mean change in HiSQoL was -15.3, the mean change in HS worst pain NRS score was -2.0, and the mean change in DLQI was -4.4. The proportion of patients reporting \"no effect\" (DLQI 0-1) or a \"small effect\" (DLQI 2-5) of HS on QoL increased from 10% at baseline to 43% at Week 8, as the proportion of patients reporting \"moderate\" to \"extremely large\" effect (DLQI 6-30) decreased from 90% to 57%.

## INCB 54707-203

## Study design and methods

Study INCB 54707-203 was a Phase 2, multicenter, randomised, PC, dose escalation study to evaluate the safety of povorcitinib (30, 60, and 90 mg QD) over an 8-week treatment period in adults with moderate to severe HS. The study included 3 cohorts. In each cohort, patients were randomised to receive either povorcitinib or placebo (3:1 ratio).

## Results

Altogether 17 patients (63.6%) receiving povorcitinib 30, 60, or 90 mg (5 [55.6%], 5 [55.6%], and 7 [87.5%], respectively) vs. 4 patients (57.1%) receiving placebo achieved HiSCR50 at Week 8. Approximately half of the patients receiving povorcitinib (30 mg, 44.4%; 60 mg, 44.4%; 90 mg, 62.5%) at week 8 (vs 57.1% for placebo) achieved an AN count of 0 to 2. The mean changes from baseline in AN count at Week 8 were -7.0, -10.0, and -12.5 in povorcitinib 30, 60, and 90 mg groups, respectively, vs. -6.0 for placebo. For IHS4, the mean changes from baseline at Week 8 were -9.4, -21.4, and -16.1 in povorcitinib 30, 60, and 90 mg groups, respectively, vs. -10.7 for placebo.

The mean changes from baseline in HiSQoL were -34.3, -39.0, and -28.0 in povorcitinib 30, 60, and 90 mg groups, respectively, at week 8, vs. -3.4 for placebo. At week 8, the mean changes from baseline in HS worst pain NRS score were -2.2, -1.4, and -3.1 in povorcitinib 30, 60, and 90 mg groups, vs. 0.3 for placebo. The mean changes from baseline to week 8 in DLQI were -7.2, -4.2, and -5.8 in povorcitinib 30, 60, and 90 mg groups, vs. 0.9 for placebo. Considering DLQI, the proportion of patients reporting \"no effect\" or a \"small effect\" of HS on their QoL was 15% at baseline, which increased to 53% among patients who received povorcitinib at Week 8 (vs 2.2% to 29% for placebo), whereas the proportion reporting \"moderate\" to \"extremely large\" effect decreased from 85% to 46% for povorcitinib (vs 78% to 71% for placebo).

## INCB 54707-312

The 52-week long-term extension study INCB 54707-312, comprising eligible patients from pivotal phase 3 studies, will provide further information on efficacy and safety of 45 mg and 75 mg povorcitinib for up to 106 weeks. The applicant has committed to submit the final study report postapproval, once available.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 5.3.5 Analysis performed across trials (pooled analyses and meta-analysis)

An integrated analysis across the two pivotal Phase 3 studies was prepared for the Pooled ITT Population and the Pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population, with the SAP dated 18 December 2024.

According to the applicant, efficacy analyses for the pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population were intended to yield estimates of the treatment effect of povorcitinib with greater precision in the proposed indication as well as to support the results of the individual phase 3 studies in the targeted population. Further, efficacy analyses for the pooled ITT population were intended to support the results of the Post Anti-TNF ITT Population and provide a larger dataset for evaluating the treatment effect of povorcitinib, particularly in participant subgroups.

The estimand (for the primary endpoint) and statistical methods, in general, matched with those applied in the individual studies except that only the primary endpoint, key secondary efficacy endpoints, and selected secondary and exploratory efficacy endpoints were to be predefined for these integrated analyses:

Primary endpoint:

- HiSCR50 at Week 12 (primary endpoint)

Key secondary endpoints:

- HiSCR75 at Week 12
- Flare by Week 12
- Skin Pain NRS30 at Week 12 (among participants with a baseline Skin Pain NRS score ≥ 3)

Other endpoints for the pooled ITT Population and the pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population:

- HiSCR90/100 at Week 12

Other endpoints for the pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population:

- a ≥ 3-point decrease in Skin Pain NRS score at Week 12 (among participants with a baseline Skin Pain NRS score ≥ 3)
- at least a 4-point increase from baseline in FACIT-F score at Week 12
- change from baseline in DLQI score at each visit
- The following endpoints at/by Week 24 and Week 52, respectively:
- o HiSCR50/75
- o flare
- o Skin Pain NRS30 (among participants with baseline Skin Pain NRS score ≥ 3)
- maintenance of HiSCR50/75 or greater response at each visit during the EXT period
- HiSCR50/75/90/100 at each visit

As a post hoc analysis, draining tunnel count along with change and precent change from baseline was summarised.

Also, demographics and baseline characteristics, baseline disease characteristics and participant disposition were summarised.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Disposition

The pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population consisted of 330 patients, of which 329 patients (99.7%) received study drug; 1 patient was randomised but not treated in study INCB 54707-302. Of these, 295 patients (89.4%) completed treatment in the PC period and 34 patients (10.3%) discontinued from treatment. In the extension period, 293 patients received at least 1 dose of study drug. Of these, 173 patients (59.0%) completed the study and 120 patients (41.0%) discontinued during the extension period. The most common reasons for discontinuation were withdrawal by participant (16.4%) and lack of efficacy (8.9%).

The pooled ITT Population consisted of 1227 patients, of which 1226 (99.9%) received study drug. Of these, 1114 patients (90.8%) completed treatment in the PC period, and 112 patients (9.1%) discontinued treatment. In the extension period, 1107 patients received at least 1 dose of study drug. Of these, 717 participants (64.8%) completed the study and 390 patients (35.2%) discontinued during the extension period.

## Demographics and baseline characteristics

The mean age was 38.6 years in the pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population and 37.3 years in pooled ITT Population. In both populations, most patients were female (approximately 63%), White (approximately 75%) or Black (approximately 14%). In the pooled Post Anti-TNF ITT and pooled ITT Populations, the majority of patients were from North America (55.8% and 52.0%) or Europe and Australia (43.6% and 46.2%); in addition, most patients were current (45.5% and 47.3%) or former (17.9% and 17.0%) nicotine users and obese (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2: 61.5% and 63.5%).

## Baseline disease characteristics

The mean disease duration was 12.28 years in the pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population and 10.28 years in the pooled ITT Population. Mean lesion counts were higher for the pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population than for the pooled ITT Population at baseline (AN: 14.4 vs 12.0; ANdT: 18.1 vs 14.8; abscess count: 3.1 vs 2.2; draining tunnel count: 3.7 vs 2.8; proportion of participants with ANdT count ≥ 11: 68.8% vs 56.4%) and there was a higher proportion of participants with Hurley Stage III in the Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population (47.9%) compared with the pooled ITT Population (35.1%).

Baseline Skin Pain NRS scores and HiSQoL scores were higher for the pooled Post Anti TNF ITT Population (6.0 and 37.3, respectively) than for the pooled ITT Population (5.0 and 31.7, respectively), and a higher proportion of patients had previously undergone local excision as prior HS procedure (27.9% vs 20.9%). The pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population also had higher baseline patient-reported analgesic and opioid use (37.6% and 11.5%, respectively) than the pooled ITT Population (26.5% and 6.7%, respectively).

Baseline disease characteristics of patients during the PC period in the pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT and pooled ITT populations is shown in Table 47.

## Primary efficacy endpoint

The proportion of patients achieving HiSCR50 at week 12 was 21.4%, 39.0% and 36.0% in the pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population and 29.1%, 41.3% and 41.5% in the pooled ITT Population, in placebo group and povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg groups, respectively (Table 48).

## 5.3.6 Patient experience data (PED)

The patient organisation HS Ireland provided their perspectives on HS. Their contribution is highly appreciated.

Summary of the HS Ireland feedback: \"Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) has a substantial and enduring impact on daily life, and current treatment pathways are often burdensome, unpredictable, and difficult to sustain. While medical, surgical, and biologic options can help some people, benefits are frequently variable or not durable, and access to specialised care remains uneven. Significant unmet needs persist, particularly for long-term disease control and effective pain management.

HS profoundly affects quality of life through pain, restricted mobility, drainage (and associate odour), fatigue, unpredictability, and social and emotional burden, with impacts extending to work, education, family, and social life. Patients with HS hope new medicines will provide sustained symptom control, improved stability, and meaningful improvements in daily functioning, even if benefits are partial. Many are willing to accept some side effects if benefits are durable and risks are clearly understood. Pregnancy and child-bearing considerations are especially important, highlighting the need for clearer guidance and pregnancy-compatible options\".

## 5.3.7 Healthcare professional engagement

Not applicable.

## 5.3.8 Overall discussion and conclusions on clinical efficacy

## 5.3.8.1 Discussion

The development program of povorcitinib consists of five clinical studies in HS patients. In addition to the completed pivotal phase 3 studies INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 in patients with moderate to severe HS, the program includes a phase 2 dose response study INCB 54707-204 and two supportive phase 2 studies INCB 54707-202 and INCB 54707-203.

Overall, the extent of the clinical program is adequate for the evaluation of povorcitinib in the treatment of patients with active moderate to severe HS. Instead of seeking approval in the whole HS population that the phase 3 studies were designed and powered for, the claimed target population is a subgroup of patients that have previously received anti-TNF treatment (i.e. Post-Anti-TNF population). More specifically, the proposed indication for povorcitinib is: \"Treatment of active moderate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa (acne inversa) in adults who have responded inadequately to, or who are intolerant or contraindicated to an anti-TNF therapy\".

The possibility of the two phase 3 studies supporting the proposed Post-Anti-TNF Population was discussed during the EMA SA (EMA/SA/0000084609). At the time of the SA, CHMP noted that this subpopulation could be either enriched from the applicant's proposed 20% of enrolled patients or evaluated in a separate study. While the phase 3 protocols or amended protocols did not specifically plan analyses in the Post-Anti-TNF Population, a separate statistical analysis plan (SAP) for this subgroup was in place and dated prior to the database lock for the primary analysis (12 weeks).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Dose response study and supportive studies

The phase 2 studies INCB 54707-202 and INCB 54707-203 were initial proof of concept studies in HS and provided preliminary efficacy data in patients with moderate to severe HS.

In the dose range finding study INCB 54707-204, HS patients with Hurley stage I, II and III received povorcitinib 15 mg, 45 mg, 75 mg or placebo. At week 16, povorcitinib demonstrated a beneficial treatment effect vs. placebo at all dose levels. The open label extension from weeks 16 to week 52 where all patients switched to 75 povorcitinib, provided some preliminary evidence of maintenance of efficacy.

In terms of the primary (AN count) and key secondary efficacy endpoints (HiSCR50), the efficacy of povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg were comparable. According to the applicant, the 75 mg provided somewhat faster achievement of clinical response in HiSCR for patients with a higher inflammatory lesion count at baseline (ANdT &gt; 11), decrease in analgesic use, decrease in draining tunnel count, decrease in Itch NRS, and improvement in the FACIT-F scores. Therefore, the applicant initially proposed to proceed to Phase 3 studies with only the 75 mg dose level. During the EMA SA (EMA/SA/0000084609), the CHMP concluded that based on the dose range finding study INCB 54707-204, the treatment effects of povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg were similar or that the differences in efficacy between the doses appeared to be only marginal. Also, given the safety issues identified with JAK inhibitors class, the CHMP recommended to expose subjects to the lowest effective dose and thus asked the applicant to consider testing both doses (45 mg and 75 mg) in one or both phase 3 studies. Therefore, the applicant's choice to include 45 mg and 75 mg doses in the phase 3 studies is aligned with the EMA SA received (EMA/SA/0000084609).

## Main studies

## Study design and conduct

The applicant conducted two identical Phase 3 studies INCB 54707-301 and 54707-302. Both studies included a 28-day screening period and an initial 12 week-double-blind PC treatment period where patients were randomised 2:2:1:1 ratio, which was equivalent to the overall randomisation ratio of 1:1:1 to povorcitinib (45 mg or 75 mg QD) or placebo. This was followed by a 42-week extension period, during which patients on povorcitinib continued on the same povorcitinib dose, and patients on placebo received (1:1) povorcitinib 45 mg or 75 mg based on randomisation at the start of the PC treatment period. The overall study design, use of placebo as a control, as well as the stratification based on ANdT count (&lt; 11 or ≥ 11) and previous treatment with a biologic drug is considered appropriate, although stratifying by region should have also been considered.

The patient population in phase 3 studies were adults with moderate to severe HS, i.e. Hurley stage II or III, who had a documented history of inadequate response to at least a 3-month course of at least 1 conventional systemic therapy (oral antibiotic or biologic drug) for HS (or demonstrated intolerance to, or had a contraindication to, a conventional systemic therapy for treatment of their HS). The patients were required to have a total AN count of ≥ 5 and HS lesions in ≥ 2 anatomical areas, whereas patients with ≥ 20 draining tunnels (fistulas) were excluded. While it is noted that the definition of moderate to severe HS based on Hurley criteria has evolved (i.e. it currently includes also Hurley IB and IC without tunnels yet having high burden of inflammatory nodules and abscesses), the used definition in the phase 3 studies can be considered to adequately represent moderate to severe HS. While most of the eligibility criteria seem acceptable, it is noted that the applicant's definition of \"conventional systemic therapy\" in phase 3 studies included documented history of inadequate response to either oral antibiotic or biologic drug. This was not in line with the given EMA SA (EMA/SA/0000084609) where CHMP stated that \"patients can be treated with biological agents however this would usually only be where there was a lack of a treatment response to systemic antibiotics used for 10-12 weeks\" and that the applicant's proposed definition of \"patients with an inadequate response to, intolerance of, or contraindication to an adequate course of systemic therapy and with a history of disease at a minimum of 3 months\" should be amended to \"patients who did not achieve a response to systemic antibiotics for at least 3 months and are candidates for systemic therapy\". Although the EMA SA was not fully followed in this regard, almost all patients (i.e. 95.5% of the pooled phase 3 ITT population and 87.6% of the pooled post-anti-TNF ITT population) had received prior oral antibiotics for HS and therefore represent patient population that are candidates for systemic therapy, which is in line with all mAbs approved for HS that are indicated in \"treatment of active moderate to severe HS with an inadequate response to conventional systemic HS therapy.\", placing them as second-line after failure to antibiotics.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

The key efficacy assessments in phase 3 studies are all widely used in HS studies. The primary endpoint HiSCR50, i.e. the proportion of patients who achieve at least a 50% reduction in the total AN count, with no increase in abscess or draining tunnel count is a validated endpoint and was agreed in the EMA SA (EMA/SA/0000084609). It has also been used as the primary endpoint in several other registration studies for HS. Also, the key secondary efficacy endpoints, including HiSCR75, flare (defined as at least a 25% increase in the total AN count with a minimum increase of 2 relative to baseline) and skin pain NRS30 (defined at least a 30% reduction and at least 1-unit reduction from baseline in the Skin Pain NRS) are considered clinically relevant measures of disease activity/severity and HS associated pain. Secondary endpoints included also PRO measures FACIT-F and DLQI, assessing the effect of povorcitinib on fatigue and QoL, respectively, as well as several other secondary and exploratory endpoints.

Use of systemic and topical antibiotics, and certain topical antiseptics for HS, were not allowed during the PC period (systemic antibiotics could only be used as rescue treatment). Allowed concomitant medications included analgesics (opioid or non-opioid) and wound care dressings (alginates, hydrocolloids, and hydrogels). Use of any systemic immunomodulators for HS, as well as HS surgery, laser or phototherapy were prohibited throughout the study. For individual lesions intralesional corticosteroid or incision and drainage of the lesion could be used as rescue treatments, when necessary. Povorcitinib is metabolised primarily by CYP3A4 and therefore the use of strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, and moderate and strong CYP3A4 inducers were prohibited. In summary, the permitted and prohibited concomitant treatments were deemed appropriate, and use of systemic and local rescue therapies were incorporated into the efficacy analysis (see section on estimands and strategies for handling intercurrent events).

Twelve weeks is an adequate timepoint for the primary efficacy analysis, also considering that longer term efficacy results are available at the intended dose levels (45 mg and 75 mg QD).

## Objectives, endpoints and estimands

For the primary analysis of primary estimand, a general non-responder imputation was applied, referred as composite strategy by the applicant. Accordingly, subsequent to study treatment discontinuation, initiation of systemic antibiotic rescue therapy or prohibited medication with effect of HS, the participant is considered as nonresponder through to week 12. It should be noted that also a missed assessment was considered as nonresponse.

In accordance with the ITT principle, clinical and PRO outcomes were also analysed using all data captured regardless of use of rescue medication or treatment discontinuation.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Statistical methods for estimation and sensitivity analysis

The primary analysis applied NRI on missing data (which often were associated with intercurrent event (IE)). The predefined sensitivity analysis must be evaluated considering the fact that few data were captured at week 12 from participants who had discontinued study treatment or initiated systemic therapy with effect on HS before week 12, the former being the predominant IE. As model-based multiple imputation was applied on the missing data, these sensitivity analyses essentially evaluated response rates in a hypothetical scenario where the IEs did not occur and assuming that data were missing at random.

Treatment discontinuation and the use of rescue or prohibited medication was overall modest by week 12 in both main studies and even among the treatment groups (further discussion on rescue medication use is provided in the context of the results.) Furthermore, responses (as per HiSCR) were rare among those whose efficacy evaluation was captured despite the IEs. Overall, for the primary analysis, the use NRI is acceptable with the sensitivity analysis providing a relevant supplementary assessment of the data.

Individual lesion(s) receiving rescue treatment were counted as permanently present throughout the study.

A post hoc sensitivity analysis was conducted with a modified nonresponder imputation. Systemic treatment with a potential effect on HS and study treatment discontinuation due to an AE or LoE were considered nonresponse, while the remaining missing data for HiSCR50/75/90/100 were imputed using the multiple imputation fully conditional specification method. In the absence of clearly articulated estimand, this hybrid approach is difficult to interpret, in principle. In practice, the results of this 'hybrid' approach are expected to lay between those of the primary analysis (composite estimand with nonresponder imputation on missing data) and its prespecified sensitivity analysis.

The statistical methods for summarising data and comparing outcomes between treatment arms are conventional and in line with the principle that stratified randomisation should be reflected by the data analysis.

Type 1 error was controlled by a graphical procedure across the 2 dose levels and 4 primary and key secondary endpoints. In short, sequential testing across three families of hypotheses was utilised. In the first group, Bonferroni procedure was used to test HiSCR50 for two doses at 2-sided α =0.025, with α transfer to HiSCR75 test for respective dose and, if HiSCR50 for one dose was not significant, it could be retested at α =0.05 only if HiSCR75 for the other dose was significant at 2-sided α = 0.025. If the α control at 0.05 was achieved for the first family, α of 0.05 was transferred to the subsequent family of hypotheses covering achievement of Pain NRS 30 and flare for 75 mg dose, which were tested using gatekeeping procedure. Following rejection of those null hypotheses for 75 mg, the last family of hypotheses covering Pain NRS 30 and flare for 45 mg dose were tested at two-sided α = 0.05 using the gatekeeping procedure. Overall, the multiplicity control for the two doses is appropriate.

Each study was planned to enrol 200 patients per each treatment arm. The sample size was calculated on the basis of expected 18 % and 15 % increase in responder rate over 30 % in placebo for 75 mg and 45 mg doses, in order to achieve power of 93% and 80.7 % power at 2-sided α = 0.025, based on chi-square test. The assumptions were based on INCB 54707-204 trial and seem reasonable. However, the studies were not sufficiently powered to detect the 15 % difference in responder rates solely based upon participants in the post-anti-TNF population, which may have resulted in lack of precision and wide confidence intervals in the respective subgroup analyses.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

As to the type 1 error control in the context of efficacy in the applied indication of post-anti-TNF population, it is noted that the trials were powered and their type 1 error control was determined for the overall population, disregarding past anti-TNF use. In SA, the CHMP had advised the applicant that type I error would generally have to be controlled for this additional analysis [specific to the subpopulation] by acceptable measures and suggested enrichment of the study population with patients who have failed anti-TNF treatment. Although the type I error control was not applied for the subpopulation specifically, demonstration of the effect in the overall HS population (irrespective of prior anti-TNF use), implied demonstration of effect in the subpopulation of patients with prior anti-TNF failure - with no further formal type 1 error control measures - given that prior anti-TNF use was a priori not expected to be an effect modifier. As to the hypothesis testing for key secondary endpoints of skin pain NRS30 and flare, the priority was given to the 75 mg dose to demonstrate an effect - but only if both dose levels first demonstrated effect on HiSCR50 and HiSCR75 at week 12. The long-term data are summarised using observed data only which is acceptable. However, results should be interpreted with caution since participants with inadequate response or severe disease may

be more likely to drop out over time.

## Results

Two amendments dated 10 April 2023, and 01 May 2023 were made to the original protocols of both phase 3 studies after review of the EU regulatory authorities. These amendments took place early, given that the first patients in INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 studies were dosed on 19 December 2022 and 22 February 2023, respectively. The modifications to the original protocols were minimal and not expected to negatively impact the validity of the studies. Altogether 864 and 877 patients were screened, and 608 and 619 randomised to placebo, povorcitinib 45 mg or 75 mg groups in INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 studies, respectively. A similar number of patients across all study groups in INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-301 studies, respectively, completed treatment during the 12-week PC period. The reasons for discontinuations and their frequencies were generally comparable across the study groups in both studies. Among patients who received placebo during the initial 12-week PC period, 92 and 93 patients in study INCB 54707-301, and 90 and 92 patients in study INCB 54707-302, switched to povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg in the extension period, respectively. Among patients that received povorcitinib during the 12-week PC period, 185 and 183 patients in study INCB 54707-301, and 184 and 188 patients in study INCB 54707-302 continued to the extension period with povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg doses, respectively. The primary efficacy analysis for the 12-week PC period was performed in ITT population that included all randomised patients. Altogether 91/608 (15.0%) of patients in study INCB 54707-301 and 88/619 (14.2%) in study INCB 54707-302 were excluded from the PP population due to deviations that were considered to affect the primary endpoint, most common reason being mis-stratification based on ANdT count and/or previous treatment of HS with a biologic drug. In addition to the ITT and PP analysis populations, all patients that received povorcitinib during the extension period were included in Extension-Evaluable Population. Besides the protocol violations affecting the primary endpoint, the overall number of protocol violations during the PC period was relatively high. Major deviations were reported for 61.0% of patients in study INCB 54707-301 and 64.6% of patients in study INCB 54707-302. Critical deviations related to the exclusion criteria were reported for 2 patients in the placebo group, 2 patients in povorcitinib 45 mg

group and 1 patient in the povorcitinib 75 mg group in study INCB 54707-301 (none in study INCB

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

54707-302). Although numerous protocol violations occurred, they were distributed evenly across study groups and are not expected to compromise the overall integrity of the studies. During the extension period, the number of protocol violations somewhat increased compared to the PC period; however, the observed increase did not raise any concerns.

Treatment compliance remained high throughout the PC and extension periods, with no relevant differences between study groups.

## Baseline data

The mean age of patients in INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 studies was 37.7 and 37.0 years, respectively. Most patients were females (66.3% and 59.3%), mostly white (72.0% and 77.1%) or black/African American (16.1% and 12.3%). BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2 was reported for 66.6% and 60.4% of patients, respectively. Most patients were current (48.8% and 45.7%) or former (17.8% and 16.2%) smokers. In general, the demographic and baseline characteristics were well balanced between the study groups in both studies.

The mean time since HS diagnosis in INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 studies was 10-11 years in all study groups. Almost half of the patients (42.6% and 48.0%) had prior HS surgery in their medical history. Most patients (61.3% and 68.3%) had moderate HS based on Hurley score. Of note, most patients (81.1% and 82.7%) had severe disease based on IHS4 score of ≥ 11. Overall, there were no relevant differences across the study groups in baseline disease characteristics, HS disease history or other medical history.

Almost all patients, i.e. 585/608 (96.2%) of patients in study INCB 54707-301 and 587/619 (94.8%) of patients in study INCB 54707-302 had received prior oral antibiotic therapy, with most of these patients having an inadequate response to oral antibiotics, i.e. 531/585 (90.8%) and 533/587 (90.8%), respectively. Prior biologic therapy was used by 35.9% and 38.6%, most commonly anti-TNF therapy by 167/608 (27.5%) and 197/619 (31.8%) of patients, and prior anti-IL-17 therapy by 94/608 (15.5%) and 81/619 (13.1%) of patients, respectively. Among the patients with prior use of anti-TNF therapy, 88.0% and 85.8% of patients, while among the prior users of anti-IL-17 therapy, 72.3% and 70.4% had an inadequate response to therapy. In both studies, the study groups were generally well balanced regarding the prior therapies used.

## Outcomes and estimation

## Primary endpoint

In study INCB 54707-301, 29.7% of patients on placebo, 40.2% of patients on povorcitinib 45 mg and 40.6% of patients on 75 mg povorcitinib reached HiSCR50, resulting in a difference in response rate of 10.6% (95% CI 1.5, 19.7, p=0.0240) and 10.9% (95% CI 1.7, 20.2, p=0.0214) with povorcitinib 45 mg vs. placebo and povorcitinib 75 mg vs. placebo, respectively.

In study INCB 54707-302, 28.6% of patients on placebo, 42.3% of patients on povorcitinib 45 mg and 42.3% of patients on 75 mg povorcitinib reached HiSCR50, resulting in a difference in response rate of 13.8% (95% CI 4.7, 23.0, p=0.0035) and 13.8% (95% CI 4.7, 22.9, p=0.0033) with povorcitinib 45 mg vs. placebo and povorcitinib 75 mg vs. placebo, respectively.

Both phase 3 studies met their primary endpoint at povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 doses, i.e. reached the predefined statistical significance level (2-sided α = 0.025). The estimated treatment effect was similar with both povorcitinib doses (approximately 12% difference in response rate vs. placebo in the pooled phase 3 data), which could be considered modest, but clinically meaningful. Based on the primary and sensitivity analyses, the results of study INCB 54707-302 were statistically robust. However, the results of INCB 54707-301 were borderline significant for both dose levels in the primary analysis. IA

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

sensitivity analysis was conducted in which missing data were multiple imputed using a statistical model called fully conditional specification, essentially assuming randomly missing data (conditional on the observed data). For both studies, as compared with the primary analyses, these sensitivity analyses imply a somewhat stronger result in terms of p-values and estimated treatment effect which is likely explained by a trend toward a treatment effect also among those who dropped out or whose data were ignored due to an IE.

## Subgroup analysis

In a predefined subgroup analysis of the primary endpoint HiSCR50 (pooled ITT population), the treatment effect of povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg vs. placebo was generally consistent across the subgroups, except for a few subgroups, most likely due to a small number of patients in these subgroups. Of note, in the subgroup of patients with BMI ≥ 40 kg/m2, the response rate of povorcitinib 75 mg was 24/81 (29.6%) vs. 29/96 (30.2%) with placebo (difference to placebo -0.6% in the pooled phase 3 population), i.e. povorcitinib 75 mg appeared less effective in this subgroup than 45 mg, where the response rate was 40/92 (43.5%) (difference to placebo 13.3% in the pooled phase 3 population). This is likely a chance finding and the issue is not further pursued. The subgroup of biologic-experienced patients had a better response to both povorcitinib doses vs. placebo than the subgroup of biologic-naive patients.

Due to the small number of patients, it is not feasible to evaluate consistency of treatment effects across subgroups within the pooled post-anti-TNF population.

## Key secondary endpoints

In study INCB 54707-301 at week 12, 15.8%, 20.6% and 24.3% of patients achieved HiSCR75 in placebo, povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg groups, respectively; 22.1%, 31.8% and 34.8% achieved Skin Pain NRS30; and 33.7%, 25.0% and 26.2% had a flare by week 12. In study INCB 54707-302, the corresponding percentages of patients were 13.3%, 25.5%, 28.4% achieving HiSCR75; 17.9%, 40.6% and 37.7% achieving Skin Pain NRS30; and 33.5%, 21.6%, 20.7% having a flare. In terms of the planned hierarchical testing, statistical significance was not reached for any key secondary endpoints in study INCB 54707-301, while it was reached for all key secondary endpoints in study INCB 54707-302. Upon CHMP's request to discuss possible underlying reasons for the discrepancies observed between studies and the overall lower performance of study INCB 54707-301, the applicant performed logistic regression on primary and key secondary endpoints for both doses and in both populations (post-anti-TNF and ITT), with study and study*treatment interaction as additional factors. Interaction tests did not reveal statistically significant evidence of treatment-by-study heterogeneity for any primary or key secondary endpoints. Overall, both doses of povorcitinib provided comparable benefits; however, the HiSCR75 response rates were slightly higher for the 75 mg dose than for the 45 mg dose.

In both phase 3 studies, approximately the same proportion of patients in each study group (≤3%) received systemic antibiotic rescue therapy during the PC period. These patients were counted as nonresponders when analysing the primary and key secondary endpoint using the composite strategy. Given the low number of patients with systemic rescue treatment and similar distribution across study groups, there is no resulting bias in the efficacy analysis. The proportion of patients receiving additional rescue lesional treatment where slightly higher in povorcitinib groups vs. placebo in study INCB 54707-301 (12.9-13.2% vs. 8.9%, respectively) and lower in study INCB 54707-302 (4.8-6.7% vs. 9.9%, respectively). This imbalance between the studies is not considered to have relevant impact on the overall interpretation of the efficacy results.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

All treatment groups in both phase 3 studies had a modest decrease in analgesic and opioid use by the end of the PC period, with no significant differences among groups.

## Post-Anti-TNF population

In addition to the efficacy analyses performed in the whole ITT populations of the phase 3 studies, the applicant performed an analysis of the primary and key secondary endpoints in a Post-Anti-TNF population, which was prospectively defined in a SAP dated prior to the database lock for the primary endpoint analyses to support the claimed indication in the post-anti-TNF patients population. The PostAnti-TNF ITT population consisted of 154 patients (25.3%) and 176 (28.4%) of patients in studies INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302, respectively, representing 26.9% of the whole ITT Population in phase 3 studies.

Neither of the studies reached statistical difference for povorcitinib 45 mg or 75 mg vs. placebo for the primary endpoint, and neither were the studies powered to demonstrate such a difference, as no power estimates or sample size calculations were made for the Post-Anti-TNF population. Nevertheless, the estimated treatment effect (difference in response rate) for povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg vs. placebo in the Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population was of similar magnitude as in the ITT population. The comparison of the pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT and ITT populations and the efficacy results in these populations are discussed below.

## Analysis performed in pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT and pooled ITT Population from the phase 3 studies

To allow estimating the treatment effect with greater precision in the targeted population (i.e. postanti-TNF), the applicant combined data across the two identical pivotal trials. This is agreed by the CHMP. The pooled analysis supports judgment on clinical relevance by reducing the uncertainty as reflected by the confidence intervals.

With respect to the methodology, the integrated analysis pooled together the data from the two pivotal studies. The statistical methods are identical to those used in the individual studies which implies that the statistical models did not account for a study effect, if any. Given the identical designs and concurrency of the studies, \"study\" is arguably an administrative factor and, as such, not necessarily included as a factor or covariate in the statistical analysis. For further discussion on the methodology, refer to the discussion on the individual studies. Neither do the results raise concerns about heterogeneity between the trials. No formal type 1 error control was implemented to the pooled analyses; therefore, all results are considered exploratory and any p-values and confidence intervals are considered nominal.

According to the HS ISE SAP, the Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population included \"all randomised participants with documented history of inadequate response to at least a 3-month course of at least 1 anti-TNF biologic drug for HS (or demonstrated intolerance to or have a contraindication to an anti-TNF biologic drug for treatment of their HS).\" Based on the disposition, 100% of patients in the pooled Post-AntiTNF ITT had received previous anti-TNF therapy. The applicant further clarified that while the majority of patients (88.6%-90.9%) in the Post-Anti-TNF population entered INCB 54707-301 or INCB 54707-302 study with a prior inadequate response to at least 1 anti-TNF therapy for HS, a smaller proportion had intolerance (12.3%-13.1%) or contraindication (1.7%-2.6%), which is consistent with the proposed indication wording, i.e. \"adults who have responded inadequately to, or who are intolerant or contraindicated to an anti-TNF therapy\".

There were no major differences in disposition, demographics or other baseline characteristics between the (pooled) Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population and (pooled) ITT Population, and the treatment groups within these populations were generally well balanced. The mean age of the pooled Post-Anti-TNF ITT

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

and ITT Population was 38.6 and 37.3 years, respectively. Only few patients were 65 years or older. In both populations, most patients were female (63%), White (approximately 75%) or Black (approximately 14%), and mostly from North America (52-56%) or from Europe and Australia (44-46%).

In terms of baseline disease characteristics, the Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population had more severe HS (47.9% Hurley stage III) than ITT Population (35.1% Hurley Stage III), including higher lesion counts and higher baseline disease scores, e.g. Skin Pain NRS scores. 23.6% and 12.4% of patients in the Post-Anti-TNF ITT Population had received prior anti-IL-17 therapy and other biologic therapy, respectively, compared to 14.3% and 4.7% in the ITT population. Overall, the patients in the Post-AntiTNF Population had more advanced HS compared to the ITT Population representing a clinically relevant patient population inherently more difficult to treat. In the Post-Anti-TNF ITT population, adalimumab was the most common prior anti-TNF treatment, reported by 96.8% and 97.2% of the patients in the INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 studies, respectively. Secukinumab was the most common prior anti-IL-17 treatment in the Post-Anti-TNF ITT population, reported by 32/43 (74.4%) and 26/35 (74.3%) of those with prior anti-IL-17 treatment in the INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 studies, respectively.

The estimates of povorcitinib treatment effects remained consistent with those from the individual studies with less uncertainty. Based on the pooled phase 3 data from the post-anti-TNF population, the estimates and 95% CI for the week 12 HiSCR50 effect vs. placebo were 17.7% (5.7, 29.7) and 14.0% (2.0, 26.0), for povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg doses vs. placebo, respectively, i.e. somewhat better than in the pooled ITT Population. These results, together with the corresponding pooled results for the key secondary endpoint HiSCR75 at week 12 [15.9% (7.7, 24.1), 17.0% (8.6, 25.5)] and flare by week 12 [-15.4% (-28.0, -2.8), -18.9% (-31.4, -6.3)] support existence of a clinically relevant effect on reducing and preventing abscesses and inflammatory nodules in the population who have previously failed anti-TNF treatment. The corresponding results for the key secondary endpoints skin pain NRS30 at week 12 failed in supporting an effect in the pooled post-anti-TNF population at nominal 95% confidence level, whereas a statistically compelling effect on skin pain NRS30 was observed for both dose levels in the pooled ITT population. It should be noted that skin pain was evaluated only among participants with baseline skin pain NRS score ≥3, leading to smaller sample size. Despite the lack of statistical robustness in post-anti-TNF population, the results for skin pain NRS30 were in line with the pooled ITT population, i.e. the estimates and 95% CI for the povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg doses vs. placebo in the pooled post-anti-TNF population were 12.3 (0.4, 24.2) and 8.1 (-3.6, 19.9). Notably, the differences in the response rates between povorcitinib and placebo in the post-anti-TNF population vs. ITT population in the primary and key secondary endpoints were largely due to lower placebo responses in the post-anti-TNF population. Overall, the results demonstrated that the benefits of povorcitinib observed in the phase 3 studies in the whole (ITT) population can be extrapolated to the post-anti-TNF population.

## Long-term efficacy

When interpreting response kinetics over time from the HiSCR graphs, it is noteworthy that response rates out of all randomised patients are presented up to week 12, whereas for the extension period, the responses are shown for patients assessed at each visit (ignoring the dropouts). Altogether 41% of the patients in the pooled Post-Anti-TNF population discontinued the study during the extension period, most common reasons being withdrawal by the participant (16.4%) and lack of efficacy (8.9%). Nevertheless, the proportion of patients who achieved HiSCR50 or HiSCR75 throughout the extension period remained stable or slightly increased in both povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg groups. In the placebo group that crossed over to povorcitinib at week 12, a rapid increase in proportion of patients gaining HiSCR50 and HiSCR75 was evident, consistent with the primary efficacy analysis. Based on further analysis requested by the CHMP, it was evident that some patients with only partial response, i.e. not reaching HiSCR50 at week 12, showed further improvement at week 24. This was reflected in the section 4.2 of theSmPC, which advises that, while consideration should be given to discontinuing treatment in patients who have shown no evidence of therapeutic benefit after 12 weeks of treatment, patients with an initial partial response may subsequently improve with continued treatment. Among patients on povorcitinib who achieved HiSCR50 or HiSCR75 at week 12, 54.5% and 73.3% achieved maintenance of HiSCR50, and 61.1% and 73.7% maintenance of HiSCR75 at week 54 in the povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg groups, respectively. While the fluctuating disease course of HS complicates interpretation of long-term response patterns, the totality of efficacy data suggests sustained benefit with long-term povorcitinib treatment, i.e. up to 54 weeks. This information has been adequately reflected in SmPC section 5.1. Patients who complete either of the pivotal phase 3 studies are eligible to participate in a treatment-extension study INCB 54707-312, which is currently ongoing. Once available, the results will be submitted for assessment and will provide further data on efficacy and safety of povorcitinib for up to 106 weeks of treatment (also see RMP).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Povorcitinib 45 mg vs 75 mg dose

Overall, the results of the primary and key secondary endpoints suggested that the efficacy of povorcitinib at 45 mg and 75 mg doses is similar in both post-anti-TNF and ITT populations. For certain secondary endpoints (HiSCR75, HiSCR90, HiSCR100, DLQI) and in a post-hoc analysis of dT counts in the post-anti-TNF population, 75 mg dose showed slightly better improvement than 45 mg dose during early timepoints (weeks 3 to 6). This pattern persisted at week 12 for HiSCR90 and HiSCR100, where the 75 mg dose continued to demonstrate better responses than the 45 mg dose in the post-anti-TNF population. The applicant also performed an ad hoc E-R analysis evaluating the impact of povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg on efficacy endpoints derived from dT counts. Compared with povorcitinib 45 mg, patients with a baseline dT counts ≥ 5 who received povorcitinib 75 mg had approximately 40% higher odds of achieving a reduction in dT counts and 40% lower odds of experiencing disease worsening. Based on the results, it was plausible that certain patients, e.g. those with higher disease burden, could benefit from the higher 75 mg dose. The applicant proposed 45 mg dose as a main dose, and at the physician's discretion 75 mg dose for patients with high disease burden and those who have an inadequate response to 45 mg. However, patients having \"high disease burden\" or \"inadequate response\" were not prospectively defined in the studies. It was noted that in patients according to Hurley stage (II vs III) or draining tunnel count (0, 1-2, ≥3), no meaningful difference in efficacy was observed between two povorcitinib doses (for pooled ITT population). Upon CHMP's request, through the analysis of several baseline disease parameters associated with higher disease burden (i.e. ANdT 20-96, dT 6-19, HiSQoL total score 44-68, skin pain NRS score &gt;7 to ≤10 and hsCRP &gt;15 to ≤210), the applicant sufficiently justified that HS is a heterogeneous disease and showed that no single disease characteristic, in isolation, is sufficient to define high disease burden. The applicant performed further post hoc analysis comparing the effect of povorcitinib 45 mg vs. 75 mg in these subgroups representative of high disease burden. When clinically meaningful responses were defined as HiSCR75, dT75 (≥75% decrease in dT count for patients with baseline dT≥1), Skin Pain NRS 0 to ≤4, HiSQoL total score 0 to ≤14 and hsCRP75 (≥75% decrease in hsCRP), it was evident that povorcitinib 75 mg led to higher responses vs. 45 mg in most of the endpoints assessed at weeks 3, 12, 24 and 54 in these subgroups. Although these analyses were performed post-hoc, they supported the conclusion that in certain cases, in patients with high disease burden, the higher 75 mg dose may be appropriate. Nevertheless, and consistent with the outcome of the Article 20 referral on JAK inhibitors (EMA/586384/2022), the final agreed posology in SmPC section 4.2 recommends 45 mg once daily for patients at higher risk of VTE, MACE or malignancy, whereas 75 mg dose may be appropriate for patients with a high disease burden who are not at increased risk of these events or for patients with an inadequate response to 45 mg. The lowest effective dose to maintain response is also recommended to be used.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 5.3.8.2 Conclusions on the clinical efficacy

Overall, the clinical development programme for povorcitinib in HS in adults was robust.

The estimated treatment effect (difference in response rate) for povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg vs. placebo in the Post-Anti-TNF Population was of similar magnitude as in the ITT population and showed a clinically relevant effect on reducing and preventing abscesses and inflammatory nodules in the population who have previously failed anti-TNF treatment.

The CHMP therefore concluded that the efficacy data in the post-anti-TNF population supports the following indication:

Povofortay is indicated for the treatment of active moderate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa (acne inversa) in adults who have responded inadequately to, or who are intolerant or contraindicated to an anti-TNF therapy.

## 5.4 Clinical safety

Please refer to the table of studies in section 5.3.2

For the purpose of this document, the following definitions apply:

'Adverse event - AE' means any untoward medical occurrence in a subject to whom a medicinal product is administered and which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with this treatment.

'Serious adverse event - SAE' means any untoward medical occurrence that at any dose requires inpatient hospitalisation or prolongation of existing hospitalisation, results in persistent or significant disability or incapacity, results in a congenital anomaly or birth defect, is life-threatening, or results in death. The definition (in line with ICH E2A) includes important medical events that may not be immediately life-threatening or result in death or hospitalisation but may jeopardise the patient or may require intervention to prevent one of the other outcomes listed in the definition above.

'Adverse drug reaction - ADR' means any untoward and unintended response to a medicinal product related to any dose administered, for which, after a thorough assessment, a causal relationship between the medicinal product and the adverse event is at least a reasonable possibility, based for example, on their comparative incidence in clinical trials, or findings from epidemiological studies and/or on an evaluation of causality from individual case reports.

The integrated safety dataset includes data from 9 studies (INCB 54707-202, -203, -204, -205, -206, - 207, -301, -302, and -312). ## 5.4.3 Adverse events

As there were no obvious differences in the overall incidences or in the types of common AEs between post anti-TNF population and all HS population the analysis of AEs is primarily focused on the all HS population (Pool 1 and Pool 2).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Overall Summary of Adverse Events

Phase 3 Hidradenitis Suppurativa Post-Anti-TNF Placebo-Controlled Population (Pool 1b)

In the Phase 3 HS Post-Anti-TNF PC Population (Pool 1b), the overall incidence of TEAEs was lower in participants in the placebo group than in those who took povorcitinib (see Table 69).

Phase 3 Hidradenitis Suppurativa Placebo-Controlled Population (Pool 1)

Similar to the Phase 3 HS Post-Anti-TNF PC Population (Pool 1b), the incidence of TEAEs was lower in participants in the placebo group than in those who took povorcitinib (see Table 69).

## Common Adverse Events

Across all pools, the most commonly reported TEAE by PT was acne, which occurred more frequently in the povorcitinib groups compared with the placebo group. The other 5 most common TEAEs across all pools included headache, upper respiratory tract infection, COVID-19, nasopharyngitis, and fatigue.

## Treatment-Related Adverse Events

Across all pools, the incidence of treatment-related TEAEs was lower in participants in the placebo group than in those who took povorcitinib. The most frequently occurring treatment-related TEAE (occurring in ≥ 5% of participants in the povorcitinib total group) was acne.

The following events were the most frequently reported treatment-related TEAEs after acne: fatigue, nausea, headache, upper respiratory tract infection, blood creatine phosphokinase increased, nasopharyngitis, and folliculitis.

Treatment-related TEAEs occurring in &gt; 1% of participants in the povorcitinib total group in the Phase 3 HS Post-Anti-TNF PC Population (Pool 1b) and Phase 3 HS PC Population (Pool 1) included acne, fatigue, headache, asthenia, nausea, upper respiratory tract infection, diarrhea, nasopharyngitis, oral herpes, UTI, folliculitis, and blood CPK increased.

Treatment-related TEAEs occurring in &gt; 2% of participants in the povorcitinib total group in the All HS Post-Anti-TNF Population (Pool 2b) were acne, fatigue, upper respiratory tract infection, blood CPK increased, headache, folliculitis, dermatitis acneiform, nasopharyngitis, nausea, oral herpes and urinary track infection.

## Long-Term Adverse Effects

The safety of povorcitinib up to 54 weeks in adults with HS was evaluated in the completed pivotal Phase 3 studies. The safety of povorcitinib beyond 54 weeks (up to 100 weeks) is being evaluated in the ongoing treatment-extension study (INCB 54707-312). At the time of data cut-off (26 November 2025), there is no evidence of a difference in the types of TEAEs observed with longer periods of exposure.

Adverse event data from study INCB 54707-204 were explored as this study provides the longest duration of exposure to povorcitinib (up to 100 weeks of treatment with povorcitinib 45 or 75 mg). Those safety data are included in the integrated safety dataset in Pool 2 (All HS Population) and Pool 3 (All povorcitinib Population). In study INCB 54707-204, the occurrence of the most frequent TEAEs for participants in the povorcitinib 45- and 75-mg groups with continued exposure through Weeks 52 (OLE period) and 104 (LTE period) was consistent with that through Week 16 (PC period). There were no changes suggestive of delayed onset of TEAEs with prolonged exposure to povorcitinib. Similarly, within the All HS Population (Pool 2) and All povorcitinib Population (Pool 3), there was no pattern of increasing probability of onset of a first event in any of the categories of interest with long-term treatment with povorcitinib.

The ADRs identified for povorcitinib by the applicant are based on the sponsor's medical assessment of each event, by individual PT or by grouped terms, to determine if a causal relationship with the treatment is a reasonable possibility. The review consisted of all TEAEs, including AESIs, ECIs, ≥ Grade 3 TEAEs, serious TEAE, fatal TEAEs, TEAEs leading to study drug discontinuation or dose interruption, and laboratory abnormalities regardless of incidence. The following factors were considered when making decisions on whether a causal relationship to povorcitinib in HS is plausible: frequency of the event, TEAE rates seen with povorcitinib (45 mg and 75 mg) vs placebo, biological plausibility based on povorcitinib mechanism of action and known effects of JAKi class, population under study (including comorbidities and prior/concomitant therapy) and incidence of Grade 3 or higher TEAEs, serious TEAEs, or TEAEs leading to study drug discontinuation.

## 5.4.4 Adverse events of special interest, serious adverse events and deaths, other significant events

## Adverse Events of Special Interest

Adverse Events of Special Interest were predefined in the Phase 3 clinical development program. These events were selected due to their relevance for safety monitoring in chronic inflammatory diseases across the JAKi class and included serious infections, opportunistic infections, herpes zoster, tuberculosis, malignancies, cardiovascular events, other embolic and thrombotic events. Cytopenias and lipid abnormalities are also part of the safety monitoring of systemic JAKis and are discussed in more detail in section 5.4.9.

Additional AESIs, including gastrointestinal perforations, hypersensitivity reactions, and HS exacerbations, were events that were selected after protocol finalisation and based on regulatory feedback. These additional AESIs were included to gather further data.

For AESIs, in addition to crude pooling, exposure-adjusted, study-size-adjusted, and study-size-adjusted and exposure-adjusted IRs are summarised for the All HS (Pool 2) and All povorcitinib Populations (Pool 3).

Serious and Opportunistic Infections

Serious and Opportunistic Infections in Pool 1 (Phase 3 Hidradenitis Suppurativa Placebo-Controlled Population) in Pool 2 (All Hidradenitis Suppurativa Population) are presented in Table 78 and Table 79 below.

The serious infection types in Pool 2 were generally consistent with those expected in HS populations and were predominantly skin/soft tissue infections (e.g., cellulitis, erysipelas, scrotal abscess, subcutaneous abscess, and sweat gland infection) as well as extracutaneous bacterial infections (eg, UTI, lower respiratory tract infection, and diverticulitis).

In the total povorcitinib group in Pool 2, the highest conditional probability of a first serious infection was during Weeks 24 to &lt;52 (1.3) and ≥52 weeks (1.3). The small number of events, particularly in the povorcitinib groups among participants in Pool 2 exposed to povorcitinib for ≥52 weeks (12 events) limits the ability to draw firm dose-response conclusions. In Pool 2, treatment-related serious infections were reported in 6 participants in the 75-mg without dose change group and 1 participant in the 15-mg group. All of these events resolved after an interruption or with no change to the study drug.

Based on the updated safety dataset, opportunistic infections were uncommon in the povorcitinib groups and no clear treatment-related signal or dose/dependency trend is described. Opportunistic infections were reported in 7 participants; 2 participants had localised ophthalmic herpetic infections (1 event each of herpes simplex and herpes zoster). Both events were nonserious, not considered related to study drug, and resolved without sequelae. Five participants had events of herpes zoster cutaneous disseminated and met the SMQ criteria for both herpes zoster and opportunistic infection AESI categories. All opportunistic infection events were Grade 2 in severity and recovered/resolved with concomitant medication. 9 events of oral candidiasis were observed among povorcitinib participants (1 in 15 mg, 5 in 45 mg, 3 in 75 mg group) whereas none were reported in the placebo group. None of the events were considered SAEs. However, the candidiasis events did not increase during longer treatment and among the observed cases, there were predisposing factors such as inhaled corticosteroids and active smoking.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

In Pool 1, there was 1 event in the povorcitinib 45-mg group and it was considered unrelated. In the All HS Population (Pool 2), the exposure-adjusted incidence rate and study size- and exposureadjusted incidence rate in the povorcitinib total group were each 0.5 per 100 PY. All of the events that were considered opportunistic infections were herpes virus related and deemed opportunistic based on the anatomic location (ophthalmic location or multidermatomal distribution). There were no Nocardia, mycobacterial, or deep fungal infections were identified. The small number of events, particularly in the povorcitinib groups, limits the ability to draw firm dose-response conclusions.

## Herpes Zoster

Herpes zoster (HZ) events were reported in povorcitinib-treated participants. All were nonserious, Grade 1 or 2 in severity, and generally involved a single dermatome. Few led to interruption or discontinuation of study drug, and most had resolved by the end of the study. The study size- and exposure-adjusted IR of HZ events was higher for the povorcitinib 75-mg without dose change group (2.7 per 100 PY) compared with the povorcitinib 45-mg group (1.9 per 100 PY).

In the Phase 3 HS PC Population (Pool 1), 5 participants (0.6%) in the povorcitinib total group and no participants in the placebo group had a HZ event, with similar incidences for the povorcitinib 45-mg group (0.5%) and the povorcitinib 75-mg group (0.7%).

In the All HS Population (Pool 2), the overall incidence of HZ events in the povorcitinib total group (2.5%) remained low, with events reported in 0.9% of participants in the povorcitinib 45-mg group and 2.4% of participants in the povorcitinib 75-mg without dose change group. No participant in the placebo group had a HZ event.

The IRs of HZ events after adjusting for exposure (2.5 participants with the event per 100 PYs of exposure for the povorcitinib total group), study-size (2.4% in the povorcitinib total group), and exposure and study-size (2.5 participants with the event per 100 PYs of exposure for the povorcitinib total group) were low. Notably, the study-size- and exposure-adjusted IR of HZ events was higher for the povorcitinib 75-mg without dose change group (2,7 participants with the event per 100 PYs of exposure) compared with the povorcitinib 45-mg group (1.9 participants with the event per 100 PYs of exposure).

To evaluate if long-term exposure with povorcitinib was associated with increased risk of HZ events, 3 separate analyses were performed: HZ events were summarised for the subset of participants in the All HS Population who had more than 52 weeks of study drug exposure, the conditional probability of a first HZ event was summarised over time for the All HS (Pool 2) and All povorcitinib Populations (Pool 3), and the time to onset of HZ events was determined for the All HS and All povorcitinib populations. The incidence of HZ infections among participants who were treated for 52 weeks or longer remained low (3.4% of participants in the povorcitinib total groups). The median time to onset of HZ events for participants in the povorcitinib total group was 291.5 days for the All HS Population (Pool 2) and 268.0 days for the All povorcitinib Population (Pool 3). Consistent with these median times to onset of HZ events, the conditional probability of a first HZ event increased with prolonged treatment with povorcitinib (≥ 24 weeks of treatment with povorcitinib).

Integrated safety dataset: HZ AESIs were reported by 41 participants (40 participants in the povorcitinib total group and 1 participant in the placebo group). None of these HZ AESIs were serious TEAEs; all were Grades 1 and 2 in severity. 10 of the 27 participants who had HZ events in the pivotal studies had single dermatomes or zoster in a single anatomical area; 1 participant had multidermatomal involvement, and for the remainder of participants, there was insufficient detail available to determine single or multiple dermatome involvement. 18 participants had at least 1 HZ TEAE that led to interruption of the study drug, and 4 participants had at least 1 HZ TEAE that led to discontinuation of the study drug (all PTs of HZ). The majority of events had been resolved at the time of the data cut-off (4 participants had events that were not resolved, ongoing, or resolving). Of these 4 participants, 1 had no reported treatment for HZ; the other 3 participants were treated with an antiviral.

## Tuberculosis

There were no treatment-emergent AESIs related to tuberculosis at the time of data cut-off.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Malignancies

The overall incidence of malignancies for the Phase 3 HS PC Population (Pool 1) among participants in the placebo treatment group was low (0.5%), and no participant on povorcitinib had a malignancy event. No event by PT was reported in more than 1 participant.

The overall incidences of malignancies in the povorcitinib total group (0.6%) and the placebo group (0.4%) in the All HS Population (Pool 2) were low and similar between the groups. Basal cell carcinoma, in 4 participants (0.3%) in the povorcitinib total group and 1 participant (0.2%) in the placebo group, was the most frequently reported malignancy. Bowen's disease in 2 participants (0.1%) in the povorcitinib total group was the only other malignancy event reported in more than 1 participant in the All HS Population (Pool 2).

After adjusting for exposure (0.6 and 1.9 participants with the event per 100 PYs of exposure for the povorcitinib total and placebo groups, respectively), study-size (0.4% and 0.4% in the povorcitinib total and placebo groups, respectively), and exposure and study-size (0.6 and 1.7 participants with the event per 100 PYs of exposure for the povorcitinib total and placebo groups, respectively), IRs were either similar or lower for participants who took povorcitinib compared with placebo. After adjusting for study-size and exposure, there were no notable differences in IRs for the povorcitinib 45-mg group and the povorcitinib 75-mg without dose change group. The most frequently reported malignancies in the All povorcitinib Population (Pool 3) were consistent with those of the All HS Population (Pool 2).

To evaluate if long-term exposure with povorcitinib was associated with increased risk of malignancies, 3 separate analyses were performed: malignancies were summarised for the subset of participants in the All HS Population (Pool 2) who had more than 52 weeks of study drug exposure; the conditional probability of a first malignancy event was summarised over time for the All HS (Pool 2) and All povorcitinib Populations (Pool 3), and the time to onset of malignancies was determined for the All HS and All povorcitinib Populations. The incidence of malignancies among participants who were treated for 52 weeks or longer remained low (0.0% and 1.0% of participants in the placebo and povorcitinib total groups, respectively). The median time to onset of malignancy for participants in the povorcitinib total group was 172.0 days for the All HS Population (Pool 2) and 172.0 days for the All Povorcitinib Population (Pool 3). No clear pattern of increased conditional probability of a first malignancy event was observed for the All HS (Pool 2) and All povorcitinib Populations (Pool 3).

Integrated safety dataset: Malignancies were reported in 9 participants (povorcitinib total: 7 participants, placebo: 2 participants). All AESIs of malignancy were considered by the investigator as not related or unlikely related to the study drug. Most of the events were recovered or recovering at the data cut-off, with the exception of 3 events: 1 fatal Grade 5 event of metastatic neoplasm in the povorcitinib 75-mg with dose change group (INCB 54707-204), 1 event in the placebo group (Grade 3 breast cancer), and 1 event of Grade 2 basal cell carcinoma in the povorcitinib 45-mg group which led to study drug discontinuation.

Three participants had a serious AESI of malignancy: breast cancer, metastatic neoplasm, and lung adenocarcinoma stage IV in 1 participant each. Three participants had at least 1 AESI of malignancy that was Grade 3 or higher; all others were Grades 1 or 2 in severity. No participant had an AESI of malignancy that led to interruption of study drug. Four participants had an AESI of malignancy (basal cell carcinoma, superficial spreading melanoma stage unspecified [diagnosed during screening, before participant received first dose of povorcitinib], breast cancer, and lung adenocarcinoma Stage IV) that led to discontinuation of study drug, which was defined in the protocol and varied by region.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Cardiovascular Events (MACE)

The incidences of cardiovascular events (MACE) were low (≤ 0.2% for each of the pooled populations). Cardiovascular events (MACE) occurred in 3 participants and included the following:

Grade 5 myocardial infarction (on Day 114) in a participant with CSU (Study INCB 54707-207) and ongoing hypercholesterolemia in the povorcitinib 75-mg without dose change group. The event was independently assessed by both sponsor and investigator as not related to study drug.

One participant in the povorcitinib 75-mg with dose change group reported a Grade 3 AESI of acute myocardial infarction (onset on Day 237) that was considered by the investigator to be unlikely related to study drug. The event led to study drug discontinuation and resolved with sequelae. The participant had a medical history of uncontrolled HS, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and was a daily smoker. The investigator considered these risk factors in context of long-standing inflammation (hsCRP 6.64 before the study) were the most likely contributors to the event.

Grade 4 ischemic stroke (onset on Day 386) in a participant with HS in the povorcitinib 45-mg group. The participant presented to an outside hospital with symptoms described as ophthalmic migraine. No additional neurologic findings were described, and no physician examination findings were made available for review. No further clinical details or source documentation could be obtained from the outside hospital. Neuroimaging, including noncontrast brain magnetic resonance imaging, brain CT, and CT angiography, showed no abnormality and no evidence of ischemia. The participant had significant vascular risk factors, including severe obesity and active smoking. The event, initially reported by the investigator as related to study drug, led to study drug interruption and was reported as resolved with sequelae. Based on the limited available information, the sponsor did not concur with the diagnosis of ischemic stroke. The event, as described, lacks clinical or radiographic evidence supporting an acute ischemic process. The clinical description is limited to \"ophthalmic migraine,\" and all neuroimaging was normal. Further follow-up was not possible as the event occurred entirely at an outside facility, and no additional records could be obtained despite multiple attempts. Given the absence of objective evidence of ischemia and the participant's substantial underlying risk factors for vascular events (severe obesity and active smoking), the sponsor considers the reported event not suspected to be related to povorcitinib.

## Other Embolic and Thrombotic Events

There were no events of other embolic and thrombotic events in Pool 1 and Pool 1b. The exposureadjusted incidence rates of other embolic and thrombotic events (combined venous and arterial) were low in both the All HS Population (Pool 2; 0.6 per 100 PY) and the All povorcitinib Population (Pool 3; 0.7 per 100 PY) and were less than estimated background rates for patients with HS in the US population-based study of over 49,000 patients identified in US healthcare claims data (3.84 per 100 PY) There were no observable trends with regard to treatment group and duration of exposure. (Table 80).
