## 7. Pharmacovigilance

## 7.1 Pharmacovigilance system

The CHMP considers that the pharmacovigilance system summary submitted by the applicant fulfils the requirements of Article 8(3) of Directive 2001/83/EC.

## 7.2 Periodic safety update reports (PSURs) submission requirements

The active substance is not included in the EURD list and a new entry will be required. The new list of Union reference dates (EURD list) entry uses the European birth date (EBD) or the international birth date (IBD) to determine the forthcoming Data Lock Points. The requirements for submission of periodic safety update reports for this medicinal product are set out in the Annex II, Section C of the CHMP Opinion.

## 8. Product information

## 8.1 Summary of product characteristics (SmPC)

## 8.1.1 SmPC section 4.1 justification

The claimed target population is a subgroup of patients that have previously received anti-TNF treatment (i.e. Post-Anti-TNF population). More specifically, the proposed indication for povorcitinib is: \"Treatment of active moderate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa (acne inversa) in adults who have responded inadequately to, or who are intolerant or contraindicated to an anti-TNF therapy\".

Although the conventional/ standard approach of aligning the wording of the HS-indication with recent precedents (involving comparable development programs and study populations) would generally be preferable for consistency, there are no regulatory grounds to refuse approval of the proposed subpopulation, provided the overall benefit-risk balance for this group remains positive.

A separate statistical analysis plan (SAP) for this subgroup was in place and dated prior to the database lock for the primary analysis (12 weeks).

Overall, the results, based on the analysis of the primary and key secondary endpoints in a Post-AntiTNF population, demonstrated that the benefits of povorcitinib observed in the phase 3 studies in the whole (ITT) population can be extrapolated to the post-anti-TNF population. The CHMP concluded that the efficacy data in the post-anti-TNF population supports the above-mentioned claimed indication.

## 8.1.2 SmPC section 5.1 justification

The main efficacy results presented in SmPC section 5.1 consist of those for the \"on-label\" indication, corresponding to the sought post-anti-TNF subgroup. The studies were not powered to demonstrate statistically significant differences between povorcitinib and placebo within this subgroup. To better characterise and estimate the treatment effect in this targeted subgroup with greater precision, data from the two identical trials were pooled and these results are presented in SmPC section 5.1. This pooled analysis enables a more robust judgement of the clinical relevance by reducing uncertainty, as reflected in the narrower confidence intervals, and hence considered most relevant way of presenting results for prescribers.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Nevertheless, the observed treatment effect in the post-anti-TNF subgroup was of a similar magnitude to that seen in the overall ITT population, in which efficacy was formally demonstrated. Consequently, results from the overall ITT population are included in section 5.1 only for the primary analysis (primary endpoint).

## 8.2 Labelling

## 8.2.1 User consultation

The full user testing utilising written readability method vs verbal face-to-face interview is considered to be acceptable, although it does not quite meet the success criteria of the EC Readability guideline: 90% of test participants find and understand information. An alternative success criteria (80% finding and understanding) specifically for user tests employing written responses has been discussed by the CMDh in their Position paper CMDh/234/2011, Rev. 01 December 2016 in section 4 \"Self-completion method\". In light of this position paper, the results of the submitted user consultation's second round, where lowest percentage for correct answers was 83 and only one incidence of not finding the correct answer occurred, are considered to be adequate proof of readability.

## 8.2.1.1 Conclusion from the checklist for the review of user consultation

The results of the user consultation with target patient groups on the package leaflet submitted by the applicant show that the package leaflet meets the criteria for readability as set out in the Guideline on the readability of the label and package leaflet of medicinal products for human use. Discrepancy is considered to be justified by the different testing method \"self-completion\" described in the CMDh Position paper (CMDh/234/2011, Rev. 01 December 2016) in section 4.

## 8.3 Additional monitoring

Pursuant to Article 23(1) of Regulation No (EU) 726/2004, Povofortay (povorcitinib) is included in the additional monitoring list since as it contains a new active substance which, on 1 January 2011, was not contained in any medicinal product authorised in the EU.

Therefore, the summary of product characteristics and the package leaflet include a statement that this medicinal product is subject to additional monitoring and will allow quick identification of new safety information. The statement is preceded by an inverted equilateral black triangle.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 9. Benefit-risk assessment

## 9.1 Therapeutic context

## 9.1.1 Disease or condition, proposed therapeutic indication

Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic disabling and debilitating inflammatory skin condition characterised by painful nodules and abscesses in early stages and draining tunnels (fistulas) and irreversible tissue damage and scarring in more severe disease. The lesions characteristically develop in the axillae and in the inframammary, inguinal, or gluteal regions. The estimated prevalence of HS in Europe is approximately 1%. For further details, see section 2.1.

The proposed indication for povorcitinib is treatment of active moderate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa (acne inversa) in adults who have responded inadequately to, or who are intolerant or contraindicated to an anti-TNF therapy.

## 9.1.2 Available therapies and unmet medical need

For a detailed description, please see section 2.1 of this document.

In general, first-line treatments of HS consist of antibiotics (topical and oral), antiseptic washes, intralesional corticosteroid injections, and lifestyle modification (e.g. smoking cessation), followed by second-line treatment with a biologic medicine. Third-line treatments include surgical intervention for patients with chronic lesions that do not respond to medication.

A significant proportion of patients do not respond to approved biological medicines, or their HS becomes refractory to therapy. The limitations of current treatments highlight the need for safe and effective new treatment options for patients with active moderate to severe HS.

## 9.2 Main clinical studies

For a detailed description of the main clinical studies supporting this application, please refer to section 5.3.2 of this document.

The key evaluation of efficacy and safety is based on two identical multicenter, randomised, doubleblind, placebo-controlled pivotal studies INCB 54707-301 and 54707-302. The study population in these studies consisted of patients ≥ 18 years of age who had a clinical diagnosis of moderate to severe HS (Hurley Stage II or III) for at least 3 months at the time of screening and who had a documented history of inadequate response to at least a 3-month course of at least 1 conventional systemic therapy (oral antibiotic or biologic drug) for HS (or demonstrated intolerance to, or had a contraindication to, a conventional systemic therapy for treatment of their HS), with HS lesions in at least 2 distinct anatomical areas and total AN count of at least 5. Both studies included an initial 12 week-double-blind PC treatment period where patients were randomised (1:1:1) to povorcitinib (45 mg or 75 mg QD) or placebo, followed by a 42-week extension period, during which patients on povorcitinib continued on the same povorcitinib dose, and patients on placebo received (1:1) povorcitinib 45 mg or 75 mg.

Altogether 608 and 619 patients were randomised in the INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302 studies, respectively, to receive placebo (n=202 and 203), povorcitinib 45 mg (n=204 and 208) or povorcitinib 75 mg (n=202 and 208). The Post-Anti-TNF population that is relevant for the therapeutic indication consisted of 154 patients (25.3%) and 176 (28.4%) of patients in studies INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302, respectively, representing 26.9% of the whole ITT Population in phase 3 studies.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 9.3 Favourable effects

## ITT population

## Primary endpoint

Both phase 3 studies met their primary endpoint HiSCR50 at povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 doses. In study INCB 54707-301, 29.7% of patients on placebo, 40.2% of patients on povorcitinib 45 mg and 40.6% of patients on 75 mg povorcitinib reached HiSCR50, resulting in a difference in response rate of 10.6% (95% CI 1.5, 19.7, p=0.0240) and 10.9% (95% CI 1.7, 20.2, p=0.0214) with povorcitinib 45 mg vs. placebo and povorcitinib 75 mg vs. placebo, respectively. In study INCB 54707-302, 28.6% of patients on placebo, 42.3% of patients on povorcitinib 45 mg and 42.3% of patients on 75 mg povorcitinib reached HiSCR50, resulting in a difference in response rate of 13.8% (95% CI 4.7, 23.0, p=0.0035) and 13.8% (95% CI 4.7, 22.9, p=0.0033) with povorcitinib 45 mg vs. placebo and povorcitinib 75 mg vs. placebo, respectively.

## Key secondary endpoints

In study INCB 54707-301 at week 12, 15.8%, 20.6% and 24.3% of patients achieved HiSCR75 in placebo, povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg groups, respectively; 22.1%, 31.8% and 34.8% achieved Skin Pain NRS30; and 33.7%, 25.0% and 26.2% had a flare by week 12. In study INCB 54707-302, the corresponding percentages of patients were 13.3%, 25.5%, 28.4% achieving HiSCR75; 17.9%, 40.6% and 37.7% achieving Skin Pain NRS30; and 33.5%, 21.6%, 20.7% having a flare.

## Post-Anti-TNF population

Based on the pooled phase 3 data from the post-anti-TNF population, the estimates and 95% CI for the week 12 HiSCR50 effect vs. placebo were 17.7% (5.7, 29.7) and 14.0% (2.0, 26.0), for povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg doses vs. placebo, respectively. The corresponding results for the key secondary endpoints were 15.9% (7.7, 24.1) and 17.0% (8.6, 25.5) for HiSCR75 at week 12, 12.3 (0.4, 24.2) and 8.1 (-3.6, 19.9) for skin pain NRS30 at week 12, and -15.4% (-28.0, -2.8) and -18.9% (-31.4, -6.3) for flare by week 12.

## Long-term efficacy

Based on observed cases in the post-Anti-TNF population, the proportion of patients who achieved HiSCR50 or HiSCR75 throughout the extension period remained stable or slightly increased in both povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg groups. Among patients on povorcitinib who achieved HiSCR50 or HiSCR75 at week 12, 54.5% and 73.3% achieved maintenance of HiSCR50, and 61.1% and 73.7% maintenance of HiSCR75 at week 54 in the povorcitinib 45 mg and 75 mg groups, respectively. While the fluctuating disease course of HS complicates interpretation of long-term response patterns, the totality of efficacy data suggests sustained benefit with long-term povorcitinib treatment.

## 9.3.1 Uncertainties and limitations about favourable effects

Due to the small number of patients, it is not feasible to evaluate consistency of treatment effects across subgroups within pooled post-anti-TNF population. However, the treatment effect observed across subgroups in the overall ITT population is considered applicable to the post-TNF population with sufficient certainty. Clinical data in patients ≥65 years are currently limited. However, based on current knowledge, no reduced treatment effect of povorcitinib is anticipated in this population.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 9.4 Unfavourable effects

Data for safety analyses during the use of povorcitinib are available from 1840 exposed participants evaluated in 9 studies (INCB 54707-202, -203, -204, -205, -206, -207, -301, -302, and -312). In HS, the integrated safety dataset consists of 1850 participants who took povorcitinib, of whom 766 took povorcitinib 45 mg and 1188 took povorcitinib 75 mg without dose change. The safety data was pooled for 5 pools as described in the safety section. For the intended post-anti-TNF indication and dosages, the exposures are presented separately for Placebo controlled population (Pool 1b, total povoriciticib participants N=230, total exposure 51.45 PY) and All HS Post-Anti-TNF Population (Pool 2b, total povorcitinib N=317, 302.69 PY). The exposure data are also presented from all HS patients for both PC population (Pool 1, total povorcitinib N=821, 184.06 PY) and total HS population (Pool 2, total povorcitinib N=1422, 1415.65 PY) as well as for all povorcitinib population that includes also participants with PN and vitiligo (Pool 3, total povorcitinib participants N=1850, 1688.81 PY). In pool 2, 474 and 767 HS-patients have received povorcitinib 45mg and 75mg, respectively, for &gt; 6months; the corresponding figures for &gt; 1 year are 260 (45mg) and 680 (75mg). In the pivotal studies, the most common TEAE in participants who took povorcitinib was acne (Pool 1b: PBO: n=6, 6.1%, 45mg n=11, 9.3%, 75mg n=12, 10.7%; Pool 1: PBO n=18, 4.4%, 45mg n=35, 8.5%, 75mg n=54, 13.2%). The other frequently reported TEAEs were headache (Pool 1b: PBO: n=5, 5.1%, total povorcitinib n=16, 7.0%; Pool 1: PBO n=19, 4.7%, total povorcitinib n=59, 7.2%;), COVID-19 (Pool 1b: PBO: n=1, 1% total povorcitinib n=14, 6.1%; Pool 1: PBO n=11, 2.7%, total povorcitinib n=30, 3.7%), fatigue (Pool 1b: PBO: n=2, 2% total povorcitinib n=13, 5.7%; Pool 1: PBO n=7, 1.7%, total povorcitinib n=30, 3.7%), and upper respiratory infection (Pool 1b: PBO: n=2, 2% total povorcitinib n=10, 4.3%; Pool 1: PBO n=12, 3.0%, total povorcitinib n=43, 5.2%). In the Phase 3 HS PC Population (Pool 1), 5 participants (0.6%) in the povorcitinib total group and no participants in the placebo group had a herpes zoster event, with similar incidences for the povorcitinib 45-mg group (0.5%) and the povorcitinib 75-mg group (0.7%). In pool 1 (all HS, PC period) the TEAEs leading to study drug discontinuation were reported in 31 participants (3.8%) in the povorcitinib total group and 7 participants (1.7%) in the placebo group. The TEAEs that led to study drug discontinuation in more than 1 participant included acne (3 participants in the povorcitinib 75-mg group), ALT increased (2 participants in the povorcitinib 45mg group) and anaemia (2 participants in the povorcitinib 45-mg group). In All HS population including longer exposure times (pool 2) the TEAEs leading to study drug discontinuation were reported in 121 participants (8.55%) in the povorcitinib total group and 11 participants (2.4%) in the placebo group. TEAEs leading to study drug discontinuation in more than 2 participants who took povorcitinib included anemia (n = 17), acne (n = 7), ALT increased (n = 6) and hidradenitis (n = 6 each), pulmonary embolism, transaminases increased, and weight increased (n = 3 each). Few participants experienced severe (grade 3 or higher) TEAEs in the Phase 3 HS PC population (Pool 1, n=12, 3.0% total povorcitinib and n=24, 2.9% PBO). The only serious TEAEs reported for more than 1 participant in this population were blood creatine phosphokinase increased (Pool 1 PBO n=1, 0.2%, total povorcitinib n=5, 0.6% and hidradenitis in 3 participants, 0.6%: povorcitinib 45-mg group and 2, 0.5% in the 75-mg group. Only hidradenitis and pneumonia AEs were considered to be study-drug related. A total of 125 participants (8.8%) in the All HS Population including longer exposure (pool 2)

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

experienced severe (grade 3 or higher) TEAEs. The most frequent severe TEAE was hidradenitis (PBO n=1, 0.2%, total povorcitinib n=21, 1.5%).

In Pool 2, treatment-related serious infections were reported in 6 participants in the 75-mg without dose change group and 1 participant in the 15-mg group. The exposure-adjusted incidence rates of other embolic and thrombotic events (combined venous and arterial) were low in both the All HS Population (Pool 2; 0.6 per 100 PY) and the All povorcitinib Population (Pool 3; 0.7 per 100 PY) and were less than estimated background rates for patients with HS. The incidences of cardiovascular events (MACE) were low (≤ 0.2% for each of the pooled populations). A total of 2 participants who were on povorcitinib (0.1% of participants each in the povorcitinib total group for the All HS Population [Pool 2] and the All povorcitinib Population [Pool 3]) had a gastrointestinal perforation. In the All HS Population (Pool 2), the overall incidence of hypersensitivity reaction events was low and identical between povorcitinib and placebo (1.1% in both groups). In the analyses of the integrated safety dataset malignancies were observed in 9 participants (povorcitinib total: 7 participants, placebo: 2 participants). All AESIs of malignancy were considered by the investigator as not related or unlikely related to the study drug.

A total of 21 pregnancies have been reported across the povorcitinib clinical development program as of the data cutoff date. Complications included premature baby, a pregnancy resulted in the birth of a baby with 21 trisomy and talipes as well as spontaneous miscarriage.

Treatment-emergent effects were observed in several laboratory measurements; lower hemoglobin levels, neutrophil and platelet counts were observed more frequently among the povorcitinib participants. Additionally, there were more participants with elevated liver transaminases, creatinine, creatine phosphokinase and total cholesterol levels among the povorcitinib participants.

The applicant stated the following factors were considered when making decisions on whether a causal relationship to povorcitinib in HS is plausible: Frequency of the event, TEAE rates seen with povorcitinib (45 mg and 75 mg) versus placebo, Biological plausibility based on povorcitinib mechanism of action and known effects of JAK inhibitor class, population under study (including comorbidities and prior/concomitant therapy) and incidence of Grade 3 or higher TEAEs, serious TEAEs, or TEAEs leading to study drug discontinuation. The analyses resulted in the identification of the following ADRs that have been appropriately included in the SmPC 4.8: upper respiratory tract infections (very common), acne (very common), folliculitis (common), urinary tract infection (common), hyperlipidaemia (common), headache (common), blood creatine phosphokinase increased (common), herpes zoster (uncommon), neutropenia (uncommon), thrombocytopenia (uncommon), Alanine aminotransferase increased &gt;3×ULN ( uncommon) and Aspartate aminotransferase increased &gt;3×ULN (uncommon).

## 9.4.1 Uncertainties and limitations about unfavourable effects

The safety analysis reflects trial populations defined by stringent exclusion criteria, omitting patients with obesity-related comorbidities, metabolic syndrome, chronic or recurrent infections, immunocompromising conditions, and laboratory abnormalities. As a result, there is uncertainty regarding the incidence of certain events-such as venous thromboembolism, major adverse cardiovascular events, serious infections, and specific haematological or biochemical findingsparticularly in the broader HS population, which carries higher baseline cardiovascular and metabolic risks. On the other hand, certain underlying clinical features in HS population, such as inflammation associated anemia and increased risk for thromboembolic events may reduce the sensitivity in the safety analyses in clinical trial settings. In order to address those uncertainties, full alignment with the Art. 20 referral for JAK inhibitors outcome was implemented, including limitation of use in high-risk patient, cautious use in patients with VTE, through warnings in SmPC section 4.4 and dose reduction in SmPC section 4.2. Further, those safety concerns will be addressed post approval (via category 3 PASS, see RMP).

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

Although the overall size of the safety database is sufficient, the exposures for the intended indication population, i.e. HS Post-Anti-TNF PC Population (Pool 1b and Pool 2b) are somewhat restricted and lower than the ICH recommendation for over 6 months and over one-year exposures for safety analyses. This is nevertheless considered acceptable as there is more substantial exposure in all HS population with crossly similar clinical features. In addition, the long-term safety profile has not yet been fully established, as relevant extension studies are still ongoing and will be submitted for assessment post-approval, once available (see RMP).

Limited exposure of patients over 65 years is noted, but the available safety data did not indicate specific safety concerns in elderly participants. Nevertheless, considering the existing uncertainty and in line with the Art 20 referral outcome, the lowest dose is recommended to be used in the elderly in SmPC section 4.2.

Several TEAEs during PC period may be treatment related and povorcitinib dose dependent, some events of clinical interest and alterations in the laboratory measurements were also noted in the povorcitinib group more commonly than in the PBO participants. Notably, some of these have been identified as ADRs for other JAK inhibitors, but do not fulfill the ADR criteria for povorcitinib at present time. This judgement may change in the future as more safety data gathers, including from participants without the predisposing factors (e.g. obesity, smoking, inherent systemic inflammation) in the HS population.

A total of 21 pregnancies have been reported across the povorcitinib clinical development program as of the data cutoff date. The outcome of pregnancies varied and some complications were reported. Further, the JAK-STAT pathway is known to be involved in early embryonic development. In non-clinical studies, administration of povorcitinib to female rats resulted in adverse effects associated with reproductive performance and embryo-foetal development in pregnant animals, and postnatal exposure via lactation. Considering the non-clinical and clinical data, pregnancy and breast-feeding have been listed as a contraindication in the SmPC section 4.3.

## 9.6 Benefit-risk assessment and discussion

## 9.6.1 Importance of favourable and unfavourable effects

## ITT population

The efficacy of povorcitinib in the treatment of active moderate to severe HS is based on two identical pivotal phase 3 studies INCB 54707-301 and INCB 54707-302. Both studies met the primary endpoint HiSCR50 at 45 mg and 75 mg QD doses at the predefined statistical significance level. While the results of study INCB 54707-301 were borderline significant, the results of study INCB 54707-302 were statistically robust. The estimated treatment effect was similar with both povorcitinib doses, i.e. approximately 12% difference in response rate vs. placebo in the pooled phase 3 data, which could be considered modest, but clinically meaningful.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## Post-anti-TNF population

The target population for the indication applied for, i.e. patients with prior anti-TNF therapy (post-antiTNF population) represented 26.9% of the overall phase 3 population. The phase 3 studies were powered, and their type 1 error control was determined for the overall population, disregarding past anti-TNF use. Given the positive results from individual phase 3 studies, pooling phase 3 data in the post-anti-TNF population to estimate treatment effect more precisely is considered acceptable, although it is acknowledged that no formal type 1 error control was applied to the pooled analyses.

Both 45 mg and 75 mg doses demonstrated a clinically relevant treatment effect for the primary endpoint HiSCR50 at week 12 in the pooled post-anti-TNF population, which was of similar magnitude to that seen in the overall population or even slightly better due to lower placebo responses in the post-anti-TNF population. This was supported by the results for the key secondary endpoints, except for skin pain NRS30 that showed numerical improvements, but failed to demonstrate a statistically significant effect at nominal 95% confidence level. Altogether, the results demonstrate that the benefits of povorcitinib observed in the overall (ITT) population can be extrapolated to the post-anti-TNF population. It is notable, that in comparison to the overall phase 3 population, patients with prior TNFtherapy had more advanced HS, including higher lesion counts and baseline disease scores, and had received more often other biologic therapies, including prior anti-IL-17 therapy, therefore representing a clinically relevant patient population inherently more difficult to treat and with fewer available treatment options. The proposed indication, i.e. 3 rd line, is well in line with these advanced patients.

The overall safety profile of povorcitinib is consistent with the JAK-inhibitor class and remained broadly stable beyond the placebo-controlled (PC) period. The safety analyses of the intented indication (postanti-TNF HS subpopulation) showed comparable safety profile to the broader HS patient pools (ITT population). However, although the overall size of the safety database is sufficient, the exposures for the intended indication population, i.e. HS Post-Anti-TNF PC Population (Pool 1b and Pool 2b) were somewhat restricted and less than the ICH recommendation for over 6 months and over one-year exposures for safety analyses. This is considered acceptable as more comprehensive safety data are available from the all HS population. Additional risk minimisation measures consisting of educational materials for health care providers and for patients and a post-authorisation safety study (PASS) to further characterise the risks have been included in the RMP.

A review of potential systemic safety concerns with oral JAK inhibitors, including povorcitinib, was performed. The necessary changes in the SmPC regarding several JAK inhibitor class associated findings, including several laboratory measurements and guidance have been appropriately implemented.

Importantly, given the adverse effects on reproductive performance and embryo-fetal development observed in pregnant animals, as well as the complications reported in several pregnancies during the povorcitinib treatment, the applicant has amended the SmPC by adding pregnancy and breast-feeding as a contraindication in Section 4.3.

<div style=\"page-break-after: always\"></div>

## 9.6.2 Balance of benefits and risks

The efficacy of povorcitinib in the treatment of active moderate to severe HS in the post-anti-TNF patient population has been demonstrated. The safety profile is well characterised, and the risks are manageable through routine pharmacovigilance and risk minimisation activities.

Taking into account the demonstrated efficacy, the generally favourable safety profile, and the manageable nature of the identified risks, the CHMP considered that the benefits of povorcitinib outweigh its risks in the post anti-TNF HS patients population.

## 9.7 Benefit-risk conclusions

## 9.7.1 At Day 210 - CHMP conclusions

Considering all favourable and unfavourable effects described above, the CHMP considered that the benefit-risk balance of Povofortay for the treatment of active moderate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa (acne inversa) in adults who have responded inadequately to, or who are intolerant or contraindicated to an anti-TNF therapy is positive.
